div.head: TO THE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: TO THE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.
PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892.

GENTLICAEN,—As you are aware, P arliament is about to be dissolved. Sir Gilbert Greenall, B art., having, to the great regret of his friends in W arrington, felt it necessary, after 45 years of faithful service, not to come forward for re-election, I beg to offer myself a 3 a candidate for your suffrages, in response to the very flattering invitation which I received in November last from a very large and influential body of my fellow-townsmen, principally composed of workingmen. In the approaching contest there is only one great issue to be tried, namely, what is called " Home Rule for Ireland," Which appears to mean, practically, Re?eal of the Union. Whilst willing to extend to Ireland, so far as is possible, the same Local Government that England has recently acquired from the Unionist Government, I am strongly opposed to the setting up of a separate Parliament in Dublin, as, in addition to its being the beginning of the breaking up of the Empire, it would be a cruel injustice to the loyal and law-abiding inhabitants of Ulster and to the large number of loyalists in other parts of Ireland. The Gladstonlan leaders conc,al from the country even the outlines of their scheme, but ameasure at all resembling the rejected Home Rule Bill of 1886 would be an injury to Ireland, as well as to England and Scotland. If you do me the honour to return me as your representa- tive to the Imperial Parliament, it will be my aim to oppose Home Rule.sna to support that Policy which during the past six years has, by restoring law and order in Ireland, re-estab- lished individual lib erty and advanced ths social and material 'welfare of ill people to a degree far exceeding all expectation; that policy which has secured six years of peace throughout the 'Enapire, and in all quarters of the world where Great nritain has any possession or interest ; and has brought about such reduction in tanation and such beneficial legislation— especially in matters affecting the artizan class—as had been achieved by no previous Parliament. I a.k you to compare theaceoraplished facts of the present Government's term of , oMie, the uninterrupted peace, during their administration.' with the failures of,Mr. Gladstones Ministry from 1880 to J. 885, and the continued,wars and .heavy expenditure on war • brought about by the vaccillating policy of his Government. ' "
I am in favour of better provision being made for the hous- ing of the working classes; nearly all that has been done in this direction having been done by Conservative and Unionist Governments.

I shall most cordially support any practical scheme of National Insurance or Old Age Pensions, or any feasible scheme which may tend to prevent hardworking, respectable people being obliged to have recisurse to the workhouse in their declining years.

I am in favour of a further extension of Local Government by the formation of District Councils ; of the reform of the many anomalies which now exist in the laws concernimg Registration and the qualification of Voters, both Parliament_ ary aud Municipal ; of further reductions of Taxation, as the necessities of the Revenue will allow, on articles of food; of a better regulated system of Imperial and Local Taxation; and of all measures which will co name to the comfort and welfare of the community at large without distinction of class. 1 As a Wars ington man born and bred, and as haying all my life hid my home in 3 our Torn, I may claim to have some knowledge of your local requirements. I Should you elect me to represent you in the House of Commons my object will be to further the interests of War- rington ; to promote useful domestic legislation; and to sup- ports policy which aims at keeping the United Kingdom and the Empire undivided, and loyal to the existing Constitution. I am, ,
Your Obedient Servant, ROBBIIT MRPOINT.
Bt. Austin's, Warrington. June 24th, 1892.
Clertion Itibreso.

DORT of the government departments —Red Tapers. ST. GEORGE was a great entomologist. He even made the dragon fly. WHY Should oil countries be surrounded by wlter 7 Because they are i/lands. Tuk cash-girl of the store is a relative of the clerks. She is assister to them all. A DjurcquE family found their canary in a pet the °thee...lay. The pet was the cat. THE elements will get into the cars, somehow. In a steeper, now, it is snore reign all night. IT is said that the Yankee who was at the point of death whittled it off with his jack-knife and got

well. ONC,' a sailor visited a city, where he said they " copper-boomed the tops of their houses with sheet lead." "JAMES, just run and put this bag on the pea- cock's tail; it's coming on to rain, and the poor dear will get wet, and his beautiful tail will be entirely spoiled " CERTAIN monks in Spain have taken to marriage. This brings them under the head of Benedict:xi' monks. THE Philadelphia Call says: "Talk is cheap." Perhaps the Call forgets how much our Congress costs us daily. "CAN you tell me what a smile is?" asked a geptlernan of a little girl. "Yes, sir, it is the whisper of a laugh." THE reporter is the philanthropic friend of the wrong-doer. Whenever he finds such a one he does all he can to write him up.

A NOTED rifle shot recently hit over 50,000 glass balls in a 60,000 glass ball shoot. The ques- tion, " What's in an aim?" seems to be thus iully answered. "So long as Ireland was silent under her wrongs,. England was deaf to her cries," is a delft:lone tot by a leader-writer in one of the foremost Nationalist newspapers. "ALWAYS try to hit the nail upon the head, my boy," said an uncle to his nephew. But the nephew's little cousin whispered to him, " Doe't hit the nail on your finger, for it hurts awful."

A FRIGHTENED visitor at Troy, during the recent land slide, left by the next morning tram, declar- ing that you couldn't make him live iu a city where the hills were running after folks. PEOPLE talk about "Lord Wo{seley's expe- dition in the Soudan ; " but there does not seem to be any " expedition " in his intolerably slow movement. THE LEAST EVIL—An old bachelor was asked why his brother married so little a wife. " Why," said he, "he thought that of all evils he should choose the least." KEEN PENETRATION.—"You don't love me—l know you don't," said a young married lady to her husband. "I gije you credit, my dear, for a keen penetration," was his consoling reply. - - -

AN American writer says :—" A man with one idea always puts me in mind of an old goose trying to hatch out a paving-stone." An editor's simile of man's career is summed up in the lines :—"Man's a vapour full of woes, starts a paper, busts, and goes." MR. PIMPS (somewhat the worse for his convi- viality)—" This is always the way with me after taking the chair at our club—so says Mrs. Phipps. The excitement of my speesh does it; but Mrs. Phipps will have it that it is tha drink. She's a most incredulous woman, is Mrs. Phipps." "Den any man ever yet make anything by opposing a woman's will ? exclaimed a tormented husband. "Yes, I have made a good deal by that sort of thing," answered his brother Richard. "But, Dick," responded the other, "you're a lawyer, and the woman whose will you opposed was always dead." RETORT COURTEOr9.—A judge, joking a young lawyer, said: "If you and I were to be turned into a horse or an ass, which would you prefer to be ?" "The ass, to be sure," replied the lawyer. "I've heard of an ass being made a judge, but a horse—never." Aar old ldy was recently brought as a witness before a bench of magistrates, and when asked to take off her bonnet obstinately refused to do so, saying: "There's no law compelling a woman to take off her bonnet." "Oh," imprudently replied one of the magistrates, "you know the law, do you? Perhaps you would like to come up and sit here and teach us ? " "No, I thank you, sir," said the woman, tartly; "there are old women enough there now." MISINTERPRETED QUOTATIONS.—‘‘ Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown. "—A head would be very uncomfortable without one. "Oh, that this too, too solid flesh would melt, thaw," &c.—lt's very evident that when Hamlet made this remark .he hadn't spent a summer in Florida. "Always speak well of the dead."—Some people will make cores remarks. A BOY in the geography class of a New York school, on being asked which is the highest moun- tain in the Empire State, answered Sing Sing, "Sing Sing I" exclaimed the teacher. "Why do you think that is the highest mountain in the State?" "Because," replied the boy, "Ben Rop- per's father went up' a year ago, and haint got down yet." • A BEAR broke into the house of a Nevada miner the other night. He was away, and his wife thought he had come home inebriated. She did not wait to light a lamp, but began operations at once. When the bear finally got away it is said that he did not stop running till he had travelled eight miles into the heart of the mountains, and he was such a sight that the other bears would not associate with him.

TREY were two freshmen who had just emerged from the literary atmosphere of Russell Library Hall—" Very nice audience." " Yes, and so literary too.' "You are very fond of literature, I presume?" "Passionately so." "You like Shakespeare, then, I dare say? " "Ah I very much. Do you ?" " Extremely ; and I like Pope too." "So do I, very much indeed." "He's grand; and I'll tell you another good writer." "Who? " 4' Milton."

DALGLEISTI, minister of Peebles, in giving a statistical account of that parish for Sir John Siuclair's immense compilation, simply stated that tne place must have derived its name from the pebbles which are found there in great quantity. The more elaborate antiquary, George Chalmers, by a tolerable pun for a man of his stamp, remarks in his "Caledonia" that the worthy clergyman of Peebles, in seeking for the etymology of the word, is content to look no further than to the stones beneath his feet! TEXAS can claim the championship for the most precocious child. Tim Kennedy, jun., the infant son of an Austin gentleman, asks the most perplex- ing questions, although he is only a little over two years old. "At what o'clock, papa, was I born ?" asked this infant phenomenon. "About one o'clock in the afternoon, my son." " Why, pa, that's not possible. You are always down town at that hour of the day." The bewildered parent did not reply, but made up his mind to enter the boy at the University of Texas as soon as the session opens. Aff old Dutch farmer, just arrived at the dignity of justice of the peace, had his first marriage case. fie dished it up in this way. He first said to his man Veil, you vents to be marrit, do you?. Veil, you loves dis woman so goot as any woman you hale ever see?' "Yes," answered the man. Then to the woman Vell, do you love dis man so; better as no man you never see ?" Lady hesitated, and he repeated :—" Vell, veil, do you likes him so well as to be his wife ?" "Oh, certainly," she answered with a kind of titter. "Veil, dat is all any reasonable man can expect. So you are marrit ; I pronounce you man and vife." The man then asked the justice what was to pay," "Oh, nothing at all—nothing at all—you are wel- come to it if it will do you any goot." II A eraL, discussing an absent friend, named Amanda, exclaimed: "What a pretty girl Amanda Is." "Ali!" said a lady, "is she blonde or brun- ette ?" "Oh, she has her dap of both," answered the admiring Mend.

The first three days of next week will be the heaviest days for polling. In many places the .returning officers object TO Monday, as, following Sunday, it does not leave proper time for fitting up the polling booths and perfecting the general ar- rangements. Tuesday is, therefore, likely to be the crux of the election, for on that day probably 200 polls will be taken. The direction in which the elections go on the first day will undoubtedly have a great effect on the ultimate result.

The Marquis de Mores, who fought the fatal duel in Paris, is a man of some mark, and will eventually • be Luke of Vallambrosa. his wife was a Miss Medora von Boffman, of New York, the daughter of the millionaire banker. The Meaquis. lived for some years " roughing it" on a ranche in California. His wife, who hares his views, is a very pretty young woman, who recently killed her first bear. Ido not think Mores will get a very heavy sentence, but the duel will have been of value to French society, if its tragic result leads to the extinction of a dangerous institution—a sort of legalised murder.

A friend, writing irow Rome, tells me that he saw Pope Leo recently, and describes him as looking extremely well, but his holiness declared he pre- teired cold to hot weather. What a pretty story that is of the Marquis who, when the Pope was Nuncio at Paris, haA the brutality to show him a snuffbox with a miniature on the lid of Venus with " nothing on." The future Pontiff looked at i t and returned it with an inquiring smile, "Charm i ! Charminc, ! A portrait of the Marchioness your wife, doubtless ?"

The "party of culture" in Salisbury have com- mitted an outrage upon Mr. Gladstone more cow- ardly even than that done by the woman of Chester,. because of its premeditativeness. In the interest of the Tories a blasphemous cartoon has been issued entitled " The G.O.M.'S Last Journey," which de- picts Mr. Gladstone with 83 years in the palm of his left hand and the Emile Rule Bill in his right, ' being dragged down to hell by an impersonation of the devil. The cartoon has so shocked the elec- tors that it has been called in, and high prices are being offered for those remaining in circulation. The incident should wreck the Tory chances of success.

-- The Earl of Harewood had been hopelessly ill for months before his death. He was an unpretending country gentleman, with no love for London life or the smart set, but affectionately regarded by his neighbours in Wharfedale. tiarewood House, where he died, is one of the stateliest abodes.in Yorkshire. Boldly placed on rising ground on the south side of the wharf, it commands a superb view of the valley bounded by the Craven mountains, 20 miles away, while eastward the great vale of York:stretches out, with York Minster rising up from it in the distance. The famous garden and lake in front of the house are only two ut the beauties of a splendid domain of two thousand acres. The Earls of Harewood have an income of £40,000 a year from their Yorkshire e6tates, and as the late Earl lived in retirement, lib is supposed to have been rich Many titled families are placed in mourning by his death. His sisters are Lady Hillinglon, the Countess Wharneliffe, and Lady George Hamilton, and a daughter is Lady IVenlock.

Truth says :—" If the by-electimns are to be accepted as a test of the general election we shall have a majority of over 100. But it must not be forgotten that these by-elections were won by care- ful organisation and hard work. I never shout until lam out of the wood. I never believe in victories until they have been won. lam an old soldier at elections. Enthusiasm goes for nothing with me ; to enthusiasm I prefer good,honest, hard work. "Glorious " meetings do not carry elections. I never, indeed, knew of an election in which we did not appear likely, so far as meetings were con- cerned, to carry everything before us. We must not, therefore, relax our efforts, or fancy that the walls of the Tory Jericho are likely to fall because we shout enthusiastically. Our business is to look up the stay-at-home people, and to win them over to our side.''

Colonel A. G. Waucbupt, LB., who is opposing the G.O.M. in Midlothian, is a member of an old Midlothian family. Be lives at Liberton, a plain but not unbeautiful district a few miles out of Edinburgh. Colonel Wauchr,pe was adopted by the Unionists of Midlothian some three years ago. .Iccordingly he has had ample time to advocate the Unionist cause, and certainly he has not been idle. Colonel Wauchope is a very nice fellow per- sonally, and no doubt a capital soldier, but he is not in the least a statesman. He will get a terrible beating, and will probably take it well.

Parliament is at last aissoived, and the writs are in the hands of the returning officers. The closing scenes were witnessed by a fairly considerable number of members of Parliament, most of them being members who have no intentien or no hope of returning again in the new ParNament. They had come to take the last glimpse of stenes of which they have been fres for many years pest, but which —apart from the slight privileges of " old mem- bers "—they have henceforth no more right to enter than the ordinary citizen. It was easy to see that in some cases these farewell visits were not made without regret, and certainly there were, familiar fates seen for the last time in Westminster which will be much missed when Parliament reassembles. It is agreed on all hands that whatever ma v be the general upshot of the election it will make sad havoc with a large number of the best known and some of the:oldest members of the House.

Mr % William Abraham u rmination not lo seek re-elsetion will be received with general regret, not only by his colleagues in the lush party, l*tit by Libtani agents in Great Britain. He devoted'a con- siderable portion of his political career to ediriating the English electorate on the Home Rule question, and there is probably not a constituenty from Land's End to John o' Groat's that he ha a not visited for that purpose. In appearance 31r. Abraham is tall and dark, with la slight stoop. He is about forty-two years of age, and was held in '4igh esteem in the Irish party for his shrewdness and busineNs capacity.

The Queen paid a number of farewell visits to the cottages in the neighbourhood of Balmoral on the last day of her stay at the Castle, and expressed herself as being very sorry indeed to leave Deeside, as she is never so well as at Balmoral, and the brac— ing air of the district exactly suits her constitu- tion. The Queen, on the other hand, always gets jaded and generally out of sorts after a few weeks' residence at Osborne, as the Isle of Wight air is far too relaxing for Her Majesty,and Osborne is a fear- fully hot place in the summer. The Queen'srevi. dences in the Isle of Wight have been greatly cur- tailed of late years, and it is probable that the ap. 1 proaching residence of the Court atOsborne will not exceed five weeks.

Mr. Douglas Henty, who has left £50,000 to foreign missions and a Bible society, was head of the biggest brewery in West Sussex. He was cer- tainly a strong Churchman, but his inclinations , were those of a sportsman. He kept racehorses, and at one time cut a considerable figure on the turf, so that this disposal of a third part of his per- sonal estate has caused some talk about Chichester, where the major portion of the ninety public- houses he owned are situated. The Hentys are one of the wealthiest trading families in the South of England. They unite brewing and banking, like many of the great brewers, who first acquire the command of public-houses, and then educate their publicans to give them the use of their money. The Cobbolds and the Lacons in the eastern counties, , and a score of others, have done the same.

div.head: EXANINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1892.
div.p: THE EXANINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1892.
THE MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF WAVRINGTON SPELTER WORKERS.
INQUEST AND VERDICT.

On Tuesday afternoon, the adjourned inquest was held at W arrington Workhouse relative to the deaths of John Connor, 37 years of age, and William Henry Yates, aged 28, who were labourers at the spelter works of Nlessrs. Kenyon. at Bank Quay. Warring- ton. Mr. Jones, deputy-coroner, presided, and there were also present Mr. C. W. Shaw, chief government inspector of the district ; Mr. D. Tinnion (partner in the firm of Messrs. Kenyon), Mr. A. Browne, who represented the firm ; Councillor Dixon, and Drs. GI °mall, Adams, Braide, and Peacock. It will be remembed that the deceased had been working at the spelter works and were taken ill. They were immedi- ately attended by separate doctors,Connor by Dr. traide, and Yates by Dr. Adams, who had certified that Connor died from peritonitis, and Yates from acute jaundice. Both doctors at the time said that the certificates were consistent with the causes of death, but from circum- stances that came to their knowledge that both were taken ill, and that a third man was similarly affected, they came to the opinion that it might bea very different reason—metallic poisoning, arsenic poisoning or fumes from a furnace.—The inquest had been adjourned for the purpose of having the foreman of the works present, and to have the contents of the stomachs of.the deceased analysed, and the works visited during operations. Laurence Spencer, the foreman, was the first witness called, and, in answer to the coroner, said that in his opinion the work was not dangerous or injurious to health. No instructions that he was aware Qf were given to the workmen to prevent danger. He only told the men to damp the stuff they were working with, and that was because it would not work if it were ground dry. He did not give any instructions as to the wearing of cloths, though he ha:. seen the men put on cloths on their own account. Ha had no idea why they put on these cloths. The two men when they came to work did not look very healthy, and they complained of being weak through not having food as they had been out of work for a long time. That was the only complaint they made to him about anything. He was not aware that the material they worked with contained any arseni?.. In answer to Mr. Shaw, witness said he had cautioned men about handling the material, because if a man happened to have a cut on his hand it made it smart and gather a little. He could not say from that that it had any irritant poison in it. They had to hammer the material, and that might cause some dust to rise, but it would be very little. He had never felt any affect of the ; dust in his mouth, and he could not say that it had a tendency to make the mouth dry. By Mr. Browne : He had worked at these works for 19 years and he had never experienced any danger from the stuff. He had never been ill with it that he was aware of. It was a man's duty to keep the material damp, and then no dust would rise from it. By Jurymen : At the time the men were working part of the material used was the ordinary stuff, but part of it was a special stuff. He did not know that the special stuff came from Germany, or that it was stronger than that generally used. He did not know that any of the men had burned their necks and backs with it.

A juryman said he had been told that the stuff was a special kind from Germany, and that the men had many times gone home with their arms and necks and backs burned with it, it being so strong. Witness said he did not know anything of that. They did not damp the stuff with vitriol. Mr. Browne : We do not use any vitriol in the place. Witness added that they used water for damping and also the" bottoms "of ammonia liquor. He could not say how many men they had had employed at the works within a certain time. He did not think there were many men left after being two or three days at the job. The Deputy Coroner then read the analyses of Dr. Carter Bell as follows:—" The following is my report upon the stomachs, liver, gall, bladders, kidneys, spleen, &c., sent by Dr. Adams, and brought to me by Inspec- tor Cox of the Warrington police force ; also the report upon a sample of material with which the deceased men were in the habit of working with. This sample from the works contained chloride of zinc, sulphide of zinc, and arsenic in small quantity. The composition of this other sample led me to think that chloride of zinc was made at these works by dissolving zinc in impure hydrochloric acid, arseniuretted hydrogen being evolved, thus causing the death. On Monday, June 20, I went over to Warrington to in- spect the works, and to see the place in which the men worked, and, contrary to my expectations, I found that no acid was used for dissolving the zinc, I have an- alysed various portions of the body sent to me and I find that zinc is present together with traces of arsenic. This agrees with the materials with which the men were accustomed to work with, but my opinion is that death conkl not have resulted from the work in which the men were engaged. The only theory which I can put forward as the cause of death is that in the reduction of the oxide of zinc to metallic zinc considerable quantities of oxide Is 4 zinc vapour with minute quantities of arsenical vapoud escape into the works. These men being new to
Lble _to withst.nd these

vapours, It is generally supposed that zinc oxide is harmless but not so when mixed with arsenical vapours. From my inspection of the works, I should not have thought it possible that men could have died from simply shovelling up the chloride of zinc and grinding it in the mill. Dr. Adams said the report of Dr. Carter Bell had con- firmed his original suspicion that metallic poison had something to do with the deaths. He agreed with Dr. Bell in the East sentence of his report as to shovelling up the chloride of sine and grinding it in the mill. He could not see how the men had got the poisonous material into their stomachs, and he could not suggest anything to prevent a recurrence. A juryman asked if the material sent for analyses was the same as that the men were working amongst. Inspector Bowen said that the visit they paid to the works was unknown to any one. Dr. Braide said that after hearing the analyst's report, he was of opinion that the deaths must have been caused by the sine or the arsenic. He would point out, however, that one of the men had DO vomiting or diarrhoea at all,which were symptoms of irritant poison- ing,. Mr. Shaw than read a section of the Factory and' Workshops Act, MI, relating to precautions that might be required to be made at certain classes of works. The Coroner said that after the report of the analyst I and the agreement of the two doctors, the jurors would have no difficulty in comin,,, to a verdict that the men died from poisoning.They'.did not need to trouble to say how they got the poison, but leave it to the proper authorities to say what remedies should be taken to pre- vent a recurrence. After a short consultAtion in private, the jury re- turned a verdict that dtath was due, in the case of Yates, to obstructive jaundice, and in that of Connor to peritonitis,set up by poisonous matter whilst at work at Messrs. Kenyon's spelter works, but how the poison got into the system they were tunable to say. Tney sug— gested that her Ma2isty's Inspector of Factories should take such steps as might be necessary to make the work, snore safe in the future. Mr. fhsw said the recommendation of the jury would, be forwarded to the proper quarter.
LIKE A STEAM ENGINE.

Mr. Gladstone is a kind of a steam engine on two legs, with heart of fire and lungs of steel, pursuing his unhasting and unresting way at a pace which leaVes all other men far behind. His distinguish- hg characteristics as a man of business are : First, an instinct of order that is dominant. Secondly,an immense faculty for eliciting the best services which secretaries and adjuncts can render. Thirdly, a phenomenally retentive memory. Fourthly, an immense faculty for concentration, and for divert- ing his thoughts from any subject at will; and lastly,a great faculty for sleep. When in the country he generally retires to rest about 11 o'clock and re- appears at 7. Add to all this a constitution of steel, and a digestion that nothing seems to upset, and you have some explanation of the amount of work which Mr. Gladstone is able to get through in the course of a day.—Mr. W. T. Stead in the " Review of Reviews."
DR. HOUSTON'S REPLY TO THE REV. E. C. E. CARLETON.
Liberal Club, Warrington, June 28th, 1892.

_ Many of your readers will have seen a letter from the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton published in last Saturday's issue of the " Warrington Observer." Dr. Houston has sent a reply to the Reverend gentleman, copy of which I enclose, and I shall be glad if you can give the same in your next issue. Yours truly, ARTHUR BROWNE, Election Agent for Dr. Houston. To the Editor of the" ExaMiner."
ECOPr.] Patten Arms Hotel, Warrington, June 27, 1392.

Dear Sir, I have read with interest your letter to the Editor of the " Warrington Observer " publishedin the issue of the 25th inst. It is the first attempt I have seen at an- swering the facts and arguments I have brought for- ward.

I take the liberty of placing in your hands a complete copy of my letters on the important question of " The Apprehensions of Ulster," to adopt your own phrase. This will place you in possession of a somewhat more extensive array of facts than those to which in your letter you refer. You do me some unintentional injustice in supposing that I am ignorant of the fact that down to the time of O'Connell the leaders of the people in Ireland were chiefly Protestants and some of them Tories. I sin quite aware that such was the case and I should be very sorry to rob my co-religionists, or political opponents, of one atom of the credit they deserve for having in those dark times stood up manfully for the cause of the down-trodden people who differed from them in creed, and possibly in politics. Their memory is cherished to this day in the humblest cabin in Catholic Ireland, and cherished more dearly because they were Protestants, who championed the cause of the poor and lowly against the selfish oppo- sition of the dominant class and creed to which they I themselves belonged. It may be my denseness of intellect, but I really fail to see how the reason you give, if it be the right one, why the Roman Catholics elected Protestants instead of Roman Catholic representatives touches my argument. My contention, as we lawyers say is, that the Irish Catholics invariably elect as members of Parliament the men whom they believe will represent their views and promote their interests, quite irrespective of creed. That the number of Protestant members of Parliament elected by Roman Catholic constituencies is now less than it was in former times, as in my letters I have shown, results simply from the fact that the number of eligible Protestants who have adopted the principle of Home Rule, and are willing to come forward and offer themselves as candidates for Irish constituences is so small. You cannot expect a Catholic and Nationalist constituency to elect a Protes- tant who is opposed to their political principles. This would be too much. There are still, however, at least 12 Protestant representatives of Irish Catholic and Nationalist constituencies, and not merely 7orB, as soma people, as you remark, assert. The number will be larger in all probablity in the next Parliament. I observe that you state as a fact, and as one of the grounds for the distrust said to exist in the minds of Irish Protestants, that the Roman Catholics of Ireland as a body,have not been very careful to keep the pledges that they solemnly gave.at the time of the passing of the Emancipation Act, and in a postscript you explain that you thereby refer to a declaration in a pastoral address of the Roman Catholic Archbishops and Bishops of Ireland published in 1886, that the Catholics of Ireland disclaim, disavow, and solemnly abjure any intention to subvert the present church establishment for the purpose of substituting a Catholic establishment in its stead. May I ask in what respect the Roman Catholics as a body have violated this pledge? Have they displayed any intention of setting up a Catholic Established Church in the stead of the Protestant Church disestablished twenty three years ago ? And if so, when and how ? Further, in the same postscript yon refer to a subse- quent part of the pastoral in which they swear that they will not exercise any privilege to which they are, or may become entitled to disturb or weaken the Pro- testant Religion and the Protestant Government in Ire- land. Again, may I ask when and in what way the Catholics of Ireland as a body have exercised any privi- lege they then or once possessed to disturb or weaken the Protestant religion or the Protestant Government in Ireland? Finally, you refer in the postscript to the following declaration made by tha British Roman Catholics 6. British Roman Catholics are charged with entertaining a pretended right to the property of the Established Church of England. We consider such a charge to be wholly without foundation. We declare that we enter- tain no pretenston to such a claim. We disclaim any right, title, or pretension. with regard to the same." I agree with you that this statement is an interesting one, and though it has no reference to the matter immedi- ately in hand which concerns only the designs of Irish Roman Catholics, I should be glad to know whether you impute to the Boman Catholics of England as a buoy any designs upon the property of the Established Church. The other ground to which you attribute the distrust existing in the minds of Irish Protestants is the increas- ing activity of the Roman Catholic clergy in nolitical affairs. I doubt very much whether there is any in- crease, at all events any prominent increase, in their political activity, though circumstances recently com- pelled them to come forward rather more prominently than they had previously done. But you surprise me very much when you say that the feeling of distrust generated by these two causes is a distrust as to what the effect of the ascendency which Mr. Gladstone wishes to create will be. ram totally unaware that Mr. Glad- stone wishes to create any ascendency. He is the un- compromising enemy of ascendency, and the champion of political equality as you cannot but know. In conclusion I have only to add that I sincerely re- joice to find that you, have candour to acquit the Roman Catholics of Ireland as such, and their church, of the odious designs against their Protestant fellow countrymen which, were imputed to them and were put forward as the pretext for holding the recent most disloyal gather- ing styled "The Ulster Convention." In this you have admitted my entire case, and I have to thank you for helping me to enlighten the people of Warrington on the point. But if you are riglat in stating "that the appre- hensions of the men of the north have reference to a set of individuals who, whatever their religious professions may be, have really no religion whatever, and whose public conduct shows that they are not controlled by any sense of religious or even moral obligation, is it not rather disingenuous for the men of the north not to say so frankly, instead of pretending that it is of Roman Catholics and the Roman Catholic Church, they are afraid? Are you quite certain, however, that the per- sons you allude to, such men as Mr. Justin McCarthy, for instance, Mr. Win. O'Brien, and Mr. John Dillon, and Michael Davitt, are not devout Catholics and men of blameless Christian lives? I remain, Sir, Yours faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON. P.S.—I am only too sadly aware that some Roman Catholics attended the Convention. There were Roman Catholics who opposed Emancipation' and there were slaves who hugged their chains.—A.ll.
DR. HOUSTON AGAIN CORRECTS THE "OBSERVER."
Liberal Club,
Warrington, 27th June, 1881.

Sir, On Saturday last the 25th inst, there anpeared in .ie Wezrington Observer," a statement concerning Dr. Houston that was not correct. Dr. Houston has written a letter to the Editor denying such statement, I enclose you a copy of his letter, and shall be glad if you will insert same in your next issue.
Yours truly, ARTHUR BROWNE, Election Agent for Dr. Houston. To, the Editor of the Examiner. [copy.] To the Editor of the Warrington "Observer." Liberal Club, Warrington. June 27th, 1892.

Sir, In your impression of the 27th inst., your entertain- ing, but occasionally inaccurate, contributor " Argus," who appears to take a lively interest in my movements, states that, on the previous Sunday, I attended—as a matter of what he is pleased to call " business "—the Corpus Christi service at the Roman Catholic Chapel. No doubt " Argus" is anxious that the information he furnishes to your numerous readers should be strictly correct, and, therefore, in their interest and in his, •I wish to say that this statement among others made by him regarding me, is not in accordance with the truth Yours faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON.

div.head: MR. GLA.L*TONE AT CHESTER.
div.p: MR. GLA.L*TONE AT CHESTER.
INJURY TO BIS EYE.

Mr. Gladstone on his way from London to Hawarden on Saturday visited Chester in the afer- noon and addressed a great open-air meeting in the centre of the city. The Liberal leader drove in an open carriage irons the Railway Station to the Liberal Club through densely crowded streets, and was vociferously cheered_ In the course of the drive a woman threw a hard gingerbread biscuit at the occupants of the carriage. The missile struck Mr. Glad- stone in the face, inflicting a slight wound on the bridge of the nose, and slightly inured the corner of the left eye. Medical attendance was forthcoming at the club, and after making aapeech Mr. Gladstone (who suffered considerable pain) had the eye bandaged and drove home. In his address to the meeting he accused the Tories of having resorted to the weapons of intimidation' inven- tion, and religious bigotry. For the first time in history. the Prime Minister of this country was the first political fireband in the land. It was a Mournful thing that the greatest offender against law and order, so far as incite- ment was concerned, should be a man who was expected to set an example to all his countrymen, instead of being a tempter to lead them astray. It was said that the House of Lords would throw out a Home Rule Bill and scrbring about a second dissolution of Parliament, but he never had admitted and never would, that the resis- tence of the House of Lords to a particular measure was a reason for dsaling with the House of Lords itself. He contended, in reply to another " invention," that it would be unnecessary to dissolve Parliament af`er the passing of a Home Rule Bill. He admitted with regret that a large majority of the Presbyterian and Noncon- forming clergymen in Ireland, were opposed to meeting the just claims of that country, and charged them with having made cruel accusations against the Boman Catho- lic ploulation without advancing a rag of proof. By statistics Mr. Gladstone showed that Ulster was not, as claimed by Lord Salisbury, the wealthiest province in Ireland, and by the same method he demonstrated that there must be a large minority of Protestants in Ulster who assisted the Roman Catholics to return a Home Rule majority for that province. He expressed • a confident hope that the coming Parliament, having disposed of the Irish question once and for all, would be enabled to pass the other reforms in the Liberal programme, including, notably, the disestablishment of the Church in Wales and local option.

THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN. Author of'' Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," " Where the North Wind Blows," &e., dac.
CHAPTER LIII. A PRAYER MEETING.

There was an extraordinary excitement amongst the more earnest and sober-minded of the Breamish folk, or at least amongst so many of them as had felt the want of some religious influence in their matter-of-fact lives.

At a time when the Church was in a state of sleepy indifference about anything save tithes and endowments, when parsons spent their days for the most part either in eating and drinking or in sport; and when sacred edifices were allowed to fall into ruin for lack of care or of funds to keep them in decent order, the followers of John Wes- ley or of Whitfield had it all their own way in country places. They managed to arouse a perfect frenzy of en- thusiasm in towns and villages, where before all had been apathy, or coarse brutal recklessness. Men lived like brutes, with no hope of heaven or fear of hell. . .

So had it been in the village of Breamish, until a year previous to the time of which I write ; when a prophet had arisen in their midst—an evangelist, who, living a life of unselfish devotion to the cause he ardently longed to further, tramped long and weary miles around the country, to pour his rous- ing and awakening doctrines into the ears of eager listeners. . . .

No distance was too great, no privation too severe for him who had vowed to carry the gospel and glad tidings of peace into the dark places of the earth. If he were hooted and stoned and driven forth from a village, he would simply turn and bless it, and be ready to re-enter its precincts at a more convenient season. But in Breamisli and among the fisher folk he found a ready field for the reception of the good seed. The eager exellatie nature of the people made them rush with delight into any outward expres- sion of mental excitement. The form ,of religion was exactly suited to them, and they received the prophet of it with rapture. The name of this wandering preacher was Abra- ham Robinson. He had followed the humble occupation of a cobbler, in a quiet country village upoh the banks of the Coquet, until the time when he received his " call " and left home and wife to fend for themselves without hesitation, while he went about his Master's business. In person he was tall, thin and limp ; walking with a perpetual stoop. He gave the impression of a weak feathery creature, liable to be blown about by every wind of doctrine.

His features also were uncertain in outline, and on the whole he seemed but a feeble sort of vessel for prophetic fire to light upon and to fill. But when once set agoing, and filled with that same fire, the effect he produced was tremendous, and was indeed probably all the more powerful for the first impression of weakness. His thin form straightened itself, his hay-coloured wisps of hair were thrown back from a lofty forehead, and his light blue eyes flashed like steel, as he thun- dered out anathemas against evildoers. For though he had a reserve fund of gospel and of grace to heal the wounds first caused by the swords of wrath and bludgeons of damnation, the ointment was never brought forth until the wounds had bled freely. It was by fear that the people must be roused from their deadening stupor, by fear and by pain. Since only through their selfish terrors could he gait any hold upon their attention and interest, then it stood to reason that their selfish terrors must be used as a lever whereby to raise them to better things. In a whitewashed room belonging to the house of the widow Ogle, or Jenny Dodd, as she was still called—according to the custom of the place, which clung to maiden names, and declined to adopt married ones, save as affixes—the meetings of the new sect were held. _ _ _

Cuddy Widdrington was head of the assembly, acting as a sort of precentor and churchwarden combined; leading the singing in a harsh un- melodious voice with a strong nasal twang, usher- ing the congregation to their seats, and keeping order amongst the younger lads and lasses; those who had come mone for the sake of some poP- fun and excitement, than from any real ' after salvation.
iorne of the lasses present also looked askance

at her. The help and guidance she wanted was a man, they whispered amongst themselves, and they were sure that nothing short of a man would con- tent her. Cuddy Widdrington was riot a bad- looking fellow, and would undoubtedly make a good husband ; steady was he, and with plenty of gear forbye. It was too bad therefore that a widow woman should get over him, when there were lasses in the village that had no chance, for the lack of men. Upon one of the back seats sat Ailsie, Bill's widow, and her father together. This sort of thing was not in the old man's line at all, but his little lass had begged him to accompany her, and there was nothing that he would or could refuse her now. Ailsie was not converted yet, had not " exper- ienced religion,'! though sometimes she had strange fitful moods that led her to long for some of the wild emotions talked of at the meetings. She was very young and very much spoiled. Father and husband had both combined to gratify every whim and fancy of the pretty creature; and the result was that she fancied the world made for her, and that everything that went amiss in her life was cruel and unjust to her personelle. When Bill died she gave way to a passion of tears and of hysterical grief that exhausted her for the time being, but relieved her all the same of further suffering. The bitterness of silent sorrow • was a thing unknown to her shallow emotional nature. She loved her husband, but loved him only as a part of herself. Before long therefore the desire for amusement and admiration awoke again within her mind ; and she could not help being pleased when a silly compliment was paid to her, as when Jim Craster declared that she looked younger and prettier than of Behrue,trawncodhmeitieheee at all the lasses were jealous because comeliness. div.head: SOME WILD THINGS AND THEIR YOUNG.
div.p: SOME WILD THINGS AND THEIR YOUNG.

The smaller wild animals take very poor care of their young. When danger threatens, the parents think only of saving their own skins and leave the little ones to shift for themselves. Particularly is this the case with rabbits. The spring batches are now nicely grown; every covert and hedge bottom is alive with them. If you approach cautiously, you will see their little brown ears cocked up in the .grass twenty or thirty yards out in the meadow. The mother is there too; but before you get within , seventy yards she is off. She does not collect her " chilluns "or tell them to "scoot ;" if she does they pay no attention, and she takes no pains to make them. They just stop where they are; and if they get home in time, it is more luck than looking after. A quick dog or cat could easily cut them off, to mention no other enemies. Other small animals are no better as regards cutting and running at the approach of danger. Mice, rats, and stoats all do the same thing. My dog—a poodle, but a mighty hunter of everything that flies or runs from a bumble-bee to a red deer—loves to turn out their nests at this time of year. I know what to expect when I see him extra keen, digging away at a hole. The old one soon makes off by a bolt-hole and leaves her bairns to be destroyed. In a mouse such conduct is excusable, but a rat ought certainly to make a fight of it. When driven to bay an old rat will turn round and offer a most extraordinary resist- ance in defence of its own dear life; but tor the children, not a bit of it. Where is the maternal instinct? Now, a human mother or a dog or a cat-1 any domesticated animal,in short—will fight as one possessed,and utterly regardless of self,for her young Even a sheep grows bola, and many other tame creatures ; but wild ones seem more callous. The stoat, a truly ferocious and determined little beast on its own account, has no more courage than a mouse on behalf of its young. It will lead them out, show them life, and take immense pains to satisfy their prodigious appetites—at the neigh- bours' expense; but it will not face danger for them. I came across some young ones, about half grown, the other day. They were out raiding with their mother, who basely deserted them at my ap- proach. Feathered things seem far more devoted to their young than furred ones. The wiles of many birds to lure the marauder from the nest are familiar to everyone. What an agony they are in! Some of the smaller kinds will all but allow them- selves to be caught, and the larger ones will face tremendous odds and win by sheer desperate bury. The old hen is the best example—a wonderful mother though a terrible fool. "Pail Mall Gazette."

div.head: WHAT DOES A SPUR DO FOR A
div.p: WHAT DOES A SPUR DO FOR A
HORSE?

Your horse is weak and weary with a long day's journey. You have ridden him since early morning. Impatient to reach a shelter for the night, you drive the spur into his panting sides. He leaps forward, and for a time trots onward rapidly. What did the spur do for him! Did it give him strength ? If so why feed him ? If not, what made him go faster? Here is a short per sonal statement which a man makes. Try if you can see any likeness between the two cases. He says : " Up to August, 1885, 1 was always in strong, healthy man. At that time I began to fee/ tired, dull, and heavy, with a faint, dizzy sensation as if I hould tumbte down any minute. I could not imagine what was coming over me. There was a bad taste in my mouth, my breath was bad, and my mouth would often fill with an offensive slimy matter. My appetite was poor, and after eating I suffered great pain, and wind would roll all over me. I had much pain at VA stomach, and was sick every morning, and threw up a great deal of phlegm. I also had a pain like the thrust of a knife cutting me between the shoulders and low down in the back at the kidneys. When at work I got tired in five minutes,. and had to stand and rest.
1 she

"I kept on with my work, however, for some time I as best I could, for I hada wife and family depending I upon me. But it was a hard and tedious task, as even stooping made me cry out with pain. After a while I . grew so weak I could scarcely crawl about, and was compelled to give up my employment. When I ventured out of doors I felt so dhay that I had frequently to stop and rest fer fear of falling, and was so bad that people would think I was in drink, and I had often to call at a chemist's and get a draught to help me home. I tried herbs and other medicines, and was attended by ,a doctor, but I got no better. In this dead-and-alive way I fingered on until April,,lB9o, when my wife got an almanac from tke druggist, and I read of a case of a railway guard at Manchester, who h 1 been cured by a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup after the doctors had given him up. So I wrote to him, and he replied that it cured him and would do me good. Upon this I got a bottle, and after a few doses I felt better, and by keeping an using it I was soon all right and back at my work, and have been well ever since. When I feel any signs of stomach disorder a few doses set me directly. I feel very grateful for the great benefit I have received, and wish others who may be ill to know of it ; as, if I had known of Mother Seigei's Syrup at the outset I would have been saved over four years' suffer- ing. I have lived in Birkdale fifteen years, and if any one wits to I shall be glad to reply. (Signed) " Tinasiss SPECE,S, "Kitchen Range Setter, " 23, Stamford Road, Birkdale, Southport."

Now, where is the likeness between Mr. Sperrin's experience and our illustration about the horse ? It is this The horse gains no new strength from the appli- cation of the spur. Of course we all see that he cannot. But the pain arouses him and makes a draft on his re- served nervous power—with a corresponding degree of exhaustion to follow. This is arlwiys Nature's way. She gives nothing for nothing. All must be paid for Losk back at Mr. Sperrin's statement where he says : "I kept on at my work, for I had a wife and family depending en me." That was his- spur. It was work or worse with him, as it is with most of us. But he had to pay for labouring when he was unable, by having to give up work altogether, and what the end would have been had not Seigel's Syrup come to the rescue nobody ears say. Possibly, the saddest thing we can think of. Any way, this triumphant medicine saved him, and he can work now without a spur.
If the reader also has indigestion and dyspepsia, with its painful and alarming consequences and symptoms, or knows of another who has, he will be able to treat himself or advise his friend.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A SWEETHE AUT.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A SWEETHE AUT.

A young labourer, named Bentock. is in cust,4dy at Ashcombe, Weston-super-Mare, charged with attempting to murder his sweetheart, a girl named Kenton, whose throat he cut on Sunday with a razor. The parties had been engaged to be married at Whitsuntide, but the girl declined to carry out the contract, and Bentock attacked her out of rerenge. The girl is now lying in a prostrate condition in the local hospital.

div.head: REDUCTION OF STEEL WORKERS' WAGES.
div.p: REDUCTION OF STEEL WORKERS' WAGES.

From July Ist. the Monmouthshire and South Wales steel workers' wages will be reduced two per cent., in accordance with the recent audit results. Notice given to terminate the sliding scale expires on September Ist. The colliers met at Aberdare on Monday when it was stated that the ballot of all colliers over 16 years of age had resulted in favour of giving notice to terminate the sliding scale on July Ist.

div.p: possibi A longing I es.tai
Jenny Dodd, the widow woman, was seated in the place of honour one evening, with all her etjt bairns spread out alongside, like a small school ate its mistress.

-- ----- They were quiet well-behaved children, all of them, save only Young Mat, the eldest ; who still required his " licks " at frequent inteivals hi order to reduce him to the precise point of good behaviour that him pious but quick-tempered mother desired in him. _ _ .

Even now, when he ought to have been listening to the emphatic denunciations of sinners Abraham Robinson was pouring forth with such voluble and terrible rapidity, he was digging his small round fists to the bottom of his trouser pockets instead, fingering and counting over the marbles he had won from Neddy Tait at the last game, 'Chat game of which the pleasant glow of victory still warmed and comforted him, even under those terribly lurid pictures of death and the judgment day. He stealthily drew forth the largest and shiniest of his treasures, and nudged his little brother Tom, to draw'the latter's attention to it. It was his way of encouraging and consoling the younger and weaker vessel, whose eyes were growing very big and round from listening too intently to the sermon. But alas for Tom, he was not by this time capable of receiving comfort, even from marbles. He was a child with big eyes and a high narrow forehead, being evidently formed by nature for receiving with avidity any amount of Calvinistic doctrines. His greatest recreation and delight was found in lookine, at the woodcuts in an illustrated edition of the Pilgrim's Progress, and in imagining himself in the place of Christian and Faithful, and undergoing all their adventures and sorrows by turns. They were all real personages to Tom, the characters drawn by John Bunyan ; though Mat's more healthy animalism rejected the possibility of Giant Despair and the man with the muck rake being actual facts. He found it much easier to believe in the existence of the mermaids and sea serpents the sailors told him of. Therefore, while Mat shut his ears and counted his marbles— thinking philosophically that his mother had religion enough for the whole family, but that he wished it would serve to soften her temper a 'bit ; and -that for his part, if he must needs be converted some day, he hoped it would not be until after he had sounded the depths of temptation, and known the pleasures of wicked- ness, because there was no sense in renouncing things before one had tried them—poor little Toni with his more vivid imagination, pictured himself as being surrounded by a set of howling fiends with horns and tails all complete; fiends who were alternately toasting him before huge fires, and throwing him into cauldrons of boiling pitch, after the manner of all early conceptions of the tortures of hell. After the sermon came a prayer meeting, and every brother and sister present was called upon to address him or herself to confessing and en- treating Heaven for grace and salvation. A perfect Babel prevailed at times ; tongues resounding on all sides, and in all sorts of strange Hallelujahs and Amens, mixed with adjurations to the Almighty which, to unregenerate ears, might have seemed to savour of irreverence or even of profanity. _ _

- But this idea of anything irreverent would have been entirely erroneous. The people were intensely in earnest, and the phraseology they used siyas merely the kind they were aecustomed to, and the kind that came simply and naturally to them. Thus when Jack Scott asked what they had done to deserve worse dealings with them on the part of Providence than fell to the lot of "them lubberly Scotchmen," since the latter had had all tchonefleusesked at th at th he e h tehr er iangghh tfi t ag that "very s e ha sa or n n d , linesa d God should be kinder to forriners " than to his own folks, the honest fellow meant no irreverence whatever. Simply he spoke to a Heavenly as to an earthly father, and fully expected a satisfactory result from the prayer for material benefits with which he closed. The mother of six who followed him poured forfor guid amostnee fluenta nd ffor helpand tvoobring audpd rietses be r, children e n in the right path. A little less prayer and a little more porridge would be the right path, her eldest hope commented inwardly, all undlitifully, as he listened to her rapid utterances, remembering that his breakfast had been docked because he had tripped twice in moue _from B4elciel.
