Fli tiloses'lr `ey brought over some time ago one of Fc doctor kigners. (Laughter and applause.), He was a 115 tea e liimselt--(renewed laughter)—ar. Renton!. dli yoe _ lui speech and found that he made jokes. But too euld not answer a joke. (Laughter.) Then he ae necdotes—(laughter)—but you coeld not answer

anecdotes—and then he told stories, and all you could do with a story was to contradict it. There Was the whole speech of Dr. Rentoul disposed of In two or three words. Recently the Tories had brought over another great gentterriart, a -Mn Murray. Before he "(Dr. Houston) left Dublin they came to him and said he was going to be annihilated, for the Tories. in Warrington had got hold of a man who was going to knock him into a cocked bat. (Laughter.) He endeavoured to keep up his coarage, and, waited until Mr.Martay should make his appearance upott the stage, and in the meantime made inquiries abect him, and found that his history was a bit curious. He was another foreigaer. The Warrington Tories never appeared to be anie to get on without foreigners. By descent, he was an thishtnan' but he was born in Virgi- nia, and he thought a good deal in his political career might be accounted for by the fact that he was born in Verginia, because the happened to be the son of a mac who owned a grebt many slaves. (Laughter.) He wits I 'born in a place where people's notions of liberty wete ?these, that you should keep it all toyourselves, and cat , nobody else have- too much" of it, for kberty, as the I Americans used to put it, , was a thing that did not agree with negroes. Accordingly, when the question of 'emancipating the Irish people was raised, he acted in the sante spirit as i! he had been dealing with negro skives—and, according to a high authority Irishmen were little better than negroes ; :they were Hottentots. (Laughtec:) The question efeemancipating Ireland was too much for Mr. Murray, and accordingly all his Liberalism appeared to have ootrtei out, and be at -once •ranged himself in the ranks of Less who had always been opposed to liberty, the Tory party. (Applause.) If they had sent him an invitation to appear oatheplatform with Mc. Murray he could have enlightened thent. ;(Applause.) They might I have pelted him with political 'questions, end nothing would have given hint greater pleasure thra to answer them, 'bat that was not what the Tories wanted. That wouldllet a little daylight into the clarkneso in which the Tory party and Tory audiences were plunged. He might have answered the 'question as to what were the privileges the English people enjoyed that the Irish did .not enjoy, by meationing trial by jaw' as one which was ,enjoyed tly the English, bitt,; in c great many cases, not by the Irish. It argued a great deal of auldacity on Mr. Ilurray's part to ' puttsuch a question when lee .knew that the people of. Ireland were suffering from perpetual coercion. Refer- ring to the Ulster Convention Mr. Murray told them that ; Uleter had made up its mind not to ght. (Laughter.) They had been hearing for c. long time that the motto which would be displayed by Ulster when Home Rule wiz established was ''.Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right." Now that needed an amendment of one ward, and then the motto would-read" Ulster will not fight, anti Ulater will be right." (Laughter and applause.) They were adopting a new policy.. They said tney would not fight, but they would ignore the laws passed by art Irish Parliament. If Ulster dieobeyed the laws it must take the consequences. But the people who called them- selves Ulster were like 'the three tailors of Tooley-st. when they ventured to speak, in the name of the Critish Empire. The IRster: Convention was a bogus convention, net a Teal one; it was a convention got cp in this countay key'thetwire-pullers of the Tory party. .ord Salisbury,vvhen:he made his wicked:and treasonable' cpeech:was one of the wire-pullers and was engineeriag this bogus convention. Mr. Murray had asked why if the Home Rulers desireddreland to have control of their , own affairs they combined with the Nationalists taeorush the Irish Local Government Bill. Because it was a sham and an imposture, and was not intended to give absolute control of local affairs and because it was acoompanied by provisions that. were nothiag less than an insult to the Irish ' people. (Applause). -Criticising Mr. Murray's claim for the Tory party that it was the party of peace, Dr. Houston cited the Afghan 'war to the contrary, and asserted that there was no party that had conduced' to so many and such expensive wars as the Tory ,1 party. He concluded with an eloquent appeal to the electors to do their duty ore Tuesday next, and resumed• his seat amongst immense-cheering. A vote of thanks wataecookeled to the speakers, and this having been acknowledged by Captain Kirwan., the', proceedings concluded. '

div.head: TORY MEETING AT ST. MARY'S SCHOOL.
div.p: TORY MEETING AT ST. MARY'S SCHOOL.

A meeting in sapport of the candidature of Mr.' Robert Pierpoint, was ...held in St. Mary's Schools Bank Quay, on Monday evening. Mr. W. C arson presided, and there were also present on the plat- form Mr. R. Pierpoint, Aldermen Francanab, Sutton, and Wright,COaflCillOr4JaleS Fairclough,Cosmcillor Muir, the Rev. E. C. E.. Carleton, Mr. It. W. Murray, (of Belfast), Mr. John White, Mr. Greenall, ate.. Near the platform were Alderman Harrison, Coun- cillors Smethurst and Woisey, and Mr. W. Diggle.; Mrs Diggle, prior to the meeting, ascended the plat- form, and entertained the audience for a short, time with a characteristic exposition of his views , on various political matters. The building was crowded. The CH/dm/cm said it was now six years since their business managers were elected to carry on the concerns of the British Empire, and by the affluxion of time they were called together again to say whether in their opinion these business managers had faithfully performed the work they had been sent to do, and ought to be returned ' again to conduct the business of tnis mighty empire. (Applause.) He criticised the policy of the last Liberal Government and especially condemned Home Rule, as- serting that as Mr. Murray had said to him that day there was now really no Irish question so far as Ireland was concerned. He claimed that the present Govern- ment had been a pacific and economical one, and while admitting that trade was not.very brisk at present, said that a better time, a time of,more steady and continuous' work for the working-men of Warrington, they had never experienced, than under the present Government. (Applause.) Mr. PIRRPOINT, who was enthusiastically received, on , rising, read a leugthy letter from Mr. Frederick Monks espresaing his regret that he could not be present. He said he made no pretence of being a Conserva- tive in the generally understood sense. His sym- pathies were still Liberal, and he fully recognised that much progressive legislation had yet to be accom- plished by the union of the Liberal Unionists and the Conservatives, and he had decided to give Mr. Pierpoint his support at the forthcoming •election. (Applause.) Mr. Pierpoint said he noticed that Dr . Houston in his address, said that Warrington had been for seven years disfranchised. He referred to Sir Gilbert Greenall's de- clining years. That gentleman had served them unflinch- ingly and staunchly and well, and it was no fault of his, but an honour to him that he had stood by the party until be became a very old man. (Applause.) When he drove about with him on Saturday, it was de- lightful to see the way in which men and women re- ceived the old accustomed face of Sir Gilbert—(loud applause)—and at the same time he was pleased to think that his own was not altogether unwelcome. (Applause.) Let them assume for a moment that Warrington had lsrteri disfranchised, and they wanted to enfranchise it would they do so by electing a man who was born amongst them, whose home had been amonnst them, or a lentleman who never came to Warrington till per- haps four months ago. (" Let him go back.") As to ' the point in Dr. Houston's address "one man one vote," he found by a return made that the pluratists numbered 120.000. Taking off 45 per cent. for absentees, that left 73,000, and it half voted on one side and half on the other side ; or supposing the majority voted on the Conservative side there was not much to make a noise about. He did not find that Dr. Houston mentioned an important point which would go with the re-distribu- tion of seats. Mr. Pierpoint made a complaint as to dis- parity of Irish as compared with English and Scotch re- presentation, with the object of showing that the 103 members Ireland possessed was an unduly large propor- tion. He condemned payment of members, and as to shorter Parliaments said if the Unionist party came in again there would to a good deal said about it, but if the Gladstonian party came in nothing. He referred to his experience atthe Ulster Convention, and said Ulster men were absolutelydetermined not to bow the knee to , a Dublin Parliament. (Applause.) This country, he said, would not tolerate the use of its forces to compel them to do so. (Loud applause.) Mr. J. B. TAYLOR moved :—" That this meeting pledges itself to use all legitimate means to return Mr. Robert Pierpoint as member for Warrington at the approaching election by a triumphant majority." As he was doing so the back of the front seat, on which Alder- man Harrison, Councillor Voisey and others were seated, partly broke, causing its partial eallapse, but after some laughter, it was supported by a chair, and several who had risen resumed their seats.

Mr. J. TircaticroN seconded, and. Alderman SUTTON supported the motion. Mr. H. W. MUIMAY, of Belfast, who was received with loud cheers supported the resolution. He said he was a Liberal in politics, and he was sorry that he was not ad- dressing there that evening a multitude of Liberals. He knew they were called Dissentients, and there was no term of opprobrium which the followers of Mr.. Gladstone had not applied to them because they had the courage of their Convictions. However, in the face ot persectiti.n , which had proved in many places to be almost irresistible they were not ashamed to stand up and express their hon.' est convictions. (Applause.) Mr. Murray Proceeded to explain that up to 1886 he was as devoted a follower ' 1 of Mr. Gladstone as he ever had, but when the Home Rule Bill was produced he declined to follow him any further. He might have the most trusty guide in the world, and he might take him through the mountain passes of Switzerland, and he might trust him most im- plicitly ; but if that guide dragged him to the edge of a precipice, but it he advised him to cast himself down, telling him that the angels would bear him up lest be cast his foot against a stone, he should come to the conclusion that at least in that leap he declined to fcllow him. (Applause.) They had heard a great deal about Home Rule and Local Government for Ireland. An intelligent man in that audience who had taken the trouble to readthe speeches of the National party in Ireland and America, if not in England, could not help 'but come to the conclusion

that so-called Home Rule was a step towards the final disintegration of this great empire. If the advocates of Home Rule were honest in their desire to give Ireland the management of their own local affairs, why wisl it that Mr. etadstone's party and the National party tried to crush out the Bill which was intended to give the Irish absolute control of local affairs? If there was any justification for the granting at Home Rule to Ireland it would be upon the condition that the people were unanimous in demanding . it. (Hear., hear.) At the Ulster Conveasion there were from 110,000. to 202000 people gathered together, and because they con- ferred under the Most solemn circumstances, they were cendemned for being so moderate. Their opponents said they did not mean what they said. Ite supposed if they had broken so many heads:, like they did in Kil- kenny, then they would have thought Stey were in earnest. (Lauver and applause.) Moir had a large number of Catholics in &eland i.vho were Etterly opposed to Home Rule. They bad Roman Catholics speaking en the platferm at the great Ulster Convention. The Ulster people would not have Homellule. They did not pro- pose to take up arms. They would not consent to be under the power of an Irish Parliament. (Loud ap- plause.) ConacillerVorsav spoke in support otthe resolution. As a Roman Catholic he deprecated )the use of language on the Home "Rule question catealated to stir up hostrlity cm animosity between tAte Protestants and and Cathelics. Ee said there were people who said 1 majorities must rule. He took exception to that state- ment. It was proper Stet maietities did rule where they ruled with unanimous consent, but in the case of Ireland,where there was a large settion opposed to Home 1 Rale, it was not right to introduce it, and thus increase •slissention. ikle considered that Home Rule woisld practically /mean •,separation from this country. He remarked that if Dr. Rouston 'could get into Parliament on the backs of the Warringtonrpeople.his first consider- ation would he to serve his own people. The motion was dedlared carried unanimously, though 41 voice exclaimed Houston' but was immediately silenced by shouts of'" put•him out," &d.—On a motion by Mr. JOHN WHITS a vote of thanks, supported by I&. ciretwr,,wasaccerded to tee Chairman, and his reply 'closed the proceedings. MEETING' IN TEE CC-OPERATIVE HALL. •

An entansiasticeneeting kr support of the candidature .61 Mr. Robert. 'Pierpoint ,waz held in the Co-operative Wiawick-street, en'Wednesday night. During the 030 urse of his speech, Mr. Pierpoint said that,while wish- ing to apeakcourteously of his opponent, he would like to refer to Dr. Houston's remarks on his address. That gentleman had been good enough in his critisista to say that kit lad a beginning and an end, but no middle. (Laughter.) Dr, Houston appealed apparently to pro- mises, but, he Mr. Pierpoint, appealed to facts. (Cheers. When one wished to employ a man or two men who presented themselves, they naturally asked" what have you got in your podket in the way of good char-. attar and credential r Take Mr. Gladstone. e had .in his pocket the record of the most disastrous five years the nation had had for half a century. (Cheers.) The records and credentials were so poor and bansiiiating that they could not ..be reprodueod, and Dr. Houston ,warrbound simply to appear before the electorate with credentials for the future. (Cheers.) Dimino. Mr. .Gladstone's administration there had been war aft:r wax and an ignominious expenditure of 19 millions. Lord faliaburthad spent absolutely nothing on war. The eleetoratelad received many benefits from the Unionist tGovernment, and they might trust them to enact many .morain the future. Mr Pierpoint also referred to the drirti question, and when he concluded was loudly ,cheered.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1892
NEWTON DIVISION.
LIBERAL MEETINGS.
COLLINS GREEN.

• An open air meeting was addressed by the Liberal acandidate for the Newton Division, at Collins• ,Green, on Monday evening. There was .a good . attendance. Mr. WAioughton presided, and after referring to current topics, that gentleman called upon Mr. Neill to address the meeting. Mr. Neill who was received with applause, said the great principle underlying Liberalism was perfect liberty and perfect equality. That was why the Radicals gave the workingman the vote. They held that one man was as good as another, and consequently was entitled to as much respect as the richest landlord or the richest plutocrat in the country. Mr. Legh was what they might call a good and consistent Tory. He ,wished that • things should remain where they were. :Dealing with free education, Mr. Legh claimed that it was a Tory measure. He would remind them that every Tory in the country was averse to free education before the present Parliament assembled. Take the County Councils, which the Tories talked so much .about. Every,Tory was pledged against Local Govern- ment. The Tories found, however, that they must , either pass soma Liberal measure that Liberals were in 'favour of, or they must go out of office. Mr. Goschen passed Free Education in the teeth of Tory wishes and their opposition. Dealing with Home Rule, the speaker said that there was not an atom of evidence to show that Catholics had bad intentions against Protestants. He believed that if Home Rule was passed, Ireland would be more prosper- ous and contented. (Cheers.) Mr. Gilmour moved,and Mrs. Rawlins seconded, the following resolution, " That this meeting believes Mr. Neill is a fit and proper person to,represent the Newton Division in the House of Corn- mons, and that we will use every legitimate means to return him at the head of the poll on the day of elec- tion:" (Cheers 4 The resolution was carried unani- mously.

tdr. Neill the proceeded to Buttonwood and addressed an oatdoor meeting, over which, Mr. Rawlins presided. A airailar resolution to that mentioned above was moved by Mr. Gavan, And adopted, and addresses were de- livered by the candidate, Mr. Taylor and Mr. Wilber- force. _ _

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

On Saturday evening a meeting for the purpose of furthering the candidature of Mr. W. Neill, for the New- ton Division, in the Liberal interest, was held in the Golbortte Liberal <Hub, at which there was a crowded attendance. Mr. -G. W. Rawlins presided, supported by the Rev. W. Graham,- Messrs. W. Neill (candidate for the division), Goele,(London), Burns (Oldham), W. P. Billington, W. H. Mitchell, W. Glover, Sandham, Roberts, Bates, Twist, Entwistle, Openshaw, Winward, R. Spencer, &c. After a few remarks from the chair- man, Mr. W. r. Billington moved, and Mr. Twist

seconded the resolution pledging the meeting te use every legitimate means to return Mr. Neill a member fer the division at the next , election. —Mr. Burns, of Oldham, Supported the motion in an ap- propriate and interesting speech, in which he ieferred to the various political topics of the present day. The motion, on being put to the meeting, was carried un- anitnously.—The Rev. 1:37, Graham then moved a resolu- tion which expressed coafidence in Mr. 'Gladstone and hi a colleagues, and hoped the time was not far distant when Ireland would be granted Home Rule. (Applause.) —Mr. Neill, on rising to second the resolution, received a very hearty welcome. He did not think it was neces- sary that he should say anything tnore about Ireland after what they had heard from Mreßurns, but he might say that, if he had been one of those in doubt in regard to Home Rate, his doubt would have been removed after reading the speech which bad recently been made ley Mr. Gladstone. they sant Mr. ladstone back to Par- liament with a majority, one of the greatest labours of his life would be settled, and then they would have time to get on withtheir owe affairs and carry out those re- forms which had been se long delayed. There was the Employers' Liability Act, which the Queen had men- tioned in her speeches in 1888-BE-90, and the Land Trans- fier Act, which were subjects of importance. He had had much difficulty in finding anything Mr. Legit was in favour of, for he was not in favour of any Eight flours Biel for miners, and that was a Bill that was much needed. But he had found that Mr. Legh in his address on the previous euening, in that district, was in favour of one thing, and that was something new, vie.—the ,endowment Of public-houses ; and there he might say Mr. Legh and he were at a different issue, for he opposed it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They must eetnembertbat a license was only granted for a year, and then the magistratewcould please themselves whether they renewed it or not,'aed why compensation should he given he was at a loss to e.ay. (Hear, hear.), , The Employers'. Liability Act was a question of con- siderableimpertance to the working-men of every con- dition, and he found that the majority of the voters in that division were working-men, and he was -of opinion that in case of accident, whether it was caused by a• fellow workman or not, the injured man ought to be allowed compensation. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of the 'Coal Mines Regulation Act, for which the Tories claimed so much credit, he could tell them that it was almost word for word with the Bill that was brought forward by two 'Liberals the year before. Were the Tories the friends of the miners? (Several Voices: .4 No.") He was in favour of an Eight Hours Bill for miners. (Hear. hear, and applause.) His reason was becaese it was an unhealthy and dangerous occupation, and to week longer hours exaggerated those dangers. He could net understandeeiners not being in favour of this mea- sure, especially if they understood it, but he thought the reason was that if the measure was brought about the wages would be reduced, and the men would be worse off. He, however, did not believe that for one minute—(applause)—for in the shortening of hours wages had 'risen. When they reduced the hours of labour for factory operatives the employers said that they would be ruined and upset, but since they cvere reduced wages had increased— (hear, hear, and applause) —and he would ask the miners not to be deceived by -such-statements as those. The Eight Hours Bill was a thing which was pashed forward by the officials of the miners, who had the interests of those men at heart, and-if the miners were to follow the example of their lenders he-thought this measure would soon become law. They knew' that many Tories said that the laght Hours Bill-should be brought shout by organisation, but he would say to them, Get well organised, and then send a roan to Parliament who will represent your views and do his best for you." (Cheers.) They knew that it was not always possible to get this representation, tut there were nine members in Parliament, men who represented the working class, who were about the most ltardwork- iag meniirrthe House. He was in sympathy with the aims and wishes of labour' and if elected he would vote for the Eight Hours Bill for the miners, and if they wanted tuget this, they must send back the man who would most nearly represent them in Parliament. He had come to that division to fight their battle, and it was to them ofenormous importance, as he had placed him- self to win that seat. He was simply like a general in the army, and they were like the rank and file, and it was for them—and they could If 'they liked—to carry the forthcoming election, arid by what he had seen through- out the division he was satisfied. (A Voice : "The colliers will do it."—Hear, hear, and loud applause.) The colliers had their work at heart, and if they would poll out and out and follow the example of their leaders, that seat would be certain. Let every Liberal pie his utmost, and he was satisfied that they would win. ,(Loud anplause.) Mr. Gomm, of London. then addressed the meeting. The motiou, on being put to the meeting, was carried unanimously. Mr. R. YATES moved, and Mr. OPIDISRAW secanded, a vote of thanks to the speakers, to which Mr. Goole suitably responded. Mr. Mutt then proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Rawlins for presiding, and in doing so said Mr. Rawlins had done a great deal for the Liberal party in the New- ton Division. He had been working almost night and day for the cease for weeks, and it was his intention to if possible win the seat. (Applause.) The Rev. W. Gnanem briefly seconded the motion, . which was carried. .

Mr. ittwutss, in reply, said he had done all he could fur the last sis.years for the Liberal cause, and now that it was the eleventh hour he would not leave it. toth the motions on being pat to the ,meeting were carried with acclamation, and the proceedings, which had been of a most enthusiastic character, terminated. During the evening a letter was read by the Chairman f rom Mr. B. W.. Molloy, M.P., who was announced to speak, regretting his inability to attend, owing to in- dispesition.

TORY MEETINGS, &c, _— MR. T. W. LEUR'S ADDRESS. In the address he issued to the electors, Mr. T. W. Leh., the Conservative candidate for the Newton divi- sion, declares himself a firm supporter of the party which, under the guidance of Lord Salisbury, had for nearly fiig years administered the affairs of the Empire with conspicuous success. The predictions that the alliance between the Conservatives and the Liberal Unionists womd nit stand the test of time have, he says, been falsified, and the country had seen that the policy of maintaining the union was compatible with steady and continuous progress in every department of public affairs. Fie claims on behalf of the Unionist Administration a renewal of the confidence of the elec- torate, on the ground that peace has been uniformly preserved,that the strength of the navy has been largely increased, that public expenditure has been economised

aud the burden of imperial and local taxation had been lightened, that popular representative government has been extended to England and Scotland, that the inter- ests of the working classes have been promoted, that school fees !Jai been abolished, aad an Act has been passed which will facditate the acquisition of small holdings of land upom reasonable ternis. Mr. Legh attributes the improvement ad prosperity of Ireland to a resolute and straightforward policy which has steadily, upheld the authority of the law ":, and he points to the attitude of the Irish 'Royal commission,tho division in the Nationalist ranks, and the apparent inability of Mr. Gladstone to produce a scheme satisfactory to the various sections of the party as showing the folly and danger of any attempt to set up a separate Parliament in Dublin. Anxious that the hours of labour should be reduced, he believes this can be accomplished by nrutual arrangement between employers and employed. And he argues that a legal limitation of the hours of adult male labour would deprive men of the right of disposing of their labour to the best advantage, and that it would censtitute an interference with the liberty of the subject.

div.head: AT VVINVVI(7K.
div.p: AT VVINVVI(7K.

A Conservative meeting iti-a7iPport of the candi- dature of Mr. T. W. Legh for the Newton Division was held in Winwick School on Saturday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. Swinton, and there was a good attendance.

The &v. if. Carson said they were all glad 'to we Mr. Legh in Winwick. He (the speaker) had been in Ireland, and was an Irishman, and he could safely say that if the 'lrish people had their own way they would not vote for Home Rule. He thought that it would be imposing a tyranny on the Irish people if they returned Mr. Glad- stone to power at the coming general election. (Applause.) Mr. Legh, who was received with applause, Raid that he would ask them to vote for him simply because he was in favour of the present Government. He always regarded Winwick ars one of those favoured spots where Liberals had no chance. Winwick was famous for its strong attachment to Conservative principles. He thought that the inhabitants of Winwick only showed their good sense. (Applause.) The present Government as far as he could see, had not given any reason why it should be changed, Why could not their opponents get a local man'? He failed to see what Mr. Weill had to do with that' part of the world. He did not wish to say anything against his opponent personally, but he thought that at the present time they had 'quite enough lawyers in Parliament. There were 150 in I the Hcuse of Commons already, and why should they return Mr. Neill? He received Mr. Neill's address a short time previous to coming to the meeting, and found, as he expected, that it was full of promises. The great difficulty was to find anything that a Gladstonian can- didate was not prepared and anxious to support. One thing that Mr. Neill was, according to his address, pre- pared to vote for was the Disestablishment of the Wplsh Church. He thought that it was a cowardly action on the part of his opponent to support such a Bill. In his early years Mr. Gladstone was one of the Church's champions, but when he found that votes could be obtained by the Disestablishment of the Church, then he consented to support such a measure. He (the speaker) thought it a very humiliating position to take up. Mr. Neill was anxious to reform the House of Lords. Plenty of Con- servatives were willing that a reform should be made there. Their opponents would like to make the House disreputable, and opposed any reform brought forward by the Conservatives. No country could get on without two chambers. His opponent was in•faveur of payment of members. Well,of all the reforins that had ever been brought forward, he thought that the payment of mem- bers was the last which the British public would take up. Was there anything business-like in increasing the national expenditure by paying members ? Mr. Neill was anxious for a reform in the Land Laws. He' went about saying that the Tories were against reforming the Land Laws. They (the Tories) would see to this, if they were allowed time. In order to see to see to these things they wanted to be returned to office again. With regard to the liquor traffic, the Liberals prided them- selves upon the fact that this question was their own. His opponent wished to have popular control over the liquor trade. But upon this question there was not so much . difference between his and Mr. Neill's opinion. With regard to the abolition of public-houses, he certainly thought that this was too sweeping a promise to commend itself to sensible persons. He thought that if puislica,ns were turned out then they were entitled to equitable compensation. Mr. Neill had a great deal to say about the hours of labour. He (the speaker) had no doubt that if the labourers were organized largely enough to affect the election, then Mr. Neill would pledge himself to support an el,g'at hours' day for labourers. They could not fix a hard and fast line far such a measure, but the Conservatives were as interested as their opponents to secure sh3rter hours. He felt that he must say a few words about Home Rule. Mr. Neill said that after being six years in power the Tories had failed to pass any feasible measure for Local Government to Ireland. (Laughter.) It was only a few days ago that the second reading of the Irish Local Government Bill was passed and the Bill would have been carried had it not been for the dissolution. Some people might have very extravagant ideas about Ireland. At one time he had an Idea himself that the Irish people were being put upon, but after paving a visit there all such ideas were banished from his mind. In Ireland at the present moment there were only four people in prison under the Coercion Act. Home Rule was one of the most successful frauds that had ever been brought forward. The Home Rule policy was always one of cowardice, and most ungenerous. The feeling of the people in Ireland was that they wanted, to remain loyal British citizens, and they would not submit to a Parliament sitting in Dublin. When they recorded their votes he hoped that they would bear the Irish question in mind. The Conservative Govern- ment had maintained peace with foreign countries. It was their duty to vote for the Conservative party, and if they failed to do their best they would be wanting in their duty as loyal and patriotic citizens. (Cheers.) The following resolution was unanimously passed "That the administration of Lord Salisbury is worthy of the utmost support, in view of the valuable legisla- tion passed during his period of office, and we pledge ourselves to support Mr. T. W. Legh as a supporter of such primciples." (Cheers.) A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman for pre- siding, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: AT ASEITON.
div.p: AT ASEITON.

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Legb was held in the Natioual Schools, Ashton-in-Makerfield, on Tuesday evening. Mr. W. Valiant presided, and there was a good attendince. Those on the platform included Rev. 11. Siddall, Mr. T. W. Leg,h, Mr. C. F. ClArke, Mr. T. Crompton, M4jor Reif, Mr. M. Rowe, and Mr. R. Murray, of Belfast.—Mr. Clarke moved a resolu-

tion pledging the 'meeting to use every endeavour to secure the return of Mr. Legit to Parliament. Mr. Crompton seconded, Mr. Murray, in supporting the resolution, referred to the work done by the Unionist Government; remarking that no Government of recent years had done so much good for the country as the Government of Lord Salisbury.—The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. Laght next addressed the meeting, and met with a very cordial reception. In the course of his iemarks he tonched upon the proposed Eight Hours Bill,stating that he thought if they had eight hours a day from bank to bank tire miner would have to work harder than he did now. The question, in his opinion,required careful con- sideration. His opponent, who had dealt with the matter in his speeches, had said that those men who had to work long distances underground would have an opportunity of making up hist time. He failed to see how that could be done. If they could prove to him that it v7aB to their interests that this bill should pass he would tote for it, but at the present time he failed to see any satisfactory reason for adopting such a course. He thought that lithe men were unanimous in desiring to obtain a measure of this kind, they could obtain it by their own exertions, and there was no necessity for them to go to Parliament. (Applause.) Touching upon the subject of royalties,Mr. Legh said if they could be shown to be uufair he would not oppose any proposal for an alteration. (Hear hear.) There was a commission on royalties now sitting, and no doubt their recommenda- tions would be acted upon by the Unionist Government, if that government was in office. But they certainly could not expect the question to be dealt with by a Gladstonian Government ; they had got to pass a Home 'Rule Bill. (Applause.) The meeting terminated with the usual votes of thanks.

div.head: AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AT WARRINGTON.

...... On Wednesday evening a meeting of the electors of the Warrington polling district, Newton division, was held in the Conservative Club,in support of the candida- ture of Mr. T. W. Legit. Mr. Joseph Davies presided, and was supported by Mr. T. W. Legh, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Aldermen Francomb and Sutton, Mr. John White, and the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. The CHAIRMAN in his address said the Conservative Government had carried on the work of this country admirably, and expressed a hope that the Conservative majority of 707 obtained last election in Warrington would be increased next week. Dr. Houston, he said, promised all sorts of things, but would do nothing. —The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON proposed "That this meeting of Conservatives and Unionists of the Warrington polling district pledges itself to support the candidature of Mr. T. W. Leigh at the ensuing election for the Newton Division. He (Mr. Carleton) had been sufficiently long in Warring- ton to know that the name of Legh was a part of the history of that district and identified with its progress, and that Warrington people had strong attachments to old families, and those who had been specially connected with their locality.—Mr. AILTHIJR BENNETT, seconded the proposition. He said the record of the Gladstonian Government was a record of disgrace, disaster, war, and extravagance, and bad trade. Lord Salisbury had not expended a penny upon war. The Conservatives made no boast of the refornas they were going to pass, but carried them out without promising what they could not fulfil. The country would be guilty of suicidal policy if it handed over again to Mr. Gladstone the power he had so wilfully abused, and as the Home Rule Bill blocked the way until Mr. Gladstone carried it out not one step could be taken in the field of other legislation.—Mr. R., Davies said, looking at thm fact that Warrington had one Irish gentleman and Newton division another (Mr. Neill) seeking their suffrages, he began to fear that his children would not use the term Great Britain and Ireland but the expression Ireland and Great Britain. ' (Laughter.) He asked if the cluntry was going to con- fer Home Rule upon Ireland with at least one-third of the country utterly opposed to it—(cries of "No ") —and urged upon the electors to oppose such a policy.—Mr. Legh then delivered his address. He said in 1880 there was a definite reason for returning Mr. Gladstone, as dozing Lord Beaconsfield's admin- istration the foreign policy of the country had excited an immense amount of opposition amongst a large section of the electors of which they had every right to show their disapproval at the polls. He did not say they were right in their view, but, at any rate, there was a definite issue before the country. Then came the five years of Gladstonian administration, and he did not think many honest poli- ticians of Warrington would claim that this had been of much benefit to the people. At any rate, he thought the subsequent six years of Conservative administra- tion would compare favourably with it. The more Home Rule was examined the more hollow it proved to be. As long as there was unity in the Irish party there was some justification in saying that Irishmen knew what they wanted and were united in their demands, but the whole situation was changed. There were at least two Irish parties, and probably a great many more. The Liberals offered a more attractive programme than the Conservatives, but what was the use of that if there was an insuperable obstacle to prevent it being carried , out P—The CHAIRMAN put the resolution, which was un- animously carried, with much cheering.— A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, on the motion of Alderman FaaNcoatn, seconded by Mr. LEGU.

div.p: DATE OF POLLING.
We are informed that the polling for the election in this division has been fixed for Monday, July 11th. The nomination will probably take place on Tuesday next, July sth.
DEATH OF SERGEANT-INSTRUCTOR McCOY.

After an illness extending over six months, Sergeant-Instructor Michael McCoy, of Mercer-st., Newton, died at his residence, on Saturday, at the age of 59 years. Be has been in failing health for about 12 months, and during that time had been attended by Dr. H. Watkins, but his long service in India when a young man had told upon his chnstitution, and he gradually grew worse until he died as stated. He leaves a widow and large family. Sergeant McCoy was for 18 years instructor to the Gr (Newton) Company of the Ist V.8.5.L.R., which at one time was known as the 49th L.h.V., and while he held that position he was much respected and esteemed by the volunteers under his charge, and in fact, by all the residents of Newton by whom he was known. He came to Newton in 1874, from Warrington, where, for twelve months he also acted in the same capacity as that which he followed at Newton. Sergeant McCoy was a soldier born and bred, and at the age of 13 years joined the 82nd Regiment of Foot; Eight years later he accompanied his regiment to the C:aimea, and he was present at the fall of Sebasto- pol. jj," earned the Crimean medal, but along with his comrades and those a the 92nd Regiment, he sacrificed it, because the Sebastopol clasp was reiused to the 92nd Regiment. _

He served through the wh-ile of the Indian mutiny and was present under Sir Celia Campbell at the relief of Lucknow. From Lucknow he went to Cawnpore, aad was engaged against the (ilwalior contingent at Cawnpore and was afterwards beseiged at Shage-han- pore. He took part in other nain•ir actions, and at the conclusion of the mutiny, he joined the 3rd West Indian regiment, as colour-sergeant. On the disbandment of the 3rd West Indian he rejoined the 82nd, and continued to serve in it, until discharged in 1873 on a pension. He received the Indian Mutiny medal and clasp for the relief of Lucknow.

The funeral took place on Wednesday afternoon, when, besides the relatives of deceased, there were ae- sent Volunteers of the Company witn which deeeased was connected, Sergeant Major Kearney, Sergt. Major, Strange, (Hussars), Sergt. Instructors Birch, Parkes, and Sullivan.—The body was interred at the Cemetery, the service being conducted by the Revs.F. W. Johnston, and T. R. Matthews.

div.head: SUPPOSED MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: SUPPOSED MURDER AND SUICIDE.

The bodies of a well-dreesed young woman and a child twelve months old were found, on Thursday,in two feet of water on the shore at New Brighton. FroKi papers found on the woman's body, she had evidently first drowned the child, and then committed suicide. Her name was not discovered, but it is believed site came from Huddersfield.

div.head: NORTH vVICH DIVISION.
div.p: THE NORTH vVICH DIVISION.
LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT NORTHWICH.

A remarkable demonstration of welcome was given to Mrs. Brunner, the wife of the member for the constituency, on her return to Winnington Old , Hall. Northwich, from London on Saturday after- noon. Accompanied by her husband, she arrived at Northwich Station at 3.30, and was met by a crowd lof some '2,000 people. After Air. Algernon .Fletcher had deliyered a short address of welcome, Mrs. Brunner was presented with two beautiful bouquets —one by Miss Marie Forgan and the other by Mr. Siicher on behalf of the Liberals of Barnton. A procession with a couple of brass bands, was then formed, and escorted Mr. and Airs. Brunner, who were .seated in an open carriage, through the town, to Winnington, a distance of close on two miles. At the park entrance the horses were removed from the vehicle, and a number of stalwart Liberals drew it to the hall, where Mrs. Brunnet was the recipient Of another bouquet. An open-air meeting was held shortly 4.:tterwards in the park, under the piesidency of Dr. Basil Hewitt. After an address, by the Rev. W. Gelley, of Blackburn,

Mr. Br-uniler, who was met with a...r; enthusiastic le- ception, said diat Mr. Whiteley, the Conservative can- didate's agent, had been asked to make a joint represen- tation with the Liberals to the sheriff that Saturday would be the more convenient day of the week for the polling in that division. So far, Mr. Whiteley's agent had absolutely refused to join in that representation ("Shame ")—and he (Mr. Brunner) had just received trona his agent a telegram that the election would take place on Monday, the 11th or 18th July, probably the latter. The 18th was the very last possible legal day. Mr. Whiteley wanted the chance of going round amongst the soap-suds—,iaughter)—popping in upon the good women who were engaged in washing, and soliciting their husbands' votes. (Laughter.) He hoped they would tell their good wives that they were going to

VOTE BY BALLOT, wild that they did not approve of Tory tricks, either in the House of Commons, the HOU% of Lords, or in the sheriff's office at Chester. (Cheers.) The rumour was abroad that he was closely donnected with the

WINNINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. This he denied. He did not, however, care who knew his opinion about co-operation. He had seen too much of the good done by it to object it. It had been proved that where co-operative societies were strongest the shopkeepers who attended to their business held their own, and did just as well as the stores. (Hear,hear.) He contrasted the present gathering with the famous Balfour demonstration held in Northwich last Thursday. The meeting he was now addressing was an open meet- ing,

div.head: NOT A PIGOT MEETING.
div.p: NOT A PIGOT MEETING.

(Cheers.) This was a meeting of Northwich people, and not of men brought by special trains from Man- chester, Crewe, and Chester. (Laughter.) This was a meeting of Gladstonians, not of Piggotists ; a meeting of peacemakers, not of coercionists ; a gathering in the interests of the public, not of publicans and brewers. (Cheers.) Mr. Whiteley told them at the Balfour meet- ing that it would be his duty to deliver that constituency from the nightmare of Bruunerisru. (Laughter.) Well, let them see

div.head: WHAT BRIINNERISM WAS.
div.p: WHAT BRIINNERISM WAS.

Bruunerism was a holiday every year to the steady timekeepers, and a week's pay with it. (Cheers.) Brunnerism was 12 hours' pay for eight hours' work in the process department of the woras. Brunnerism was not contracting out of the Employers' Liability Act, and no insurance of employer against accidents. There had been compensation to every man who had be3a injured, and to families when death had occurred, and there had never been a moment's hesitation as to whether Brunner, Mond, anti Co. were legally liable or not. (cheers.) They had got a day school, a night school, a wood-workinr, shop, and were putting up an iron-work- ing shop, ital. all were to be absolutely free. They had got a good playground, a gymnasium, and a fine recreation ground. And that was all Brunnerism. (Loud cheers.) Outside that place he had done a good dealof work for the public. Brunnerism had made since 1879, when he first became a guardian and a member of the rural sanitary authority, broad roads, good wide back passages, and put an end to the filthy evil-smelling slums; it had secured a pure and wholesome water supply to one village after another until they had supplied nearly a score, and it had been instrumental in the saving of 'nearly 700 lives in the Northwich Union, and 5,000 cases of sickness. (Cheers.) He hoped at the next election they would not wake out of their nightmare, but that they would vote forl3run- nerism. (Cheers.) He saw in a paper that his opponent Mr. Whiteley,was addressing, the workmen at a builder's yard, when his agent asked for a show of hands, but someone called out" intimidation," and the agent sub- sided. (Laughter.) The same thing was done in one of the works of the Salt Uaion, and there was nobody there at the time with pluck enough to say " Nay " and so, in the face of the foreman, the men were called upon, and did show their hands for Mr. Whiteley. He did not blame the men for holding up their hands when the foreman was looking on but he did blame the candidate for Parliament who asked them to do it. (Cheers. Mr. Wynne Humphreys, of Runcorn, and others after- wards spoke.

It appears that Cameron and two other men, named Grant and Whiteleg, went out for a walk together, and when they got as far as Howley they sat down by the river Side. leg to-day, but goes back as far as the Reform Bill of 1832. In that year 43 Protestant mem- bers were returned by Catholic constituencies; 40 were returned in 1848 ; 33 in 1868; and 28 in 1874, --that is even after the Home Rule question began to come to the front. But where are the Protes- tant constituencies in Ireland that have returned Catholics? They are not to be found. It comes to this then, reading Lord Salisbury's manifesto in the light of modern history, that, although the 'Catholics have shown themselves tolerant they are not be trusted ; trust only is to be reposed in the Orangemen of Ulster, who have by • cotoparison shown themselves intolerant ! We 'roust confess to a feeling of shame that Eng- lishmen, who pride themselves on their fair-play 'and love of liberty, should hesitate in regard to Irishmen to do by them as they would be done by. What is the use of giving the franchise to the people of Ireland, if we are to pay no heed to their voice ? What is the use of preaching ernocracy, which means the rule of the majority, xf we are not to practice it ? We ask the Liberal Unionists whom these lines will reach to reconsider 'their position—even at the last moment. As a !actor which may possibly be a determining one ba various elections, they take upon themselves a grave responsibility if they either vote Tory, or . 'decline to vote at all. The policy of Coercion has been tried for ninety years; and it has utterly failed. Surely it is not too much for them to say --" We will reject the rash counsels of Lord galisbury ; and will try Conciliation, along with a Plan of Home Rule which, while giving Irishmen 1 ; . Power to manage their own affairs, shall leave them in Imperial affairs subject, as at present, to lbe control of the Imperial Parliament."

On the Eve THE electors in this and ether of Battle. parts of the country are being flooded on the eve of the General tlection with a mass of political literature—issued by both parties—which is intended to assist them in coming to a right decision. It is almost impos- sible for them to read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest the whole of it; but if they glance at the main features of what is laid before them they will see that the Liberals, on one side, present a definite Programme of reforms, whilst, on the other side, the Tories cannot be said to have any programme, *ltcept that of opposition to Home Rule. It is true that Lord SALISBURY and his followers make various references to social and domestic changes; but they are careful not to bind themselves to anything specific, so that they way be at liberty to 40 anything or nothing, if, by a strange chance, they should be again returned to power. Let the working-class electors ask themselves what they have to expect from the Tories when, as history Shows, they have always been on the side of class Privileges. They will do nothing in the direction Of removing the iniquitous Mining Royalties, be- cause they would thereby interfere with the rested interests of landowners. It is a matter of course for them to stand by vested interests, for they occupy a central position in the struggle be- tween the classes and the masses. Take the case Of the proposed compensation to license holders. The Tories were prepared to sacrifice scores of millions of money in the interests of the drink traffic ; and at this moment Tory candidates are, for the most part, pledged to watch the interests Of the trade rather than the interests of the pub- lic. The Tory candidate for Warrington is bound hand and foot to the beer barrel, and citizens, Who, though not teetotallers, are inte rested in the progress of temperance, will do well to remem- ber in giving their votes that he is opp osed to Local Option and Sunday Closing, and in favour of compensation to brewers. Railway men who Study the replies of candidates, will find that their Only hope of shorter hours, and full protection of life and limb, rests in an alliance with the Libe- ral Party. Trades Unionists generally surely cannot forget that, during the pre sent session,the Government refused to amend the law which per- imits working-men being indicted for conspiracy, When by means of picketing they seek to protect themselves in case of a strike. The fact that working-men will be able to vote at all during the ensuing week is due to the untir- ing efforts of the Liberal party. Lord SALISBURY resigned office rather than be party to even a small extension of the franchise in boroughs; and he brought the country to the verge of revolution rather than concede the extension of the franchise to counties. And what of the ballot—that splendid Safeguard of the freedom of the elector? It is notorious that the Tories opposed it tooth and nail when Mr. GLAD3TONE brought the matter before Parliament; and it is an opensecret that the Tories detest the ballot unto this day. But it txists ; and we trust that all classes of electors Will make use of it in the full assurance that they Will be perfectly safe in relying upon its secrecy. It is through the ballot box that Payment of Members and "one wan one vote" may be car- ried, that is if the electors vote for Liberal Candidates, for the Tories have made it evident that they are utterly opposed to both of these re- forms. It is hardly necessary to remind Irish electors that in voting Liberal they will be voting for the redemption of their race. Further, Ile Liberal, English or Irish, should be absent f rout the poll who is in a position, whatever the sacrifice, to record his vote. It has happened before that an election* has been decided by a single vote; and we should not envy the feelings of the Liberal elector, who after failing to vote When be might have voted, discovered that he ilad lost an election. Another thing, voters who are not actively working for the party can render Food serx;ico by taking care to vote early. There 12"3r often a great deal of time and energy wasted in king after electors who delay polling until late '4 the city, with a result that there is more Work to do in the last hour than can be satisfac- ily accomplished. Our last word is, let each ;inter go to the poll as a free citizen, conscious w.a.t be is exercising a privilege which carries asith it a great responsibility, and give his vote his reason and his conscience may direct. He et then go wrong, for, as Emerson finely saYs, "the soul's emphasis is always right."

ELECTION NOTES.
Our r4aders are referred to our first page :or Addresses of Candidates.

The holidays in Warrington may interfere with voting somewhat ; for it is a good deal to ask an elector that he should return for the polling day, when his pleasure trip goes beyond it. But let him think of those who have been working in the election campaign for weeks, and months, and remember that if his abstention from it should lose an election,it will mean that these labours are thrown away. And to lose an election by a single vote would be sufficient to make an absentee miser- able for the rest of his life.

Tory canvassers havo shown themselves indus- trious in circulating the statement that Alderman Platt was so disgusted with the Liberals that he would neither vote nor take part in the election. This is one of those lies in which is " half a truth," and therefore amongst " the blackest of lies." Alderman Platt is as good a Liberal as ever; but he is away in Switzerland. He has taken care, however, to pair with a Conservative—Dr. White, who is with him on the Continent.

Our Tory contemporary says :—" The list of questions sent by the Warrington Temperance Federation to the candidates for Warrington was signed by the Rector the (Rev. F. W. Willis),the RZY. C. E. Jackson and others. We understand that the Rector and gr. Jecksoa do not authorise their signatures to be attached to the questions, and in consequence of the Federation making use of the names as they did, Mr. Jackson has written to the secretary, Mr. W. Roberts, resigning his con- nection with it." We are in a position to give a flat contradiction to the above statement. The circu- lar setting forth the questions bore the names not only of the gentlemen named, but of every officer and vice-president of the Federation, permission in every case being obtained before the name was attached. We are quite sure that this will not be denied by the Rector, or the Rev. C. E. Jackson. They at any rate, will not be party to the false statements which are, as usual, circulated at the last moment.

The fact is, Mr. Robert Pierpoint has gone "the whole hog" on the drink question ; and, as the Tories know that there are men in the Church who will not vote for such a candidate, they wish to confuse the issue by suggesting that the cl:,•rgy- men named, were not party to the questions being put. It is an old dodge, but it has failed before and it will fail again.

Mr. R. W. Murray, was brought all the way from Belfast to influence Warrington voters, as a former resident of Warrington. But he might just as well have stayed at home. He told the audience at Bank Quay, that he hadn't prepared a spech—a fact which was obvious as he proceeded, for his re-hash of worn-out arguments was neither coherent nor convincing. And what of his sup- port to Liberalism in the past? When he was here before, Mr. John Crostield, as treasurer for the Liberal party, said that when Mr. Murray lived in Warrington, he never receiv3d as much as a shilling in support of the party from Mr. Murray. How much, then, was his Liberalism worth? Elevenpence-half-penny ?

Irish electors who read Lord Salisbury's mani- festo will see that it is penned in the vein which led him to compare the people of Ireland to Hottentots. He denounces the methods they have adopted for" the last fifteen years," quite oblivious of the fact that in 1885 he and the rest of the Tory leaders went down on their knees, so to speak, to secure an alliance with the Parnellites. It is not fifteen years since 1885; and Lord Salisbury in condemning the Nationalists is himself con- demned.

But the most impudent thing in this direction is the republication, in our local Tory contempor- ary, of the Parnellite Manifesto of 1885. The Tories were Parnellites in 1885; but since then they have been Pigottites. Can it be, that they wish to pose as Parnellites, in 1892 P This repro- duced Manifesto will at least serve to remind Irish- men how shamelessly they were betrayed by the Tory party in 1885 ; and it will have the effect of making them work all the harder to give the traitors the punishment they deserve. It is another piece of impudence as coming from the Tories, to ask working-men—" Are the Irish to be allowed (if Home Rule is granted) to impose protective duties ?" It is notorious that when Lord Carnarvon as a member of Lord Salisbury's Cabinet consulted Mr. Parnell about a Tory scheme of Home Rule, it was the Tories who sug- gested that Ireland should have power to impose protective duties. The Liberals are opposed to such powers, and the Nationalists do not ask for them, for they know that protective duties would be the ruin of Ireland.

Wide-awake working-men are not to be caught by such clap-trap. They know that when Ireland has power to manage her own affairs, thousands, aye tens of thousands of Irishmen in this coun- try and America, will return to their native land. They will toil in peace with a knowledge that the fruits of their labours will not be seized by rapacious land-owners, and they will thus relieve the English labour market. There is not a lab- ourer in Lancashire and Cheshire whose wages will not rise when, Irishmen, under a Government of their own, remain in, or return to their own country.

Add to this the opportunity that will be given to English workers, when, with Borne Rule out of the way, the Liberal party can carry out the reforms to wirich they are pledged—reforms which, by restoring-the land to the people, will give an enormous impetus to the demand for labour in the country. At present, because the labourer is denied access to the land, he tramps into the town, competes with the workers of the town, and thus tends to bring down wages. Reverse the operation; open the way to the land ; the agriculturallabourer will return to it ; and, by returning to it, he will benefit himself, and improve the chances of those he leaves behind in the present over-crowded cen- tres of population. But Home Rule first, and all the rest will follow.

On Saturday evening, Lord Cross addressed a meeting in support of the candidature of Colonel Mellor, the Unionist candidate for Radcliffe-cum- Farnworth. His lordship said that if they would take the trouble to read the election addresses of Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Balfour, they would soon be able to come to a decision who was the most energe- tic, who spoke as if it was spoken from the heart, and who spoke that which was light and just, and who it was that had written election addresses simply for the purpose of catching votes. When the Home Rule matter was understood, the voice of England would be just as strongly against it as in 1886.

TOTAL ABSTINENCH On Sunday last three open air mnetings were held in connection with this mission, two at the usual plarie,at the end of Bewsey-st., both conducted by Mr. J. Tanner, who was supported at the after- noon meeting by Messrs. J.Drury, T. Rigby, J.Price, R.Storey,and W.Beswick. All the speakers showed the urgent need of tenaperance reforms, and ap- pealed to those who had the welfare of the nation at heart, to vote only for men as Parliamentary candidates who had laid the drunken state of this town to heart,and therefore pledged themselves to support all needful reforms. At the evening meeting Mr. J. Tanner was again supported by Messrs. Drury, Rigby, Price, R. Gout, Councillor Dixon, T. Dale, Bigginson. and R. Storey. In the evening a meeting was held at Town's End, which was addressed on the same subject by Messrs. Price, Rigby, Councillor Saye, and other friends. Seven pledges were signed during the day.

women got the franchise, religion would be joined with politics, they could make their minds easy about that. (Cheers.) The sooner we be- came religious in reality, the less they would be inclined to fight each other about party,and the more truly would they see to it that the National conscience should be something that would bring peace and good-will to men. (Cheers.) Mrs. Chant took her seat amid an extraordi- nary burst of cheering,which continued some minutes. The motion_ was carried with one dissentient. . .

Mr. A. R. Norman proposed a resolution -a—na—ending a hearty vote ot thanks to Mr. Brunner fOr his past ser- vices and declaring him to be a fit and proper person to represent the Northwich Division in Parliament. Mr. Jepson seconded the motion,which was carried by acclamation. .

Mr. Brunner, on rising to reply,was greeted with loud cheers and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow." He had been asked by some good friends of his, who were very proud of banners, and he (Mr. Brunner) was proud to be near them and to be behind them. He was asked by some members of the Friendly Societies to speak in Runcorn about old age pensions. They knew that on Whit-Monday—when he certainly did not.bemean him- self—(cheers)—he spoke upon the subject of the scheme which had been put forth by Mr. Chamberlain. Since then a scheme had been brought forward by a Parliament- ary Committee which was a considerable improvement upon Mr. Chamberlain's scheme, and Mr. Chamberlain's plan had disappeared like the three and twenty plans he had for Home Rule. (Cheers.) In both schemes the payment for 40 years and Sc. a week pension was com- mon to both schemes. Now he hoped that both they and he were going to do better for England at the end of 40 years than ss. a week for a man at 65 years. kCheers.) We were very far from having done our duty to the poor, but nevertheless much had been done in the last 40 years. There were now only one-half the number of people in proportion to population whose end was the workhouse or who received relief at the bands of the State. During the last 23 years, since the passing of the Elementary Education Act, there had been a reduction effected in the number of criminals in our gaols of two- thirds. People lived longer, people lived more healthily, and a very marked change was that not nearly so many children of school age,s to 13,died now as died before the passing of the Education Act in 1870. That Act was described by the Tories as a godless Act. If they con- ceived the amount of misery and sorrow that had been prevented in thousands of hemes through the saving of the children, they would see that it was no godless act but one they ought to thank God for. (Cheers.) Look- ing back, was he not justified in saying that if they went on during the next 40 years as they had marched during the last 40 years, they would get much beyond a miserable ss. a week for people of 65 yearn of age? (Cheers.) They must remember that during the last 40 years wages had risen in every trade, and his desire was that workmen should get higher wages than they did that day, and that they should continue to rise. (Cheers.) How was that to be attained ? Why was it that some men got much money and others got little money ? When they came from the hand of God as little children they were ilk. What made the difference in them in after life ; what made one man worth much and another worth little? It was education, education,education. (Cheers.) If we held on the course mapped out for us and that we had trodden during the last 22 years, since 1870, and especially if all communities of the country followed the excellent example of Runcorn and adopted the Technical Education Act, the poor people of this country would have a free opportunity offered to them to get as good an education as the children of the rich, and their wages would rise and rapidly rise. (Cheers.) They had much more to do than educate the people. They were bound in iustice and in kindness to give to every man as much right to protect himself against the nuisance of ;the liquor trade as the magistrates had to do. (Cheers.) There was now spent 140 millions a year in liquor and they could surely save out of that amount without put- ting every man to inconvenience that, poor 17 millions needed to establish pensions and he believed if they passed the one beneficient law to put into the hands of the people themselves the control of the liquor traffic, they would save long before the end of 40 years many times over that 17 millions which was necessary. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner condemned the proposal to pro- vide for these pensions out of the taxes; which were principally paid by the poorer classes, and he counselled the working-men as self-reliant men not to bind them- selves for forty years to a cast iron scheme, which took their money every year, not to put themselves under the control of this scheme, but to stand by their friendly focietieS the rules of which they rrx..-.1; themselves t which they could alter for themselves, which were worked by men like themselves for the benefit of men like them- selves the country ova. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner said two questions had been addressed to him. The first was "Are you in favour of the abolition of the Vaccination Acts, and if you are would you endeavour to bring in a bill for their repeals ?" As at present advised he was hoe., in faYQUI 91 VII abolition of the Vaccination Acts. (Applause.) But this he WB5 in favour of, that no man who objected to having his children vaccinated should, as the law allowed at present, be fined timil after time. (Applause.) The second question was" Are you in favour of the abolition of canvassing a voter for his vote 2" Mr. Brunner said there was a great difficulty in thls matter, because they would have to define canvass- ing by Act of Parliament and they must settle exactly what canvassing meant. Be should like a candidate forbidden to pop into a house uninvited, whether the voter was at home or not, and whether the mistress was prepared to receive visitors or not. He wanted to grant the right to exclude any unwelcome visitors to every man and woman in that constituency, just as he claimed the right for himself and his wife when they lived at home. (Cheers.) He wanted that consideration and respect for the household. (Cheers.) •1 On the motion of Mr. A. H. Norman, seconded by Mr. Brunner, Mr. Speakman was heartily thanked for pre- siding, and the proceedings concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN IN ELECT ONEE RING.

The fight in the Widnes and Northwich Division is becoming keener as the polling day draws nearer, but there is plenty of time left, in fact too much, for speaking and working. The Widnes election has been fixed for Thursday, the 14th, and Northwich for Monday, the 18th, the latter being the last possible day on which an election could take place. In botk these constituencies Saturday would have been the most suitable day, but the powers that be have a unique way of their own of settling those matters.

W. Handley, agent to Mr. Brunner, wrote to ' Mr. C. J. Hughes, the Conservative agent, asking him to join with him in prevailing upon the Sheriff to fix Saturday for Northwich Division,but he received no reply to his communication or any help in having the day fixed as desired. Monday is the next best day, and this has been secured, but a large number of working-men will be disfranchised. and they should remember to whom they owe that fact.

The Liberal meeting at Runcorn on Tuesday night was one of the most enthusiastic ever held in Runcorn. Mrs. Chant was the special success of the evening. Her impassioned eloquence again and again evoked tremendous cheering, and when she resumed her seat the audience rose en masse, and there was a perfect storm of cheering for some moments.
Owing to his unfortunate deafness Mr. John Simpson takes no part in public meetings ; but his heart and sympathies are with the Liberal party.

To the vote of confidence in the Leaders oi the Liberal party there was only one band held up against and apropos Mr. Brunner described how he had been continually cheered when driving along the roads to the meeting. He had remarked to Mrs. Brunner—"They are in the majority." Now,he said, amid much laughter, the man who had held up his band against was in the minority.

The prospects of the Liberal party in North wich Division are very bright, and there appears no reason to doubt, notwithstanding the activity of his opponent, that Mr. Brunner will be again returned by a substantial majority. In 1886 he was defeated by a majority of 458 by Mr. Robert Verdin, who polled 4,416 votes to Mr. Brunner 3,958. In the previous election, 1885, Mr. Brunner had received 5,023 votes against 3,995 given to Mr. NV. H. Verain. These figures point most strongly to the fact that Mr. Brunner's supposed defeat by Mr. Verdin was through Liberal abstentions. In 1887 most of these had returned to the fold, Mr. Brunner receiving 5,112 votes to Lord Grosvenoes 3,983, or a majority of 1,129. There is no reason to believe that the Liberal party will on this occa- sion desert a tried Liberal and neighbour like Mr. Brunner for a stranger and a Conservative from Blackburn.

Mr. Deacon has addressed meetings in all parts of the Widnes Division this week, and he has had splendid and enthusiastic audiences. Both he and his supporters are confident of the result of the con- test. He has a minority of 792 to convert into a majority and if Mr. Deacon with his personal popu- larity, sound political convictions, and a band of ardent workers cannot do it, we shall have to set down Widnes Division as hopelessly Tory.

The Federation of Trades and Labour Unions connected with the shipping, carrying, and other industries have decided to support Mr. Wade- Deacon in Widnes Division. Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q C., in St. llelens; Mr. Herbert Lewis, in Flint; Mr. J. T. Brunner, in Northwich Division ; and Mr. W. , H. Lever in Birkenhead.

A number of temperance reformers have ad- dressed a number of questions on the direct veto, local option, Sunday Closing and Compensation to Publicans to the candidates for Northwich Division and replies have been received, but they are not to be published at present until other communications have passed.

The thirty-second annual meeting of this society was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Friday. Mr. W. H. Arnott, C.C., one of the trustees, occupied the chair. There were also present Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, Mr. John Adams, secretary, Mr. William Appleby, auditor, Mr. Sankey, chairman of the managers, Messrs. Liptrott, Crouchley, Simpson' Jackson, Ilibbert, Wilkinson, Gibson, Ritchie, Howard, Singleton and a fair number of the mem- bers. A copy of the report had been sent to each member and it was taken as read. The principal portion was as follows : Three of the Properties have been sold during the year at a loss of £548 2s. Bd., and the sum outstanding on Properties in hand has been reduced from £11,154 17s. Bd. to £8,470 Us. 6d., and the net receipts are £321. One of the Properties sold has been mortgaged by the pur- chaser to the Society. Advances have been made this year on five lots of Property amounting to £3,010. Three mortgages have been repaid, representing £1,301 6s. id. The interests received from these Properties is £564. 13s. 2d. The profits for the year are £9Bl 18s. 3d. Out of this it is proposed to pays dividend of four and one- half pounds per cent. per annum, which will take £BOB us., leaving £173 7s. id. to be carried to the Con- tingent Account, which, after allowing, for the loss on Properties sold, will make that Account £3,681 4s. 4d. This is over 43 per cent. on the amount outstanding on Properties in the Society's hands. In December last a careful examination of the affairs of the Society was made, with a result so satisfactory that it was unanim- ously resolved that the General Business Should be re- sumed, and that those persons holding Retention Money should be paid in full. We are pleased to state that over one-half of these persons agreed to make their Re- tention Money into Shares, and the remainder have since been paid, except the sum of £36 10s., which has not been claimed. The Society consists of 313 members, holding 1,8644 invested shares. and 2,4224 purchased shares. Also six persons who have withdrawn, and left Retention Money amounting to £36 103. The Chairman said he considered the report was very satisfactory, and he thought it would be accepted as such by all parties interested. The improvement in the Society's affairs in the last two years was very marked. He had not been very long a trustee, but during the time he had held the office he had not been altogether idle. The managers deserved great credit for the able manner in which they had pulled the Society through its troubled waters, and he was pleased to be present and take part in the proceedings that night. The Society was now paving 20s. in the pound which it was con- sidered it was well able to do, and which was a source of great gratification to the managers as well as to the persons receiving the payments.
