div.head: CCIDENT TO A CRICKETER.
div.p: A CCIDENT TO A CRICKETER.

During the progress of a Cricket match between the second elevens of Earlestown Wesleyans, and of Warrington wire works, at Warrington on Satur- day, Ed. Wolfe, one of the Earlestown players, was struck in the e 5 e by a ball and seriously injured. He was taken to Warrington Infirmary, but as the sight had been injured he was ordered to Man- chester Institution, where he remains an in- patient.

div.head: FATAL FALL AT ST. TIELENS.
div.p: FATAL FALL AT ST. TIELENS.

On Wednesday midnight, Nathaniel Jackson, 44 years of age, a labourer, residing at 33, Cowley-st., St. Helens, was killed by falling downstairs whilst under the influence of drink. The deceased went to bed intoxicated about eleven o'clock, and an hour later was heard to fall downstairs. His wife ran to see what was the matter, and found him lying dead at the bottom with his neck broken and his skull fractured. COLLAPSE OF A HOUSE AT ST. HELENS.

On Thursday morning, about half-past nine, an alarming accident occurred at Parr Stocks, St. Helens, by which a family named Daniels had a narrow escape. The Daniels lived in one of two houses standing together in Parr Stocks-road, and at the time stated the gable end of Daniels' house suddenly collapsed, bricks,. mortar, and other material falling with a crash into the yard. One of the children was playing close by, and was almost surrounded by the falling debris but escaped injury. NEW MAGISTRATES FOR ST. HELENS. In connection with the distribution of "honours" by the present Government before Parliament is dissolved three St. Helens gentlemen have been offered seats on the magisterial bench. Mr. Alfred Walmsley-Cottam, who already occupies a seat on borough bench, has been asked to accept a similar position for the St. Helens county district. The three new borough magistrates will be the Mayor (Councillor F. B. Dixon-Nuttall), Councillor E. Johnson (ex-Mayor), and Mr. B. B. clover. Mr. Dixon-Nuttall is a glass bottle manufacturer; Mr. Johnson a chemical manufacturer; and Mr. Glover a colliery proprietor iad roperaaker.

div.head: ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT RUNCORN.

James Clarke, of Warrington, was summoned before the Runcorn magistrates,on Monday,to answer a charge of cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state.—Edward Lunt,contractor, Warrington, was summoned for causing the horse to be worked.—P.C. Fryer said on the 21st June he was in Halton-road,when he met Clarke driving three horses attached to a lurry laden with barrels of beer. He noticed the shaft horse was in pain, and he found on its shoulder underneath the collar, whieli was saturated with blood, a large raw wound.—Mr. W. H. Jenkinson,whe defonded,said Clarke took the horse from the stable without asking for per- mission, but the wound was then quite healed. But through the heat, and the fact that the animal had been fed on grass, it broke out afresh. The horse was in splendid condition.—The Bench dismissed the charge against Lunt, and fined Clarke 2s. 6d. and costs. JOSEPH PRITCISARICS sale shop is 51,11igh-st., his workshop 4' Bridge-st.—Adrt.
TIRED OF LIFE AT WIDNES.

Alice Drury, aged 18, of Sankey-st., Widnes, was brought u; at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, charged with attempting to commit suicide. On Satur- day morning last a man named Jos. Tonkies was walk- ing along the St. Helens canal, when the prisoner came to him and said, "I am going to drown my self; lam tired of life." She then suddenly jumped into the water, and Tonkies pulled her out by her clothing, and placed her on the bank. She cursed him for saving her life. P.C. Dickinson took her into custody, and in an- swer to the charge, she said she had nothing to live fcr. There was no one to take care of her and her young baby, and she was as well at the bottom of the canal as alive. —Mr. Timmis said it was highly probable that the prisoner would make another attempt on herseif if re- leased, and the most humane thing would be to commit her for trial. She was then committed to the Quarter Sessions. Both PRITIIIKARIVS Shops are under personal snpersisien.and customers may rely upon reeeivineevery attehtlos.—Advt. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF Mrs. GEORGIE WARD, OF

div.head: RINCORN.
div.p: RINCORN.

The mortal remains of Mr. Geo. Ward, of Church-st., Runcorn, were committed to the grave in the conse- created portion of Runcorn Cemetery, on Monday after- noon. The deceased, who had died on the previous Friday, was a member of a family that had been con- nected with Runcorn for a very long period. His father was sexton and apparator at Runcorn Parish Church for 38 years. Mr. Ward commenced life at Runcorn Gas Works, and he was there employed for 27 years, during which time he ably filled several responsible positions. On the retirement of Mr. Wright from the relieving officership of the Runcorn district of Runcorn Union, in 1884, Mr. Ward secured the post from upwards of a hundred applicants, and he has performed the duties to the satisfaction of the Board of Guardians and to the interest of the ratepayers. An enthusiastic Oddfellow, Mr. Ward was a prominent member of the Ebenezer Lodge, and he had goae through the various chairs. For many years he was a member of the local corps of Volun- teers. His death at the comparatively early age of 49 years is a source of great regret to a wide circle of friends, and a widow is left to mourn his loss. At the funeral besides a number of relations there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. E. Aaron, and Mr. T. Lea, representing the Board of Guardians; Mr. W. R. de Prez, relieving officer of Great Budworth District, and Mr. W. Howard, deputy relieving officer, Runcorn. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. J. Holden. On the coffin were a number of beautiful floral offerings from friends and relations.

div.head: EXA MINER, SATURD ,V Y. JULY 2, 1892.
div.p: THE EXA MINER, SATURD ,V Y. JULY 2, 1892.
WIDNES DIVISION.
MR. Fl. WADE DEACON AT HALEBANK.

On Wednesday evening, a meeting of the friends and supporters of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, the Liberal candi- date for the Widnes Division was held in the large room of Mr. Dainteth's Wireworks, Halebank. Mr. J. Jackson " presided, and there was a crowded attendauce. The Chairman said if they sent Mr. Deacon to Parlia- ment, he was sure that he would make one of the best representatives they could possibly have. (Applause.) Mr. H. Wade Deacon, who was warmly received, moved "That this meeting expresses its confidence in the leaders af the Liberal party, and believes that under their guidance the question of Home Rule for Ireland will be Axially settled in the new Parliament." He re- marked that he was pleased to see such a large and en- thusiastic meeting. His prospects were most favouraole, and he hoped that they would manage to pull off the election. (Applause.) His opponent (Mr. Gilliat), in speaking at Hale last night said, "God bless the Crimes Ant," Mr. Crilliat did not say God had blessed the Crimes Act, for no man living could say that. God had not blessed the Crimes Act. Ho (Mrr Deacon) said God bless the dawn of a brighter day for Ireland. (Applause.) What had the Coercion Act of the present Government done in Ireland? It had persecuted perfectly lawful combina- tions of the tenants, broken up public meetings, and sent members of Parliament, mayors, and clergymen to gaol. (A. Voice: "As criminals.") In addition, trial by jury in most importaat cases him been suppressed by it. 'The question they had to decide at this election was whether they would give Ireland a measure of sail-government, reserving to the Imperial Parliament the supremacy of safe-guarding minorities, or whether they would go on with this perpetual coercion for ever and a day? If thee returned him to Parliament he would support Mr. Gladstone in granting Horne Rule to Ireland. (Applause.) If they believed in freedom let them record their votes for the Liberal party. (Ap- plause.) Mr. W. Knowles secnnaleil the resolutiem Mr. W. H. Manning, in supporting the res.ution, said he was not a separatist. Tha, Liberal party were not separatists. The real eniontstra or the United King- dom of England and IrelanA were to be found in the ranks of those who feAlowed Mr, Gladstone. (Ap- plause.) Other speeches fellowed, and the reselution Was qaapi. MOUSIY
--a-. CHURCH BAZAAR AT RUNCORN,

div.head: ADDRESS BY MR. WHITELEY.
div.p: ADDRESS BY MR. WHITELEY.

There was commenced in Runcorn Public Hall,on Thursday afternon, a three days' bazaar in aid of the building fund of St. Michael's Church. It had been intended to hold a bazaar in a field behind Stanley Villas but the heavy rainfall of the previous day rendered the change necessary. Considering the hurried manner in which the promoters had for their task the stalls were admirably arranged and decorated, and the room preser.ted a pretty appear ance. The stalls were well laden with choice and costly articles, and every arrangement had been made to attract and . entertain the visitors to the kazaar. The opening ceremony was performed by Mr. G. Whiteley, the Conservative candidate for the Divisian, who was acc9mpanied by Mrs, Whiteley, and then was a large company present, including a fair sprinkling ef those who were aptly termed " Our friends, the enemy." The Rev. Canon Wo-d, said there bad been some- thing like £5,000 spent on St. Michael's already, and they were spending another .£1,500 of which they wished to raise .£3OO by that bazaar to enable them not only to discharge all liabilities with regard to the church and chancel,but:also to put into proper condition the nave, and to make the land surround- ing the building into a garden. The church was a link in the past. It was built before his incum- bency, the chancel had been built in the present, and they would leave the erection of the tower to a future generation, so that the church was a link with the past the present and the future, so that everybody who supported that Union must be very good Unionists indeed. (Laughter.) On the other hand the Church was absolutely free, a fact which would commend itself to their Radical brethren,and be there present Unionist or Radical if they would put their hands deeply into their pockets they would consider them truly Liberal. (Laughter and applause.) They all knew Mr. Whiteley now, and some of therm would like to think he was going to be a resident amongst them for a long time, and politics apart, some of them hoped he would get the " sitaation " for which he was aspiring. (Applause.) Mr. Whiteley had a cordial greeting, and after a few prefatory remarks he said he had had the pleasure of going round the church in Green- way-road, and he was in agreement with Canon Wood that when it was completed., architecturally considered it would be an ornament to the town. It was quite true there was a great deal of spout about it. (Laughter.) But now-a-days, especially in election times there was a good deal of spouting. (Rene,ved laughter.) He was bound to confess that when he came into the town for the first times few , months ago he was agreeably surprised. Abroad Runcorn had not that good name it ought to possess, probably because it was very near the town over the ! water, which odourously speaking, was not very pleasant and whose buildings were hardly in nine- teenth century form. But in Runcorn they had good streets, good buildings, and good houses, and they had a batter appearance than those who had not been to the town could have expected. Mr. Whiteley referred to the antiquity of the Parish Church, and said it was only in the last few decades that a large increase in the population had taken place, and along with that increase there has been an extension of church work and church accommodation, and from what he heard the good folk of Runcorn had not been slack with their energies nor with their liberality. (Applause.) They believed as Churchmen —although he owed a great deal to Nonconformists—that the church, and indeed all religious bodies were doing a grPat work amongst the masses, and he hoped that the great Council of the nation in the years that were just before them, would be able to devote mere of its time to social matters and those matters affect- ing the work and interests of great masses of the population. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. E. Imison, seconded by Mr. J. B. holland. a hearty vote of thanks was ac- corded to Mr. and Mrs. Whiteley. The ladies then commenced the sale of their wares. There was a crowded attendance in the evening, and both the stalls and entertainments were well patronised, as evidenced by the fact that the sum of .t 180 was raised. _ _
Yesterday the bazaar was held in tents off Green- way-road, and amongst the attractions were sports.

At the Cheshire Quarter sessions, on Monday, Sir Horatio Lloyd, in charging the grand jury, expressed satisfaction at the state of crime in the county. The death is announced of Sir U.S. Atkinson ex-Pre- mier of New Zealand.

div.head: MASS MEETING OF LIBERALS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MASS MEETING OF LIBERALS AT RUNCORN.
SPEECHES BY MESSRS. BRUNNER, LEVER AND ARMSTRONG AND MRS. CHANT.

A mass meeting of electors in support of Mr. Brunner's candidature was held ut Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday night. The building was packed in all parts, and the proceedings were of the most en- thusiastic description. The room was appropri- ately decorated with flags and mottoes and a capital portrait of the G.O.M. occupied a prominent place over the platform. The time previous to the com- mencement of the meeting was spent in singing the election songs composed by Mr. llandley, the audi- ence being led by Messrs. R. Crosby and T. Clegg. Amongst those on the platform were:— Mrs. Ormiston Chant (London), Revs. ft. A. Armstrong (Liverpool), C. Finch, J. Martin, J. Pulford Williams, and John Simpson ; Messrs. W. H. Lever, Liberal can- didate for Birkenhead ; J. T. Brunner, M.P., W. Carroll, I'. Leach, B. Crosby, G. Bellany, S. Coventry, J. Lee, W. Epps, E. Marshall, T. Lee, J. Bridgewater, J. D. Jows, T. Clegg, W. Millington, W. Jepson, W. Musdin W. Yates, B. Posnett, W. M. Sowerby,J. It. Frith, J. Wilson,

James Handley, J.P., E. lig: - Humphreys, A. R. Norman, T. Handley, H. Parker Lowe (London), A. Riley and W. Handley (agent and secretary). The Chairman said it gava him great pleasure to accede to the request of his friends to take the chair that night. They had got a great battle before them in Runcorn ; he ventured to say such a fight as Runcorn had never seen before. (Elear,hear.) A great deal was said about Mr. Brunner's opponent. He (Mr. Speakman) did not think they need say much about Mr. Whiteley at all. What they were anxious for was that the principles of Libera- lism that most of them had been cradled in, should be kept nailed to the mast. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone, by his Home Rule policy had laid the foundation stone of justice to Ireland, and the present Government had put stone after stone upon that foundation stone. Measures that hal been sketched by the Liberal party had been taken up by the Unionist party, and in his opinion if they could only have kept them in office a little longer, they wGuld have given Home Rule altogether. (Cheers.) The time for that had passed, and he hoped that Mr. Gladstone would be able to crown his last battle by 1 passing a full measure of justice bit Ireland. (Cheers.) Ile nad been asked by those on the other side "Why do you support such men ?" He replied, " I support principle first and men afterwards. (Cheers.) lie had been also asked" Why do you Nonconformists support a policy that would give over to the Roman Catholics all the Protest- ants in Ireland ?" His reason was that he was a Chris- tian, and being a Christian he wished to live in brother- hood. The Roman Catholics believed in the same Jesus Christ that'the Nonconformists believed in, and they had a right to • o all that they had in common. There- fore what the English people had to do was nct to be set aside by this or that, but go forth determined that jus- tice shall be done to all ia the empire. (Cheers.) Mr. Jno. Withineton proposed" That this meeting expresses its unabated confidence in the Right Hon. W. Gladstone, of the Liberal party and believes that under his guidance a satisfactory measure of Home Rule for Ireland will be submitted in the new Parliament consistent with the unity and intergity of the Empire. The meeting trusts that an early settlement of the Irish question will enable the Liberal party to devote itself to those great reforms embodied in the Newcastle programme, and which deeply affect the welfare of the peeple of the United Kingdom." Lord Salisbury had sent forth a piteous cry to the Non- conformists to help him in his fight against Home Rule. Lord Salisbury should be more consistent with his Nonconformist brethren before he appealed to them (Cheers.) Did they ever know the Tory party appeal to the Nonconformists of this country except at a General Election when Home Rule was in question. (Cheers.) They were not going to help Lord Salisbury. (Renewed cheers.) He remembered a time when the Wesleyans asked Lord Salisbury for a site for a chapel, and he ' offered them a piece of land near a sewage outfall, where it was not fit for a pigstve and it was within sight. of one house and that was the workhouse. (Laughter and cheers.) And now he asked for their suffrages. He would not get them. (Loud cheers.) Mr. J. R. Frith seconded the motion. This would probably be the last time, he said, he should have to record his vote for Mr. Gladstone, and he meant to do it and to de all in his power to send Mr. Gladstone for the fourth time as Prime Minister of England. (Cheers.) He would be the only man who had occupied that position for a fourth time. (Renewed cheers.) He knew a few of the Tory dodges, and he understood they were trying to get people not to vets at all rather than vote for Mr. Brunner. ("Shame.") Don't be guided by them (hear, hear) kSt.it be determined that every vote should be recoraed. The vote was a privilege obtained for them / by Mr, ciladstone, and in justice to tliefllrlYos, to jets- tice to their country, acd in justice to the GrailLl Old Man record that vote for him alone on the 18th July. (Cheers.) He was sorry the election had been fixed for the last day, but he supposed that was another Tory dodge (laughter), but in spite of it they would give their opponents a good thrashing. (Cheers.) Mr. W. H. Lever supported the motion, and showed the system of canvassing adopted by the Primrose League, by means of misleading leaflets. Ile scented the" Separation League," and said the Liberals saw in Home Rule only an extension to Ireland of those liberties which we enjoyed in England. (Cheers.) In Canada and in the Channel Isles, where there was Home Rule the people were intensely loyal to England, and their past experience showed that to have a united and strong empire there must be given such a measure of local self government as would make the people contented happy and prosperous, and without that they could never have true unity. (Cheers.) Mr. Lever then dealt with some of the reforms in the Newcastle programme. The Rev. R. A. Armstrong, in supporting the motion, said the Tories were at their old game. they ware ap- pealing to bigotry and prejudice in order to obscure the path of reform. For some years he spent his life as a Protestant minister in the Province of Ulster. He was tho son of a man who was an episeopalian clergyman in Ireland, and he was subsequently a Nonconformist Christian pastor in the same County Down. Twenty years ago he cause to the conclusion that there never could be peace and true prosperity in Ireland until the Irish people had the right to manage their own affairs. (Cheers.) The fact was that the Protestant in Ulster had so long enjoyed a religious ascendency that the very conception of religious equality was unknown to them. (Hear, hear.) It appeared to them that if persons of oppesite religious convictions lived side by side either the Catholics must govern the Protestants or the Protestants must govern the Catholics. They could not understand a commonwealth of brethren of different religious convictions living side by side in harmony, sustaining the same laws of justice, righteous- ness and progress, and they could not conceive other- wise than that as they had hitherto exercised ascendancy over Catholics, so the Catholics when their turn came would exercise ascendency over them . (Cheers.) He was convinced from what he saw of the tone and temper of the Catholic population in Ireland that it only re- quired that the Catholic should be emancipated, that he should feel himsslf a citizen with the destinies of the , the esuntry in his own hands in order for ever to put an end to this miserable feud and bring about the peace and prosperity for 'which Ireland yearned. (Cheers.) The Orange spirit was the narrowest, most bitter type of bigotry which the world had ever seen. (Cheers.) He WAS certain as a man could be of anything that had not been fulfilled already, that a generation or two after the great measure of Home Rule had been passed which Mr. Gladstone was about to carry the Protestants of Ire- land would thank God that their fathers were defeated. (Cheers.) Mrs. Ormiston Chant, who had a most enthusiastic reception, described her visit to the Ulster Convention. It spoke well for the Nationalist party that they shared good humouredly in the fun of the Convention, and not atstone was thrown or a threat used. It was because the Nationalists felt safe in the kind love of the English people. (Cheers.) They had sent a message of hope across to Ireland, hope that maketh not ashamed, and Irishmen were trnsting their word, and it would be to the lasting disgrace of the English nation if they did not clench the hope by making it a reality when polling day came. (Cheers.) The manifesto of Lord Salisbury was a direct appeal to the most mean and most bigoted and most greedy side of human nature. Home Rule was an appeal to the most elevated and most noble and most unselfish feelings ef our nature, and thank God there was unselfish kindness and patriotism in England yet. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner was before them not only as a delegate, as it vvere,for their resolve that Mr. Glad- stone should in his last years hive the crowning honour that he so richly deserved above all other men—(cheers) but he stood for the defence of the great and noble prin- ciples that were animating England to-day. (Cheers.) And at the head of their programme, there WAS not selfishness, or snobbery or toadyism, asking that they should take care of those who were well able to take care of themselves. At the head and front of all for whom their suffrages were asked through Mr. Brunner, stood the ragged, bare-footed, sweated starveling from the sweater's den in the East end of London, and she asked them to keep that notion before them. (Cheers.) Reform of the Poor Law was one of the objects of the Newcastle programme, and surely in the fay end of the nineteenth century they could do do something more for their old poor people who had used up their bodies in lives of toil, than send them to the Workhouse. (Cheers.) Then they wanted Parish Councils, and a system of land tenure that would permit the land to be used to produce more food instead of re- ceiving it from foreign countries. (Cheers.) The Allot- ment Aet had turned out a sham, a fraud, and a delu- sion, because there had not been given compulsion and protection with it. (Cheers.) She lived in London and knew about the slums and about the insecurity of the house life of the poor, and said to them tenderly and solemnly that one of the first acts of a civilised coun- try should be to make the home life of the very poorest as secure as the home life of the rich. (Cheers.) Of the first importance it was that the children should be well fed. well clothed, and have plenty of time for play and plenty of space for play. They ought to see that their ' Councils provided playroom and playgrounds for little children. (Loud cheers.) Objections were often heard to mixing politics with religion ; but when

div.p: THE CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY'S SHOW AT WARRINGTON.
APPOINTMENT OF JUDGES.

A meeting of the Cheshire Agricultural Society was held at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-st., Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon, with the object of making arrangements for the Show which is to be held in Warrington, in August. The Rev. J. R. Armitstead, Vicar of Sandbach, presided, and there were also present—Messrs. James Edwards, C. Welch, E. braith, J. Dickson, C. R. Hall, J. J. Tricket, C. Thornhill, J. J. Balmer, T. Balmer. J. Bosley, Hy. Barnett, T. Richardson, John Edwards, W. Coomer, N. Turner, C. Edwards, John Barratt, J. Hill, W. Wl.itlow, J. Lea, Beecrolt, Lockwood, T. T. Dutton, Baxter, J. Dickson, T. Baxter, W. Harrison, S. Rey- nolds, J. Tinsley, and the following members of the local Committee: —Messrs. Ed ward G reenall,Gilbert Greenall, 11. Milling, J. E. Davies, J. Knowles, C. Macl ver, and H. Greenoug h .The business transacted was the appointment of judges, stewards, show yard committee, &c., ana the following are the names of the gentlemen who were appointed to the various offices :—Judges of farms and cottages, Mr. Charles Sherwin and Mr. Parton ; judges of cheese, Mr. Boothby and Mr. Charles Griffiths; judges of butter, Mrs. Joseph Rigby and Miss Maidment ; judges of cattle,Mr. Joseph Hill and Mr. Ashhurner ; heavy horse judges, Mr. John Edwards and Miss Beecroft ; Shire Horse Society judges, Mr. George Simpson and Mr. Henry Smith • light horse judges, the Rev. Lee; judges of implements, Mr. W. Coomer and Mr. N. ' Turner; judges of local exhibits, Mr. Gilbert Greenall; Mr. Cohn Mclver Mr. J. Knowles ; stewards of cheese, Mr. J. Balmer and Mr. Baxter ; butter, Mr. Tricket ; cattle, Mr.H. Barnett and Mr.J.J. Balmer; heavy horses. Mr. Bosley and Mr. Barratt light horses, Mr. Welch, Mr. Dutton, Mr. T. R. Boote ; sheep, Mr. Charles Thornley ; pigs Mr. James Edwards and Mr. Balshaw ; seeds and implements, Mr. Challinor and Mr. Thomas Dickson ; show yard committee, Mr. Russell Hall, Mr. Baxter, Mr. Joseph Knowles, Mr. Whitlow, Mr. Tinsley, Mr. J. THE BOLIDAYS.—The works in this district osed on Wednesday evening, and will remain closed 1 Tues- day morning, thus giving the hands five elea ays for pleasure. lira WarEa SUPPLY.--The supply of water to the Junction end of Lowton has for some time been a ques- tion which has much agitated the minds of the house- holders. Some tune ago the Newton Improvement i Commissioners, n a letter to the Leigh Sanitary Auth- ority, stated that they were willing, subject to the ap- proval of the railway company,to supply the Authority with water by meters fixed near the Bull's head at Is. per 1,000 gallens, the minimum charge to be ' 10s. per quarter, and the Leigh Authority to bear all expenses in maintaining all pipes, meters, connections, Sec. It has now been decided that the Clerk to the Authority (Mr. F. E. Williams) shall inquire whether the Newton Commissioners are still willing to adhere to their_ offer. No doubt the wants of the people will now be attended to.

THE bASE OF WOUNDING. Thomas Savage, living behind School Brow, was charged on remand with unlawfully wounding James Owen.—The Chief Constable said the complainant was still in the Infirmary and there was no improvement, and the earthenware which was supposed to be on the brain was still not removed. He was conscious, and declined to take chloroform. The prisoner was remanded till to-day (Saturday). He applied to be allowed release on bail, but the magistrates refused. AN OLD OFFENDER SENT FOR TRIAL. On Thursday, at the Warrington Police Court, James Towey, described as a loiterer, of no fixed abode, was charged on remand with having stolen two keys, the ' property of the committee of the Warrington Infirmary. • Prisoner was seen by the House Surgeon on Tuesday • night, to be on the top of a shed hear the Infirmary Dective Sergeant Monaghan was afterwards informed of the occurrence, and of the fact that the keys had been missed from the Infirmary. He apprehended prisoner, and found them in his pocket. He had been convicted before, and was now sent for trial to the next Caunty Quarter Sessions to be held at Liverpool. AN AUDACIOUS SWINDLE. A middle-aged woman giving the name of Elisabeth Hennessey, of Liverpool, pleaded guilty on Thursday, before the borough magistrates, to 24 charge of having, on Wednesday, stolen 10s. by means of a trick from Peter Worrell, market-gardener, who has a stall in the market. From a statement made by the Chief-Constable it appeared that the prisoner purchased three bunches of turnips, of the value of 4, from prosecutor, and tendered a sovereign in payment. Mr. Worrall counted out Sonia change and had handed prisoner 103. when she said he might give her the sovereign back, and she would pay him a shilling. Redid so, and prisoner handed him a shilling. Another woman came up and took the prosecu- tor's attention and the prisoner retained the remainder of the change he had handed her, and walked away with it. sho aybsevenrly apprehended, and was now sent to jail for a month:— -- -- MORE LODGING HOUSE MYSTERIES UNVEILED. ArmlElart, widow, of Knight's Yard, was charged at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, by Mr. Nor- man, sanitary inspector, with keeping a lodging-house on the 10th of June without having it registered.—The evidence disclosed that the house Consisted of only one living,room and one bedroom and that one bed out night of Use 10th of June cofitained—thrtteferiflant, son, aged 27, and her daughter aged 12, and another bed on the floor contained a woman and her daughter. There were two others sleeping in the living room. Three of the seven persons were lodgers.—Alderman Harrison (to Mr. Norman) : I should think this is one • of the worst cases you have had.—Mr. Norman : Yes, even in a moral point of view.—Alierman Harrison : Bad in other ways.—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs ; in default 14 days.—Elizabeth Thomason, 4, Knowles's Yard,was charged by Mr. Norman witlakeep- ing lodgers, on the same date without having her house registered. The house was occupied by eight persons, two of them lodgers, this it Was shown being a case of overcrowding. Ole of the lodgers, a man, the defend- ant said she intended to make her husband, as she was " punished " by her children.—She was fined £1 and 7s. costs, in default a month's imprisonment. A DRUNKEN RUFFIAN AND HIS WIFE.—SUPPOSED USE OF THE KNIFE.
the. i from her --

At the Warrington borough magistrates' court on Monday, Patrick Farrell, of 7, Croppers' Brow, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and with assaulting his wife Mary Farrell, on Saturday night.— Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said tho defendant was drunk and struck his wile and knocked her down. He picked her up and found her bleeding from a sharp cut. He found a knife hidden up the prisoner's sleeve. The cut might have been produced by a fall on a stone.— Inspector Spinks corroborated. Fhe woman he said had cuts on the eye and the head, and was covered with mud through having been rolled by her husband. The cut on the head was done, he thought, by a fall, but that on the eye by a severe blow. The prisoner was prevented from assaulting her a second time.—Mrs. Farrell said the prisoner had her "on the floor" kicking her. She appeared very faint and weak, and somewhat hysterical. —lnspector Spinks said the police had had repeated com- plaints about the prisoner's abuse of his wife, since he came home from the army. The senses were almost thrashed out of her.—The prisoner said he came home and found she was out drinking. She came in about a quarter past 11 drunk and used filthy. language to him. He told her if she would not go he would throw a bucket of water over her. She would not go, and he went towards her, but before he could reach her Mr. Monaghan had his hand on him. She fell and cut her head, outside. He never had a knife on him.—The pris- oner was sentenced to 4 months' imprisonment with hard labour.
MINO tt CASES.

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (chairman), Alderman Chandley, Messrs. L. Voisey, R. Garnett, and J. Geddes. DRUNIEENNESS•—EIIen Connor, in Scotland-road on the 28th inst.' one month.—Annie Jackson in Buttermarket- street, 25th inst., ss. and costs. SLEEPING cur.—James Loftus was committed to pri- son for seven days' hard labour for sleeping in a behind Bank Quay Station, on the 25th inst. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—The following persons were fined for not sending their children regularly to school :—.Arthur Miles, Samuel las, Joseph Griffiths, Edward Walker, and John Goddard. ALLEGED NEGLECT.—Jehn Carr, labourer, was charged with deserting his wife and children, and leaving them chargeable to the Union.—He was £6 in arrear.—The case was adjourned for a month, in order to see whether the defendant made any contributions. DEFRAUDING A RAILWAY COMPANY.—WiIIiam Bridge. was charged with travelling on the Midlanl Railway from London to Warrington without having previously paid his fare, and with intent to defraud.—The prisoner , pleaded guilty and was fined 103. and costs, or, in de- fault. 14 days' hard labour. THELHATHEIIO HIS WlFE.—George Henry Ward, a labourer, was charged with using threats towards his wife, Annie %Yard, whereby she was afraid he would do her grievous bodily bann.—Defendant was bound over in the sum of £lO, and find two sureties in glO each to keep the peace for six months.. THEFT OF MONEY.—Catherine Smith, alias Connelly, was charged with stealing 10s., the moneys of Thomas Cunningham, on the previous evening.—From what was stated by the Chief Constable, it appeared that the prisoner and the prosecutor, who belongs to, the militia, were in company on Friday evening, and a police- constable heard the man say to Smith," Give me that money." The woman denied that she had taken his money, and the constable brought both of them to the Police Station. The man again asked the prisoner for the money, and after a little hesitation, she produced half-a-sovereign and 9s. in silver.—The prisoner was committed for one month with hard labour. THEFT BY A SERVANT.—Annie Barry, a young woman, residing at 5, Bakehouse-yard, Latchford, was charged with the theft of a sovereign from the dwelling-honse of William Bayley, Foundry-street. The prisoner was further charged with stealing £2 17s. Bd. from the same place on Friday, the 24th inst. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—The Chairman said the prisoner had just come out of a reformatory, where she had been for five years, and almost immediately she came out she-went into the house of these people whom she had robbed to the extent to which she had confessed that morning. The prisoner was committed to prison for two months with hard labour.

Aldermen Francomb and Harrison,

Maxmum BoaAviota.—Mary O'Reilly, a Yorkshire woman, for this behaviour in Gladstone-st., on Sunday night, was sent to jail for three months with hard labour. ViGRANCY.—John Jones, engineer, was charged with being found sleeping in a hayloft belonging to Mr. Briggs in Battersby Lane about a quarter past one on Sunday night. Ile was sent to prison for seven days with hard labour.—Kate Elliott, for being found sleeping on the premises of Mr. Hutchinson. in Wilderspool road.— seven days' hard labour. STLUSET Onsraccrion.—Joseph Caldwell, greengrocer. 152 Winwick-road, was charged with allowing five bar- rels of potatoes to stand on the footpath a long and unreasonable time, on the 17th inst,—The defendant said the constable who appeared against him, P.C. Oboper 20, refused to come into the house to have the matter explained, and was very 'saucy.—Alderman Francomb said the case was one which the constable might have settled with the defendant without bothering the Bench about it ; and they dismissed it. THEFT B A LAD.—James Barry, aged fifteen, son of Michael Barry, 5 Bakehouse-yard, was charged with stealing on Saturday afternoon 103. ed. and three pawn tickets the property of Sarah,wife ot Thomas Alc'Donald, 8, Dallam lane. She sent him to the pawn-shop with the money and tickets, and he was not seen again till four o'clock on Sunday afternoon, when he came home and handed 2s. sd. and the tickets to his mother. She handed them over to the complainant. At the police station he said the complainant had given him the money, and he had spent it with some other boys in the cricket field, at the theatre, and in some mince pies. The magistrates cautioned him and recorded a conviction against him. DRUNK AND DISORDSRLY.—Patrick Cain in Winwlck- road, on Saturday night, ss.—Martin Ford, in Rose Yard, the same night, 53. and costs.—Arthur Pallett, and Elizabeth Yates, in Mersey-st., that night, ss. each. Ellen Carty, at Friar's Green, that flight, 53..--Margaret Stokes, in Foundry-st., on Saturday night, 53. and costs.—Frank Mahoney and James Finn, in Fennell-st., on the 21st of June, 53. and costs each.—Bessie Taylor, in Bold-st., on Saturdaz night, 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour.—Margaret Griffin was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Brick-st., on Saturday night. She had been assaulting her husband with a clog, but it was stated that he" beat her scandalously "; and it was also said that the children were much neg- lected. The husband was about to go away for training with the militia, and the Bench expressed some anxiety as to what would become of the children ia his absence. The case was, however, dismissed on account of his hav- ing to g) out with the militia. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest (chairman) and
R. Garnett.

DRUNK IN Crum:He OF A floask.—Patrick Quinn, drunk in charge of a Horse and cart in Bewsey-road on Monday night, was fined 10s. and BOAS. ABSENT FROM MILITIA TRAINING.—James McGarry, charged with being absent from militia training was handed over to the military authorities. A DISREPUTABLE CHARACTER.—Brid;.,et Murray, for unseemly conduct in Tanner's-lane, on Monday night, was sent to prison for 14 days' hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERDY.—Margaret Denapm, was charged under a warrant with being drunk and dis- orderly on the 20th July, at Latchford. She was fined

55. TREFT ram( THE BAURACBS.—John McKeen, chemical works labourer, of Widnes, was charged with stealing from Orford Barracks, about half-past one on Monday asternoon, two pairs of boots, one pair of socks, and one pair of braces, value £1 03. lid, the proporty of the military authorities.—The Chief Constable said the pri- soner, in company with tIo men from Widnes, who belonged to the militia, Caine to barracks for training with the militia and he was seen by Col.-Sergt. Cairns and P.C. Hollingworth with two bundles which were found to contain the stolen articles. Each militiaman on commencing training was supplied with a new pair of boots, which became his property at the end of 28 days' training. The prisoner would have worn the old boots he wore at last training and disposed of the new boots for which more would ha given if unworn.— Col.-Sergeant Cairns, and P.C. Hollinsworth, 6, corro- borated this statement.—The prisoner said the two men who where with him were his brother-in-law and a friend, and they asked hint to bring the articles out to them.—Mr. Hunt said he thought the prisoner had re- ceived the goods knowing them to have been stolen.— The Colour-sergeant said the other men might have stolen.them from the barracks. He thought the prisouer ought to be resnauded and t%ll three men charged.—T he Chief-constable of Widnes had given prisoner a good character, and the Bench, disposed to accept his state- ment, dismissed the case. WEDERSDAT.—fiefore Mr. John Fairclough. _ . _
DRUM—George Smith, drunk in Bridge-st., the previous night was fined ss. TiniELSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (in the chair),
Captain Ridgway, and Mr. J:Faii•clough.

Davmaskriass.—Bridget Burke, factory Sand, last from Manchester, was fined ss. and costs for drunken- ness. SLEEPING OUT.—Patrick Leonardy, Frederick George Poole, and Ernest Poole, lads, were charged on remand from Thursday with having been found- sleeping in a railway carriage, at Dallarn-lane sidings, without having visible means of subsistence. The boys were cautioned and dismissed, and Poole, who had wandered to this borough from Manchester, was told that the police would see him in the train for home. BAD BEILATIOUR.—MichaeI Cunningham, labourer, 38, Flowcock-st., and Elizabeth El len Fleming, no abode, were charged in custody with indecent behaviour. In- spector Spinks.described the conduct of the prisoners as disgraceful, and Fleming called him a liar. She used impertinent language to other officers. Cunningham (17th appearence) was fined 10s. Lnd costs, and Fleming (39th appearance) was sent to hard labour for a month. ASSAULT ON A Sisrmi-IN-Law.—William Tallon, 81 Hoyle-st., was summoned for having assaulted Hannah Vernon, his sister-in-law, on the 27th inst.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, appeared for the complainant, and Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, for the defendant. It was alleged that the defend ant went to a shop kept by the complainant, used abusive language to her, and then struck her on the face. It was also complained that defendant had annoyed his sister-in-law on previous occasions. From the evidence it appeared that there was some family dispute, defendant claiming an interest in the business, but it was stated that Miss Vernon had carried it on for twenty years, had really made it, and was the recognised holder of a pa wnbroker's license. Mr. Longton admitted that there had been a bother ,and contended that it arose through the action of the com- plainant. Defendant would undertake not to go near the shop of Miss Vernon again. The magistrstes ordered defendant to find a surety i n £5 for his good behaviour, and to be bound over in his own recognisances.

div.p: TIM EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1892.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The ordinary meeting of this Board was held on• Wednesday morning. There were present Messrs. Heaton (in the chair), Balharry, Hibbert, Dobson, Piling, Jolley, Hood-Wright, A. J. Jolley, Coun- cillors Hill and Muir, Messrs. Gill, J. Houghton,- Smith, Ratcliffe, Turton, Humphreys, , and Mather. —lt was resolved, to advertise for a new registrar for the Newton division, applications'to be opened at the next meeting of the hoard.—A vote of thanks was returned to Sir A. B. Walker for his kindness in entertaining the Guardians at Osmaston.—There was no other business of interest.

CHA RGE OF ATTENIPTED SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Borough Police Curt on We lnesday Morning, before Mr. John Faircleugh, Annie Moseley, a married woman, living in Lovely- lane, was charged with attempting to commit suicide the previous night by cutting her throat. P.C. Bell said he was in Lovely-lane on Tuesday night, when he beard cries of "Police," and on going in the direction of the voice, saw the defend- ant's husband outside his house, and he told him that his wifo had attempted to destroy heraelf by cut- . . .

_ ting her throat. He afterwards went into the man's house and found the defendant lying on a sofa, with a cut in her throat about an inch and a half long. She made various accusations against her husband,and said he was not sober, and added" See the state he is in." She also said "1 have cut my throat, and I intend doing it. Ha took her to the Infirmary, and had the wound dressed. —The prisoner's husband now stated that she had cut her throat not on Tuesday night but on Tuesday morn- ing, and the prisoner herself said she had done it on Monday night, and her husband saw on Tuesday morn- ing what she had done, but took no further notice but at night came in, under the influence of drink, and ,went out and called for the police.—The Bench, after hearing these conflicting statements, contented them- selves with binding the woman over fot six months.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY
AUTIIORIIY.

The ordinary meeting of this Authority was held on Thursday. There were present the Rev. G.F. Roberts (chairman), and Messrs. Humphreys, War- burton, Houghton, Long, Owen, Mather, Kilshaw, Fairclough, A. Jolley, and S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), Wm. Owen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (inspector.)—A letter was read from the executors of Mr. A. Clarke, 41, Bolton-st.,Moses Gate, calling the Board's attention to ,the matter of the purchase of an acre of land at Hollins Green from them for' the purposes of the proposed ceme- tery at Rixton and Glazebrook, and asking the Authority to confirm, the same. They also offered to lend the Authority the money for the purchase on the security of the rates at 31 per cent. for 3 or 5 years.—The Clerk explained that the Authority would have to borrow the money for 30 years at least.—The Clerk was directed to write to the Local Government Board enclosing a copy of the letter from the executors of Mr. Clarke,and asking fordircetions.—The Chairman, , in accordance with notice, proposed that the Authority adopt the Infections Diseases Notification Act, 1891, and the Infectious Diseases Prevention Act, 1890.—Mr. liumpkreys secOnded . After some discussion it was unanimously resolved that the Acts be adopted.—Mr. Houghton, pursuant to notice, pro- posed that the resolution of the Authority passed on the 4th of September last making lighting expensesa general charge upon the vhole district be rescinded, and that all such charges be declared in future special expenses upon the townships lighted.—Mr. Owen seconded and the Chairman supported the motion.—Mr. Long said he had been in favour of inaking such expenses general, but if the Board wished them to be special he would withdraw his opposition.—The resolution was carried unanimously —The Inspec'or made a report as to Orford water supply and it was decided to leave it to Mr. Owen to see Mr. Mortimer, the owner of most of the property affected, with a view to arranging with him as to a water supply. There was no other business of importance.

div.head: MR. PLIMSOLL AND THE TORY ' UNIONIST UOVERNMENT.
div.p: MR. PLIMSOLL AND THE TORY ' UNIONIST UOVERNMENT.

The following is the text of a letter addressed by Mr. Henry Halliday to Mr. Samuel Plimsoll on tho subject of his invitation to the electorS to restore the Tory Government to power on the ground that they are the true friends of the seamen : June 22nd, 1892.—Dear Mr. Plimsoll I, have read 'with amazement your letter in this morning's " Standard." Without questioning any of the statements, which corn- lug from you, everyone will know are made in perfectly good faith, what do your charges against the Liberal leaders come to ? The Ist is : That Mr. Gladstone during a Parliament, in which his labours might becom- posed to those of Hercules, was too busy to see you en°. morning, before your name was associated with those reforms with which it has since been so honourably con- nected, whereas Lord Salisbury, not in office, under circumstances which render his complaieance not wholly unintelligible to the ordinary politician, received you. But how about the Tories when they were in office? Some of us remember a dramatic incidant in the House of Commons on July 22nd, 1875, wherein you played an important part, which did not leave the impression that you were then enamoured of Tory enthusiasm for the cause of the seamen. Nor did we imagine that it was the action of Tories in the country that ultimately egm- yelled the 'Grove.intatent to fulfil the duties which they had undertaken but Were endeavouring to shirk. Coming to later times, you tell us that for three ses- sions bills in favour of the seamen have been passed, presumably with Liberal support, and yet you make it a point against the Liberal leaders that they don't in- clude measures of this character in their programme for the next Parliament. Is not the ease and silence with which these measures are being passed happy evidence that they are, as they ought tebe, non-contentieus, and have the support of both parties ? But the astonishing part of yoor letter lathe conclusion to which you come, even if we suppose your chargea to be more serious than is apparent on the lace of them. I have a vivid recol- lection of your vehement indignation with this Govern- ment early in 1889,and of your active cmoperation in the " National protest" which made Mr. Balfour eat his own words, and alter his disgraceful treatment of politi- cal prisoners. I have heard from your own lips your very strong opinion of the treatment meted out to a nation by the Government, and yet now, op the ground that the Lib- erals are not as eager as they should be in the promotion of certain excellent measures which you justly advocate, you advise the people of the country 'lO keep a Govern- ment in power who are active in the commission of National crimes, in the destruction of National liberty, hnd in the perpetuation of a feud of centuries, which Liberals are trying to terminate. We must suppose that your absorbing enthusiasm on behalf of those whose cause you have so nobly advocated has for a time excluded from your consideration other and larger subjects, and we may hope for your own reputation's sake and in the interest of your own specie. subject you will feel able to withdraw the appeal you have made,and so relieve yourself from the odium which must attach to all who, in full knowledge of this Government's crimes against Ireland, would support their misrule.

"Mr. Halliday'could with equal force have shown that the Liberals had done their share, and more than their share, in the work of amending the law, in the in- terests of seamen. In 1873 they passed "the Merchant Shipping Act," providing for the appointment of sur- veyors of ships suspected of being unseaworthy, by rea- son of their defective state, or overloading, or improper loading, and etnpowering the Board of Trade to detain such unseaworthy ships until they had been put into a safe and satisfactory state. In 1880 they passed " the Merchant Seamen (Pay Ment of Wages and Rating) Act." securing the payment of the sailor's wages to himself, or to those to whom he may have directed that they should be paid. In 1833 they passed " the Merchant Shipping (Fishery Boats) Act," by which the interests of the am prenticev anti the seamen generally engaged in the fish- ing service were carefully protected. 'Mr. Plimsoll will Ino doubt repent of having written so ill-timed and ill- tempered a letter, when he comes to reflect calmly on the matter, sees the injustice of his charges, and the in- jury he may have wantonly- and deliberately done to that parry from whom the class he champions have received so nandh attention. ' THE 'LONDON POISONING CASE.
Thomas Neill, the man 'charged with attempting to blackmail Dr. Harper; of Barnstaple, in connection with the Stamford-street poisoning mysteries, was further re- mended at Bow-street, on Monday.

div.head: MR. GLADSIONE'S MIDLOTHIAN CAMPAIGN.
div.p: MR. GLADSIONE'S MIDLOTHIAN CAMPAIGN.
ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION.

Mr. Gladstone left Hawarden Castle oa Wednes- day morning shortly after" nine o'clock for the purpose of fulfilling his political engagements in Midlothian and the West of ScOtlancl: The right 'hon. gentleman, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Miss Gladstone, and Mr.. Henry Gladstone, drove to Sandycroft Station, on the London dud North- Western Railway, and there a special saloon carriage was placed at his disposal for the journey north. Mr. Gladstone stated that apart from the injury to his eye, he was in excellent health. The wound has now entirely healed, but, in order to shield the eye from the glare of the light, Mr. Gladstone is compelled to wear a pair of very dark-coloured spectacles. The right hon. gentleman has been put to considerable inconvenience through being pro- hibited from reading. A quick run was made to Chester, and there the saloon was attached to the ordin- ary train for Crewe. Just before the train left the station, Mr. W. C. Deeley (president of the Chester Liberal Club) visited the saloon, and asked Miss Glad- stone to convey the heartiest wishes of Chester Liberals to Mr. Gladstone, and to state that in consequence of some misunderstanding an address and bouquet had not then reached the station, but that they would be for- warded by the next train. As the train moved away at ten minutes past ten, loud cheers were given, and many people ran down the platform waving their hats and wishing Mr. Gladstone God-speed. Dr. Granger, who has been attending Mr. Gladstone since the assault upon him, joined the train at Chester, and travelled with the party as far as Lancaster. His report was of a very favourable character.

div.head: AT CREWE.
div.p: AT CREWE.

Upon arriving at Crewe, it was found that the North express from London, to which the saloon was to be at- tached, was half-an-hour late. A reservoir had burst near Stafford, flooding the tun nel, and completely block- ing the Irish' and Scotch mails. The saloon was accord- ingly run into a siding to await the art ival of the express, which took place at a quarter past eleven. A number of people gathered round the saloon, and a message was conveyed from M‘Laren, the late member and present Liberal candidate for Crewe, expressing good wishes. Mr. Gladstone heartily returned these, and then three cheers were called for, and lustily given, for him, and "one more for Mrs. Gladstone." The' journey north was resumed at half-past eleven,or twenty- eight minutes late, amid cries of." Success to you," and " Victory," Mr. and Mrs. Gla,dstone b.) wing their than from the carriage window.

div.head: SPEECH AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SPEECH AT WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday morning Bank Quay railway station was a scene of considerable animation in consequence of it beingS announced that Mr. Gladstone would make a short ' stay there on his way to commence his electoral campiign in Mid- lothian. Tickets for admission to the platform had been issued by the Liberal Club, and at first none but those holding these were admitted, except indeed many who purchased passenger tickets in or- der to gain access to the platform, .but ultimately a number of others were passed through and Mr. Glad- tone on his arrival had an enthusiastic reception irom a crowd of some hundreds of persons. The follow- ng members of the Warrington Liberal Association were present with the object of presenting through Dr. Elcus- ton, who with Mrs. Houston, accompanied them, an illuminated address to the right hon. gentleman. It had been hoped that Mr. Gladstone would come direct from Chester to Warrington in which case he 'would have been able to be half-an-hour or more at Warrington, but in consequence of his coming by Crewe, only a few minutes' halt were practicable. The train was due at Warrington at 11.37, but through an accident occurring on the line at Stafford Mr. Gladstone did not arrive till five minutes to 12. Among those ' present were Dr. and Mrs. Houston, Councillors H. Roberts, A. Browne (Dr. Houston's election agent), Plumpton, Dixon, Mr. and Mrs. W. Pierpoint, Mr. and Mrs. John Fairclough, Mr. John Crosfield, Mr. C. J. Holmes, Mr. W. Roberts, Mrs. Holford, Mr. H. Roberts, Miss Dutton, the Revs. John Yong, and J. Davies_ Mr. James Plinston, Mrs. Loughlin, Mr. James Summersgill, Mr. Kiernan, Mr. S. Kenyon, Mr. Tinnion, Mr. J. Winser, and Mr. Gough. As the train was sighted, a hearty cheer was given, and as it steamed in the cheering was enthusiastically renewed, and a scene of no little excitement and struggling for places was witnessed. The police, under the control of Inspector Spinks, aided by the busy co-operation of Mr. Ashton, the station-master, preserved good order, and all passed off pleasantly. Mr. Gladstone promptly stood up at the carriage window and bowed, apparently highly pleased with his reception, to the crowd. Dr. -Houston- then handed- to him a handsome illuminated address, of which a copy had been sent to him the previous night, and which was therefore taken as read. The address, the artistio part of which had been executed by Messrs. Brooks and Son, of Bridge-st., read as follows:—" To the Right Hon. William Ewart Gladstone. Sir,—On be- half of the Liberals of Warrington and our candidate, Dr. Houston, Q.C.' we desire to greet you on your way to the field of your labours in the favoured constituency which is about to do itself the honour of once more re- turning you as its representative. We beg to assure you that you have no more ardent admirers, and no more devoted followers than those whom we represent, and that there are not more staunch supporters of Liberal principles than are to be found in this borough. We earnestly hope, and we confidently trust, that your splendid efforts in the cause of justice, liberty, and pro- gress are about to be crowned with a signal and endur- ing success. Heartily we wish you God speed." The address was signed by Messrs. John Rylands, John Cros- field, A. H. Crosfield, Win. Pierpoint, J. H. Gornall, C. J. Holmes, Arthur Houston (the candidate), Arthur Browne, and Henry Roberts. Mrs. Houston, on be- half of the association, handed to Mr. Gladstone a bas- ket of choice fruit, intermingled with some Grace Dar- ling roses, and to Mrs. Gladstone,who accompanied him, a magnificent bouquet, which had been exhibited on high, for ,the edification of the crowd, like a sort of floral standard, and ras much admired. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone thanked Dr. and Mrs. Houston, and shook han.gs cordially with them both.. The right hon. gentle- man then spoke as follows: I thank you Dr. Houston and gentlemen. I have had the opportunity through your kindness of reading this address. You speak here of the hope with which you look forward to the approaching contest. I well recollect that in the dis- astrous election of 1888 the Liberals of Warrington never lost heart—(cheers)—and they showed that constancy in defeat which is the best pledge and guar- antee of the exertion necessary to gain vic- tory. (A voice : " Home Rule.") I meet you now, gentlemen, under very different circumstances. We are looking forward to a strong and decided pro- nouncement of the national will in favour of the opinions, in favour of the issues,for which we then struggled. We are confident, and I believe our opponents are not less aware of it than we are ourselves, as to what is to be the issue of the coming election. And you, gentlemen, I hope, will take a prominent and decisive place in the ranks which we believe will unite with the result of victory for the cause and for the principles oh justice. I have much pleasure, Dr. Houston,in wishing you person- ally success, and hope we shall meet again before many weeks are over. (Loud cheering.) The right hon. gentle- man and Mrs. Gladstone then shook hands again with Dr. and Mrs. Houston and with a number of other ladies and gentlemen,Mr. Gladstone expfessing pleasure at the reception he had met with, and the train carried him on his way to Edinburgh, amidst enthusiastic plaudits and waving of hats and handkerchiefs by the crowd, until
he disa-ppeared from sight. FURTHER NORTH. _ . .

On erring at Wigan the Liberals gave him a heary welcome, and Mr. Gladstone, speaking hopefully of the result of the strugele, said even their Tory friends were not sanguine about it, and they knew a thing or two about electioneering. At Preston. Carnforth, and several other stations north he gave words of earnest encouragement to the electors ; and, speaking at Carlisle in acknowledgment of an address, he said the Liberals were the ,true champions of union with Ireland, fsr the union they 'sought was founded upon justice. There was, he said, only one voice that came to .them—the voice of hope, courage, cheerfulness, and confident anticipation. They were fully justified in believing that they were going to retrieve, and more than retrieve, the disaster of 1886. Another address was presented to him at Carstairs, and in reply he said the new Parliament had before it some of the noblest and most arduous work in his recollection. They wished to clear the Irish difficulty out of the way first, and then they could address themselves to the wants of the coun- try. On reaching Edinburgh Mr. Gladstone had a magnificent reception, and was followed and cheered by many admirers on his drive to Dalmeny.

div.head: SBEECFI IN .EDINBURGH:
div.p: SBEECFI IN .EDINBURGH:

Mr. GLADSTONE delievered the first of his Midlothian Speeche4 on Thursday night. The meeting took place in the Edinburgh Music Hall, and was very enthusiastdc. The right lion. gentleman said he had never met the electors Of Midlothian with greater confidence, and after a refe- rence to the Government's contrivance for preventing a Saturday poll in , the boroughs in order. to limit the working man's vote where they they could not get rid of it, he declared it was still as profcundly true as ever, and more significant than over, • that Ireland for the moment stopped the way. The address of the Premier to the constituencies showed that in the ectimation of the Government the question of Ireland was the question of the day, and that he anticipated that there would he a Horne Rule Bill. Undoubtedly the first duty of a Liberal Government would be the preparation and the introduction of such a but. The declarations he (Mr. .Gladstone) made as to the princi-

pies of the Home Rule Bill in 1886 had never been re- tracted. What the Liberal Government stated then was that the object of the Bill was to give Irelaid full and effective conttol of her own properly local affairs, under conditions which included the supremacy of Parliament, a fair adjustment of pecuniary burdens, special care of minorities,: and equal treatment with England and Scotland. Those acquainted with.the last Home Rule Bill I knew a great deal about the new one. In obedience to the voice of the country another condition was imposed —namely,the retention of Irish members at Westminster, but the details of that retention—whether they should be allowed to vote on all questiohs, and whether there should be one set of Irish members or two—were matters which must be approached in a practical spirit when a Liberal Government was established. In proof of the reality of the intended supremacy of the Imperial Parlia- ment the right hon. gentleman pointed to our colonies, and said it was impossible to suppose that in any of teem which were under a constitution of local autonomy the majority could practise gross injustice against the minority. That disposition nowhere existed, and it existed no more in Ireland—it existed less, if possible, in Ireland than it did even in , some of tha colonies. Nor was it to be supposed that Parliament would remain inactive and suffer such op- pression to go on. Turning to the opposition of the " classes" to Home Rule, he said the leisured classes, the educated classes, the wealthy classes, the titled classes had almost always been in the wrong, and he then spoke of the conciliatory spirit in which cencessiqns had been made by the Irish people and their leaders. Much would be heard during this election struggle of the party pledges of 1886. The Irish local government measure was a wrong and an insult to the Irish nation. Some • Conservatives said it would be reintroduced in the next Parliament, but he did not believe their party would have the opportunity. In conclusion, he ex- horted his supporters to go forward with the good work they had in hand. Let them not put their trust in squires or peers, not in titles or in acres, not in man as man, but in the Almighty God, who had ordained the principles'of right and equity and freedom to be the guides and masters of our lives.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. •
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. •
HOUSE OF LORDS.-SATURDAY.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at twelve o'clock.
The Burgh Pollee (Snotland) Bill was read a third time and passed. _

THE WITNESSES' (PUBLIC INQUIRIES) PnoTscnox BILL. .—On the motion to go into comjnittee on this Bill, Lord MORRIS, who contended that there was no demand for the Bill, moved that the House go into committee this day six months.—Lord HERscasix defended the Bill. In such a case as his noble and learned friend had set forth the man would be dismissed, not for giving evi- dence. but for the theft. rime House divided, when there were—For going into committee nine ; against 19; majority, 10. THIRD READINGS.—The Contagious DiSeases (Animals) Bill, the Expiring, Laws Continuance Bill, the Technical Instruction (Scotland) Bill, the Mauritius Loan Bill, the Banks of England and Ireland (Payment) Bill. the British Columbia Bill, the Telegraphs Bill, the Salmon and Fresh Water Fisheries Bill, and the Strop Hours Bill were read a third time and passed. At five minutes past one, the House adjourned until three c'clock on Monday. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDAY.

Their lordships met at three o'clock. THE ROYAL ASSENT.—The Huai assent was Riven by commission to several public and a large number of private Provisional Order Bills. THE WITNESSES' (PUBLIC INQUIRIES) PROTECTION BILL.—Lord MORRIS with the leave of the House, with- drew his amendment put on Saturday, which prevented their lordships going inta committee on this Bill. The House then went into committee on the Bill, which was agreed to. On the motion to read the Bill a third time, Lord Morris entered his protest against important mea- sures being forced through their lordships' House with- out adequate consideration. The Bill Nato; then read a third time and passed. The sitting was then suspended at five minutes past four to await certain Bills from the House of Commons and was resumed at twenty-five minutes to five, the Earl of Morley (chairman of committees) taking his seat on the woolsack.
_ The CLERK a,t the tables informed their lordships that the House of Commons had agreed to their amendments to the Public Works Loans Bill.
At a quartet' to five the }louse adjourned.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAT.

Tho Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Bhortly afterwards the Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod (Captain Butler) appeared at the table' and summoned the House to appear at the bar of the Upper House to hear the Royal Assent given to various Bills which have passed both assemblies. The Speaker, accompanied by most of the members present—between 20 and 30—then pro- ceeded to the House of Lords. The SPEAKER, 01, his return, announced that the Royal Assent had been given to the Appropriation Act, 1892, and to others. THE WITNESS PROTECTION BILL.—MT. BREISER asked the President of the Board of Trade whether he had any information to give the -

Witness Protection Bill, which was not proceeded with in the House of Lords on Saturday.—Sir M. Hicks Blum said he had no information whatever. THE TELEGRAPHS BILL.—On the consideration of the Lords' amendments to this Bill, Sir Joule Lamb= said that the County Councils bad had no time to consider the effect of the amendment, and it was useless to do more at that period of the session than make a protest against it. A division was challenged, and the amendment was confirmed by 65 toll. LORDS' AMENDMENTS.—The House next proceeded with the consideration of the Lords' amendments to a number of Bills, including the Shop Hours Bill, the Coroders' Deputies Bill, the Burgh Police (Scotland) Bill, with regard to which Dr. Clark made a faint protest, the Technical Education (Scotland) Bill, the Belfast Corpora- tion Lunatic Asylum Bill, the Witnesses' (Public In- quiries) Protection Bili, and other measures. No serious , opposition was offered in any case. The House adjourned at 4.25.

div.head: DISSOLUTION. PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: THE DISSOLUTION. PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-TIIESDAY.

The seventh session of the twelfth Parliament of the Queen and of the 25th Parliament of the United King dom of Great Britain and Ireland was terminated on Tuesday by Royal Commission. The interior of tho House of Lords, as usual on these occasions, was rend- dared additionally bright and picturesque by the pre- sence of a large number of ladies, who occupied seat- on the benches on both the Opposition and Ministerias side of the chamber. The Strangers' Gallery was also largely filled by members of the fair sex. There were between thirty and forty peers present. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at three o'clock. Prayers having been said by the Bishop of Gloucester. Lord DENMAN rose and said—my Lords, I move that this house at its rising do adjourn until the 2nd of Sep- tember.

div.head: ROYAL ASSENT TO ACTG.
div.p: ROYAL ASSENT TO ACTG.

The Loan CHANCELLOR, without taking any notice of the motion, left the chamber and shortly afterwards returned, accompanied by the Earl of Coventry. the Earl of Limerick, the Earl of Yarborough, and Lord Windsor, who as Royal Commissioners all wore peers robes of scarlet and ermine. The Commissioners having taken their seats on the bench placed for them in front of the throne, which was uncovered, the Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod (Captain Butler was directed to summon the Commons. After the lapse of a few minutes, the Speaker, accompanied by the Sergeant-at-Arms, without the mace, and followed by a large number of iegislaturs from the Lower House, appeared at the bar. The Lord Chancellor then, in his usual formal language, announced that the Queen, not thinking fit to be present in person, bad issued a Commission under the Great Seal, which he called upon the reading-clerk to read. The Hon. SLINGSBY BETHELL, ham,' read the Com- mission, the Royal assent was signified to the Allotments (Scotland) Bill, the Coroners' Deputies Bill, the Drainage and Improvement of Land (Ireland) (number two) Bill, the Public Health Act Amendment Bill, the Accumula- tions Bill, the Burgh Police (Scotland) Bill,the Telegraph Bill, tke Expiring Laws Continuance Bill, the Public Works Loans Bill, the Shop Hours Bill, the Technical Instruction (Scotland) Bill, the Witnesses' (Public In- quiries) Protection Bill, and a number of private Bills. TILE QUEEN'S SPEECH.

MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,— The time has arrived at which it is expedient that the electoral body of this country should be consulted by the assemblage of a new Parliament. I have therefore summoned you for the proroga- tion of Parliament at an earlier period than usual. I am glad to record that the friendly relations I have maintained with Foreign Powers remain un- altered. The treaties have been duly razified which refer our differences with the United States in res- pect to Behrings Sea to arbitration. The ratifica- tion alSo of the final act of the Brussels Conference for the suppression of the slave trade has after many delays bean completed. The Government of France, however, has made reservations in regard to some of the provisions which affect operations against the maritime slave trade. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.--,- I recognize with satisfaction that before separat- ing you have made full provision for the require- ments of the public service. - MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN.— I have gladly given my assent to several Bills which you have been able to consider and to sanc- tion notwithstanding that the duration of the session has been exceptionally short. The arrange- ments you have made for enabling labouring-men

to become purchasers of small agricultural holdine will increase the class of cultivating owners, whin is of great importance to the State. The application to Ireland of those educational measures which have been recently adopted in Great Britain will confer great beneAts on the poorer classes of that country. You have sanctioned valuable provisions for re- forming the police administration in Scottish burghs and for extending to Scotlend the facilities for the hire of allotments which were given to the People. of England and Wales a few years ago. At the. same time, you have done much to lighten the bur- den of local taxation in that country, and to'toster the interests of secondary and of university educe- The Act for strengthening the discipline of the Church of England in regard to moral offences ac- complished a necessary reform which has been too low-, delayed. r have willingly accepted a measure for imProv- ing the constitution and proceedings of the legisia" tive Ctuncils in India, which will, I trust, enable my Government in that country more fully to Boer' tam n the opinions and wishes of the various races and classes of my subjects, and to secure the co: operation of those best qualified to give advice and assistance in the conduct of affairs. I have assented gladly to the measures vfhich you have wisely and generously adopted for the , relief of my subjects in the island of Mauritius under the unexampled Calamity which has over- taken them. In closing this Parliament, which has been un- usually laborious, and has also been highly fruit° in beneficient legislation, I thank you for the sa: sidous performance of your momentous duties dur ing the last six years, and I heartily commend ru to the favour of Almighty God.

PRESENTATION TO A TRADES' SECRETARY AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday evening, a considerable number of members of the Iron and Steel Wiredrawers' Society met at Mr. Eittlewood's, Unicorn Inn, Winwick-rd., on the occasion of a presentation to Mr. E. Williams, of Arpley, late district secretary to the society, in expression of appreciation of his 17 years' service in that capacity. The present consisted of a hand- some walnut cabinet, supplied by Messrs. S. E. and it. Johnson, of Bridge-st. Mr. vv. flaigh,district president, presided, and Mr. Vim. Wood, vice-president, occupied the vice-chair. Among those present were Mr. Thomas Wadsworth, general secretary; Mr. Evans, manager of wire works at Manchester ; Mr. S. Taylor, manager for the Wire,Mattrass Co. ; Mr. H.lRathbone, manager for Messrs. Smith and Sons' Wire Works, Dallarn-lane, at 1 which place Mr. Williams, who was formerly at floug,h- ton's Wire Works, Sankey, has recently been appointed to the managership of the music wire department Mr. Sermons, representing the Manchester, and Mr. Hood, of the St. Helens district of the society, were also pre- sent. A letter was read from Mr. George Smith, of the Friar's Green mill, Warrington, treasurer of the society, expressing his regret at being unable to be present to testify to the exceptional ability, and straightforward integrity of Mr. Williams.—The Chairman, in making the presentation, deplored the loss of Mr_ Williams as secretary, anti expressed satisfaction that was felt at his remaining in the district. He was an upright and honest man, who, whatever his lot might be, would be just in all his dealings, and who would always be appreciated, as he was by these present. The chair- man concluded by handing to Mr. Williams the key of the cabinet which was then being exhibited at Messrs. Johnson's.—Mr. Williams briefly thanked the society, and Messrs. Rathbosie and Wadsworth (general seers- tary)subsequently made remarks highly eulogistic of the charailter of Mr. Williatns.—Pianoferte performances were given during the evening by Mr. Burton. and songs, Rm., by Messrs. Taylor, Reddish, Scarisbrick, Cook, Highley, and Whitham.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse,on Tuesday,under the presidency of Mr. Mclntyre. Present Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Rev. J. W. W. Tanner, Mr. P. Speakman, CC,, Mesers. J. Weir, E. Aaron, T. Lewis, P. Hall, H. E. Heywood, J. Brandreth, W. Pickering, T. Lee, A. It. Norman,. T. Baxter, C. C. T. Wilkinson, W. Whitlow, J. M. Williams, J. Ashton (clerk) and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: DEATH OF MR. WARD.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. WARD.

The Clerk reported the death of Mr. Geo. Ward, re- lieving officer for Runcorn District. Mr. Speakman said they must all regret very much the sudden demise of Mr. Ward. It was only a fortnight ago that he and (Mr. Speakman) reported that Mr. Ward, seemed very much better, but he became much worse, and was now dead. Mr. Ward was an officer highly appreciated by the Board and he proposed that a letter of condolence be sent the widow.—Mr. Weir seconded and Mr. Lea supported.—The motion was carried unanim- ously.—Mr. Speakman said, with regard to the appointment of a successor to Mr. Ward, that it would be to the interests of the Board if the selection was left to the Guardians of Runcorn and District.—Mr. Norman seconded, and remarked that the Guardians of the district the relieving officer had to serve were best qualified to judge of the candidates that would be forthcoming, and it was only reasonable that they should have the appointment.—Mr. Heywood said recently the Guardians of Frodshain district by 9 votes to 2, supported one gentleman for the medical officership of Frodsham, but they had the whole of the Board against them.—Mr. Brandreth said the question was for the whole Board to decide.—Mr. Lewis proposed that a com- mittee consisting of three members from each relief dis- trict,ane: this amendment was carried by 12 votes to four. —Mr. 1N orman moved that the five Runcorn Guardians be placed on the Committee.—Mr. Lea seconded. This 'notion was defeated by nine votes to seven, and the Committee was constituted as follows : Messrs. Aaron, Lea Taylor, Weir. Baxter, Whitlow, Heywood, Bran- dreth and Peter Hall.
