div.head: -TELEGRAPH AND TELEPHONE.
div.p: -TELEGRAPH AND TELEPHONE.

An application from the Postmaster General for per- mission to erect telegraph poles from Frodsham to Frod- sham Bridge was :referred to the Frodsham Parochial Committee. The Authority decided that they had no ob- jection to telephone poles being erectedon the main road between Stockton Heath and Grappenhall by the National Telephone Co.
INFECTIOUS DISEASE.
Mr. Brandreth proposed that all the sections of,the Infectious Diseases (Prevention) Act, 1890, be adopted, and that the Act come into operation on August 9th.— Mr. Aaron seconded.—Carried.
WATER SUPPLY WANTED.

With regard to the water supply of Ashton, Dutton, and Preston-o2th-Hill, a letter had been received from the Local Government Board, stating that the Board were advised that it was only in cases where water could 'e supplied within a reasonable distance at a cost to each house, considered separately, which did not exceed that limited by section 3 of the Public Health Water Act,lB7B, that the Rural Sanitary Authority were empowered to require the owner to provide a supply. The London Board asked for further information to be furnished.— After discussion, it was resolved that tenders be asked for from well sinkers in the district as to the amount for which they would provide water for the townships by pump and well. DIPTHRIZIA. AND TYPHOID FEVER. The Medical Cfficer reported three cases of diptheria at Frodsham. two at Antrobus, and one each at Lower Stretton and at Five Crosses. There were also two cases of typhoid fever at Manley, and one at flelsby. There was a case of scarlet fever at Kingsley. The doctor had issued the usual preventive orders.

SUTTON PUMP. The Inspector reported that the water from the bore- hole to the Sutton Pump well had been condemned, and the analyst suggested that another sample be obtained, and the inspector was directed to comply with the sug- gestion. A WESTON POINT SEWER. The Inspector reported that an extension and:a fur- ther improvement of the sewer at Weston Point had been made in a very satisfactory manner at a little or no cost to the ratepayers, but there was a defect in the sewer at the lower end, and he asked for an order to have the same examined .—Order granted.
PLAT: APPROVED.
Plans were submitted and -approved for a new house at Stockton Heath, proposed to be erected by Mr. Jack- son Lee.
CHMICH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY AND THE ELECTION.

The following circular has been addressed to the members of the Church of England Temperance Society by the Executive : The approaching General Election gives the members of the Society an opportunity of pressing earnestly on candidates for seats in Parliament the importance of legislation with a view to promote the cause of temper- ance. This society is not attached to any political party. Its aims are independent of all party objects. Its recommendations are such as can be supported by men of all varieties of political opinion. It is not, there- fore, within the province of the Society to take sides directly or indirectly, in the approaching political con- flict. But the promotion of temperance affects the happiness of so many thousands of our countrymen, bears so directy on the moral tone of the whole naticn, that the executive deem it a duty incumbent on all members of the Society to press upon all candidates for whom they vote the imperative necessity of support- ing by every means in their power such legislation as will diminish the temptations to intemperance, at pre- sent the cause of such widespread mischief. There are certain legislative proposals which all workers in the temperance cause are now united in supporting, and which the time is now ripe for pressing to final adoption. Stated broadly and without details they are these :- 1. Sunday closing of public-houses. 2. Registration and regulation of clubs which supply intoxicating liquors to their members.

3. Prohibition of serving of liquor to children. 4. Abolition of grocers' licenses. 5. Speedy diminution on some equitable plan, of the number of public-houses. 6. Control, direct or indirect, by ratepayers over the granting of licenses. It is not suggested that these questions shall over- ride all others. On the main issue now submitted to the nation every elector will no doubt decide in accord- ance with his own conscientious convictions. But it is well known that constituents can exercise a very power- ful influence on the candidates whom they support, and that influence ought to be used to the utmost of their power by the members of the society in furtherance of the purposes for which the society exists. (Signed) F. LONDIN, Chairman.

Sir,—May I ask you to allow me through the,medium Of your celumns to emphatically deny a rumour that is being, Addifluously circulated by the ConservitiVei !tit !as retiring from his candidature Mn trheLliatnhuatsmico;"dll.d4:p4 isiion. This rumour appears in a ideal Tory piper, and is only one of a similar class of " alleged rumours " that are being started by a series of local TOPS' papers. Last week it was a Liberal candidate in another divison of Cheshire who was about to retire, a statement that was entirely devoid of truth. If these are samples of the accuracy of the news (?) disseminated by this series of Tory Journals people will soon think that statements appearing in a Tory print are utterly unreliable and misleading. Sir,—NotvAthstanding the enormous development which has taken place in recent years in gas and elec- tricity, there can be no doubt that oil lamps light the homes of a larger number of persons throughout the world than any other illuminant. Even in the Uuiteal Kingdom alone, it has been estimated that over 10,000,000 lamps are in use. No wonder then that newspaper readers are every now and again startled by the recital of terrible accidents, too often resulting iniagonising death. Mr. Alfred Spencer, of the London County Council, stated at an inquest on the late Lord Romilly that he estimated that there were 300 deaths a year caused in this country by ungafe lamps. Mr. Sheen, of the Fire Brigade Association, expressed the opinion that 10 per cent. of fires are caused by paraffin lamps, and Captain Shaw, the former Superintendent of the London Fire Brigade, reported 158 fires in one year caused by the upsetting of lamps in London. Wilt a friend to human- ity in each corlstituency ask the candiaiates, whether Liberal or Conservative, to pledge themselve, to support a short Act of Parliament compelling every lamp to have affixed to it an automatic extinguisher, as recom- mended in the reports of Sir Frederick Abel, Mr. Boyer- ton Redwood, and Colonel Majendie, or must we wait until a Bishop or a Royal Princess is burnt to 'death ?-4 am, dear sir, yours obediently,
The intend.

div.head: HUMANITY_
div.p: HUMANITY_
"BE JUST AND FEAR NOT." HOUSTON FOR WARRINGTON t

- - - .Sir,—Once more we are on the eve of a. great political struggle, and once more it behoves us, one and all, to Weigh well and consider how we shall best acquittpur, , selves lathe great trust reposed in us by our fellow citizens. This time the issue is momentous and likely to be epoch-making. And I would appeal, sir, through you, to such of my fellow electors as .may yet be undecided 'lbw to. cast their votes to adopt what I believe to be Mr. Gladstone's motto : " Be just and fear not." Let us do what we can to atone in some measure for our past barbaric treatment of the Sister Isle. Let us give our neighbours the privilegeof minding their own business, whereby we shall be in a better position to do the same. And for this there is much need. Don't let Lord Salisbury's political Bogie-man affright you. Be just and fear not the Ulster corner-man—that sore place in the Irish body politic—the ulcer of Ireland.

People who threaten to break the law if the law is not made to suit them,must be dealt with as the law directs. Don't let the Tory flags so liberally displayed, or the Tory placards, induce you to give your vote to a cause requiring such appeals to uphold it. I see much is made of Mr. R. Pierpoint's being a native of the town. Well, so was Tatney Dutton, Billy Cliff, and Sammy Snigg, but I am not arguing that these celebrities represent us in Parliament. Person- ally, I much prefer a Dublin man who will vote right for true reform and progress to a townsman who aspires to add weight to the Tory brake to impede and imperil the many useful measures of reform now and for so long awaiting settlement. Faithfully yours, JOHN PEERS. Penketh, Jane 28th, 1892.

P.S.—I note that these said Tory placards contain ist I large letters the word " Progress "—Tory progress ! Se cloth the little sea-side crab Progress in sash a way As he scuttles o'er his native strand. His oyes turned t' other way 1 The party of borrowed plumes— the party whose sole function in life is to stop progress has now the glaring inconsistency to inscribe oa its banners the word—to them really so obnoxious—" Progress." After this let us wait a little while—to find them claiming Home Rule as a Tory measure, as they have claimed so many other measures against which they fought,and screamed, and threatened.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 2, 1892.
THE TIME HAS COME.

Sir,—The time has come for the electors of the 'United Kingdom to declare at the polling booth whether or not they are in favour of Home Rule for Ireland. Let every voter and every Englishman ask himself this question. If tie were an Irish man living in Ireland governed as Ireland has been governed and treated as Irishmen have b: au treated, would he be contented or would he want lime Rule ? It is the duty of those who suffer from injustice to make it known that it may be redressed, and those who would suppress the agitation are guilty of oppression and tyanny„ but happily for mankind the days of oppression are passing away. I notice that many of the Tory organs endeavour to make light of Mr. Glad- stone's desire for justice, and it answers their purpose to do so because the majestic beneficient and abiding power of justice is not upon their side, for it is to mistrust, self-interest, and prejudice that the Tories appeal, and the triumph of the party depend- ing on these qualities is disastrous to the nation's welfare. The Liberals of Warrington have a splendid candidate and a noble cause, and I trust that we shall each of us do what we can to win, for if we do our success will be so great that I might almost say that we shall all of us have won it If putting aside personal and selfish considerations the electors will act without prejudice and do their duty, I think their votes will be decisively in favour of Dr. Houston and the Grand Old Man who is, thank Heaven, so undecayed and strong. With the enclosed verses I conclude—

Be wise in time, nor let oppression stay, For progress sweeps offensive laws away ; Balfour's firm rule will never lead us right, Immortal Gladitone is the nation's light. He knows that only liberty can save Our sister country rising from the wave; Her gentle reign might all our troubles end And peace o'er Erin once again descend. Oh! white-robed peace• unto this world of strife . . .
Thou bringest all the happiness of life; But with coercion thou can'st never be--
Thou dwellest only with sweet liberty.
Then give the Grand Old Man, sublime and strong, In wisdom gathered through a life so long, Your votes and power, these sea-girt shores to bless With freedom, justice, peace, and happiness.
S. KENYON.

div.head: TO THE VITESLEYANS OF WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT.
div.p: TO THE VITESLEYANS OF WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT.

Sir,—l trust you will find me a little space in order that I may address a few words to my co-rel igionists in Warrington and district on the subject of the Liquor interest in relation to the coming election. I am not going ta take any extreme standpoint ; but I confess to a strong anxiety that the Wesleyan vote in this district should go to strengthen the cause of local and national sobriety. The manifesto of our dear and respected father in tho faith, Charles Garrett, is very clear and te the point, and who can doubt but that if John Wesley were again with us he would be on the temperance side. I have stood face to face with you many a time in the various pulpits, and I know your kindliness and sympathy and Christian energy, but I am afraid some of you are likely to go to the poll in fright, so to speak, and record a vote for a party from whom you can never expect the slightest concession to temperance reforms. Why this panic about Home Rule? Does not the Drink ravage Ire- land as well as England ? I grant you that Home Rule may turn out an evil thing; but—and this is the point I want you to notice—will you by voting Conservative support an admittedly terri- ble evil for the sake of guarding against what is only a ireagii/e eei/ ? Will you by your vote and interest up- held the greatest foe our church has to contend with, merely because you happen to be a Conservative or a Unionist, or because you happen to have the idea that Home Rule will not be a good thing for Ireland ? I fully believe that your good common sense will lead you , to perceiva that you will not do either yoarself, your ) Church, or your country due justice in allowing a purely Irish question to monopolise your votes. It is not for me to tell you how human nature on the average behaves in front of temptation. You know these matters ntultiply the temptation to drink, and, as human nature is, you multiply the consumption of intoxicants with all its attendant evils. What will you do then to help your country best; to support your pastors in their work of Christianizing men and women ; to assist the men who without a halfpenny do the bulk of the ministerial work of your church ; to rouse poor erring human nature ? If in your capacity as citzens of this town you wish to thwart the work of Christ, then you may do so by casting your vote for the Conservative p?rtr ; if; on the oth,7 hand, you are desirous of rernalfiink Late b your religious tfalninti 149 d. to, the trad).tion of your church, then shut your Gai); to the confusing hubbub of the plitkiltn rd vote solidly fAr Liberalism—not, mark ' ytvd, because it is Liberalism, but because in the great battle between the powerfully entrenched Liquor interest and poor defenceless humanity, it has promised to take the part of humanity.—l remain, very sincerely yours, A WESLEYAN LOCAL PREACHER OF THE WARRINGTON CIRCUIT.

div.head: PRESENT STRUGGILE
div.p: THE PRESENT STRUGGILE

Sir,—r wish to say a few words to my fr,ilow electors on two of the questions that have to be decided by the present contest. The first of these qmstsions .is Ulster, as to which I would advise tny townsmen and fellow-Non- conformists not to be led away by mere clap-trap. I be- lieve it is a fact that many Nonconformist ministers in Ulster have been influenced in 'their attitude towards Home Rule by a few rich men in their respective con- gregations. It is an unfortlimste circumstance tfiarin • ) a great many congregations the ministers ire- unduly influenced by a few persons of wealth and position on whom they are largely dependent for due payment of their salaries. If the opinions of the pooret and largest bodies of the people could be ascertained, they would be found to preponderate in favour of Home Rule. And now a word as to the recent Ulster Convention. We have been told of the immense number of delegates who attended. There is small matter for wonder at that, for I have been informed on good authority, that passes and expenses and handsome badges were to be had fez- the asking. Who would decline such a jolly nice holiday on such terms as these? But, Sir, -money is being lavished with an unstinted hand,and no means are being left untried by which a Tory majority may be returned. The other question I would speak about is the Temper- ance Question. All honour to our candidate for his out- spoken fspressions on this subject. We have nothing to fear from accepting this question in its entirety. I know that some of our friends ere a little disquieted, and fear that it may lose us some votes, but I know for a certainty that it will also win many votes for us. One gentleman I knew who would not lift his Anger to help the Liberals, has_ gone out canvassing, with might and main for Dr. Houston, and will lend his horse and trap on the day of the election all because the Doctor nap so, unreservedly ttireolvn in his lot with the Temper- ance cause. And yestetday, a well-known - Conser- vative, a friend of mine, told me that he feared sr adoption cf the Temperance cause had done his party almost irretrievable damage. When I suggested that it had probably damaged the Liberal party he said he did not think so for a moment. Well, I know that certain friends of his are Liberal Unionists—and very strong ones too, andl believe they have been won over to our side solely because of our complete adoption of Temper- ance. It must have been bitterest gall to right thinking' men amongst our Conservative friends—to hear or read the stinging and forcible words of Dr. Houston the other night when he said, referring to the distinguished ser- vices of Sir Gilbert Greenall, that he, Sir Gilbert, had voted once only in seven years and that that was in support of compensation of publicans.' What an act of disinterestedness ; a sight, surely, for men and gods ! But it is only of a piece with the rest of Tory legislation. ,They are always precious careful; ,of their own personal interests. I rejoice that the day of revenge is drawing.near.The publicans-areethoroughly alive to their danger. They were never -so -scared as —.. • . t 13: t,

they are to-day, and we of the Temperance party are beginning to see the position of our hopes. We begin to feel that the arduous labours of many years will soon meet their reward in the social purity and improved material condition of the masses of our people, by the removal of these dens of infamy and debauchery which have so long disgraced our dear old town. Let all friends of Temperance and progress do their utmost to return our eloquent and scholarly candidate at the head of the poll on Tuesday next.—l am, sir yours truly, AN OLD TOWNSMAN.

div.head: TILE CONSERV AT IVES AND REFORM.
div.p: TILE CONSERV AT IVES AND REFORM.

Sir,—We are on the eve, in Warrington,of a great poli- tical contest. We have on the one side Mr. R. Pierpoint, but lam at a loss to know what to call him, as in his first platform speeches, he titled himself a Tory of the old stamp. A little further on he was a Canservative- Unionist ; now he is a so-called Unionst. More than that, he claims to be a Warrington bred and born gentleman, which it would be unjust to doubt,. But I may say for myself that I have lived in Warrington close on 30 years, and I have not had the pleasure of knowing that gentleman yet. I was speaking to a friend of mine who is close on 60 years of age; he tells me that he never had the pleasure of knowing Mr. Pierpoint until he called to solicit him for his vote. He also claims to be a War- rington bred and born citizen. Further, he never heard of Mr. itobert Pierpoint being connected with any works or supporting any of our valuable insti- tutions, and yet Mr. Pierpoint and his supporters are claiming to have the support of the working-men of Warrington. Now, sir, that appears to roe to be an unjust claim. Further, Mr. Pierpoint and his supporters claim to give us all the good measures that we are possessed of, such as the franchise, also free education, as Mr. Pierpoint calls it. But I call it sham free education. The follow- ing will show from facts how the two above-mentioned measures have been passed, and 1 shall leave it to my Tory friends to judge for themselves how Lord Salis- bury gave us the franchise and how Mr. Balfour and his friends gave us the free education bill. Lord Salisbury and his friends deserted the late Derby and Disraeli government,to give us the present franchise our Tory friends are claiming so much credit for, in the following manner: Lord Cranborne, now the Marquis of Salisbury, in one of his speeches against the late Disraeli Reform Bill of 1867, made a somewhat vehem- ent speech, in which he arraigned the leader of the Con- servatives for treachery to the party. He declared that Mr. Gladstone's imperious demands had been obeyed by Mr. Disraeli, and that the Conservative Reform Bill was really the fulfilment of Mr. Bright's wildest dreams. Lord Cranborne, now the Marquis of Salisbury, was one of the greatest critics and the bitterest enemies of the Reform Bill of 1867. He fought the bill at every step of its progress through the House of Commons, and when it had received the Royal assent, he published in the " Quarterly Review "an article entitled "The Conser- vative Surrender," in which he vehemently attacked the Bill and its authors, and predicted the most doleful results as certain to flowlrom its operation. " Unscru- pulousness " and " facility "were the words he used to describe the policy of Mr. Disraeli and Lord Derby, and both were roundly accused of having beers actuated by fear of the mob and by a desire to retain office at the expense of a sacrifice of principle. Three years ago Mr. Balfour remarked that a large section of the Conservative party had over and over again stated that they had objected to the principle of free education. Sir H. Howorth, Conservative member for Salford,in a letter to the " Times " is June last year, said :—" It is well known to everyone in the House of Commons that there are very few supporters of free education as a principle upon the Tory benches." And Mr. Bartley, Conservative member for Islington, said in his place in the House of Commons :—" In the division of the second reading less than half of the Conservative members voted for it."

Through the Liberals of Warrington not being able to get a Warrington local gentleman to come out as a Liberal candidate for them, they had to seek elsewhere for one, and their choice fell on Dr. Houston, who, for his qualifications to represent them can not be surpassed, as his intelligence will lead him to both speak and vote in our English House of Commons for true Liberal prin- ciples. And if all Liberals in Warrington will do their duty on the day of the election, as he is doing, and will, if elected, do in the future for us, he will get returned as the member for Warrington. We say nothing about his being Irish and a foreigner,but trust to him doing his duty to us the same as the Irish generals and the Irish soldiers hays always done in the fields of battle for mar country.—Yours, Sm., June 29th.
NO MONOPOLY.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
ANOTHER FATAL ACCIDENT.

On Monday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner held an inquest at the Three Pigeon., Inn, Tanner's- lane, concerning the death of Arthtr Messiter, aged 17, fireman on tho Ship Canal, at Moore, and son of George Messiter, of 52, Pierooint-street, a fitter,employed on the Ship Canal, at whose house he died early on Saturday morning. The deceased's father said about half past 2 o'clock on 'I uesday morning he was informo that his son had had a fall while at his work. He went and found this was the case, and that he had cut his head. He explained to him that it had happened while - he wag wheeling a barrow of coal over some planks, to the engine. Oae of the planks was missing, and he fell a distance of 3 to 4 feet. He was con- veyed home, and elied on Saturday morning about five minutes to two o'clock. He had previously had good health.—Dr. Adams deposed to calling to see the deceased on Wednesday morning, and afterwards three times a day, up to the time of his death. There appeared at first to be nothing seriously wrong with him. He was perfectly conscious, and the only indication of trouble was a slight scar behind the right ear, and merely a little skin brushed off. He explained that he fell while trying to wheel a barrow of coal over planks, of which there ought to have been threa, but one was missing. He fell, and the barrow dragged him down, and some- thing hit him on the right side of the head, and he Was dazed and funny for a time. After witness left the house on Wednesday afternoon, the 'deceased gradually became dull and lethargic, and his condition indicated that rupture of a blood vessel and large hemorrhage. There was no doubt that his death was the result of injury from the fall, but his case had taken a somewhat unusual course. The jury returned a verdict of •,Ae.,lo.e4.tgd death."

TIIE NEW CONTRACTS. It is understood that the final contracts have been let within the last few days for the completion of the main worke of the Manchester Ship Canal. The line of canal from Runcorn to Manchester was, by direction of the executive consmittee of the directors of the company, divided into five fairly equal sections. div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council is sum- moned for Tuesday evening next, but owing to the election on that day, it is expected that the meet- ing will be adjourned. Amongst the business men- tioned on the Council summons are the following items.

div.head: TIIE AUDITORS' HONORARIUM.
div.p: TIIE AUDITORS' HONORARIUM.

The borough auditors, namely, Mr. James Muir, (Mayor's auditor), and Messrs. john Harrison, and James Bolton (elective auditors), report that they have examined the accounts of the Corporationfor the year ending March 25th,and certify the several statements to be correct. The Finance Committee recommend that the sum of E,75 be voted to the auditors for their services.

div.head: QUESTIOW.
div.p: A QUESTIOW.

Councillor DIMON has given notice of the follow- ing question: "To ask the Chairman of the street Improvement Committee if any error had been made in allowing the property to be erected by Mr. Wm. Jeffery, in Padgate-lane, and if one has been made, will he give me full particulars, and who is responsible for it ?"

div.head: LONGFORD DEPOT.
div.p: LONGFORD DEPOT.

The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contains several resolutions with regard to Longford depot. They are as follows :—(1) That the tender of Messrs. Bryan, Donkin, and Co., Limited, to supply Perret's bars for Longford at £l6O be accepted. (2) That Mrs. Beamont, the owner of the land at Longford, be requested to refer the question of the sale of the field adjoining the depot, and containing about 'an acre of land, to Mr. Wm. Owen, to fix the price t) be paid by the Corporation. (3) On the recom- mendation of the Longford Sub-committee, the ' tender of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, and Co., Limited, bra steel boiler, with all necessary destructor iron- for the sum of .E 669 be accepted. The work to be completed within eight weeks from date of contract. (4) That the Borough Surveyor be in- structed to prepare drawings and specification, and obtain tenders for the construction of the destruc- tor, with all necessary alterations to buildings.

div.head: NEW BA.THS.
div.p: THE NEW BA.THS.

The Baths Committee recommend that the ten- der of Messrs. Thomas Bradford and Co., to supply and flic the whole of the engineering work for the new baths, according to specification, at £557, be accepted.

div.head: NEW BAND STAND.
div.p: A NEW BAND STAND.
The Parks, &c., Committee, have approved of a plan of a new band stand, and recommended that the tender of Mr. R. W. Collin to construct and erect it for .£265 be accepted.

div.head: "MOCK AUCTIONS IN TEE MARKET.
div.p: "MOCK AUCTIONS IN TEE MARKET.

The Markets Committee propose that the charge to auctioneers and persons selling by auction in the market, be fixed at 7s. 6d. per day, or any fraction of h day, except on days other than market days, when the charge for half-day or less be 3s. GI

div.head: REDUCTION OF METER RENTS.
div.p: REDUCTION OF METER RENTS.

The Gas Committee have decided to reduce gas meter rents from the 25th March last as follows : Three lights from 3 to Is. GI per annum ; five lights from 4s. 6d. to 3s. per annum ; 10 lights from 6s. 6d. to ss. 6d. per annum -; 15 lights from 9s. to Bs. per annum ; 20 lights from 9s. 6d. to Bs. 6d. per annum.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND THE GAS MAINS.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND THE GAS MAINS.

The Gas Committee report that the Manchester Ship Canal Company having agreed to lay a new main over the high level vehicular bridge near Wash-lane,Latchford, and to pay the sum of .£l,OOO in lieu of their constructing the Knutsford-road subway under the Canal, the Committee have in- structed the Town Clerk to prepare an agreement for carrying the arrangement into effect.
THE GAS WORKS PROFITS.-PROPOSED REMOVAL OF THE WORKS.

The Gas Committee recommend that the sum of £1,617 15s. 91, part of the net profits of the gas undertaking, for the year ending March 25th, 1892, be carried to the reserve fund, and that the net surplus of the gas revenue, namely .El,ooo,be carried to the Borough Fund.—The Committee have also considered a report of Mr. Thos. Newbigging, C.E., on the proposed transfer of the Mersey-st., works to Longford. They are of opinion that it is desir- able that the Mersey-st.,works be eventually trans- ferred to Longford, but that they cannot see their way to adopt the scheme immediately. They, how- ever, recommend that the Town Clerk apply to the Local Government Board for permission to bor- row the sum of £20,000 for extansions at Longford works.

div.head: MARKET HALL AS A CONCERT 'TALL.
div.p: THE MARKET HALL AS A CONCERT 'TALL.

The General Purposes Purposes Committee report that the borough surveyor having reported upon the excessive cost and unsuitability of utiliz- ing the Market Hall as a Concert Hall, they have resolved that the question be deferred sine die.

div.p: COUNCILLOR DIXON STICKS TO MS TEXT.

div.p: PENKETH.

div.p: OPEN Am MEETINGS.

div.p: GGPORNE:

The officers are : Messrs. W. Molyneux (secretary), W. R. Mitchell (treasurer), J. Garton (captain), and R. Halliday (sub- captain.) It is expected that over a thousand scholars will take part in the proceedings. LEADBEATER'S CHARITY.—OR Friday evening, a üblic meeting of the ratepayers of Golborne, took place in St. Thomas's school, for the purpose of electing trustees for the management of Leadbeater's Charity for that town- ship. The Rev. T. W. Richardson, rector of the parish, wesided,and there was a large attendance. Fen gentle- ,en were nominated, and after a lengthy discussion of a friendly character, it was agreed, on the motion of Messrs.-Caunce and Winward, to elect the following as being equally acceptable to Churchmen and Nonconfor- mists alike. via.—Messrs. J. Robinson, J. Dobb. John Unswirth, jun., and W. Glover. The Chairman con- gratulated the ratepayers present upon the suitable manner in which they had conducted the proceedings, thus avoiding the expense of a poll. A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the proceedings.

A Teheran telegram reports a considerable decrease in thio mortality from cholera at Meshed. it was resolved at a meeting of the North Wales Miners' Federation on Monday, to support only those Candidates who will support an Eight floura Bill.,

div.head: BAZAAR AT THELWALL
div.p: BAZAAR AT THELWALL

A most successful bazaar was held at Massey Hall, Thelwall, kindly lent tor the occasion by Mrs. Peter Rylands, on Wednesday, Thursda, and yes- terday afternoons in aid of the Thelwall National Schools. The objects of the bazaar were : 1. To pay off the debt,a growing one,which now embarasses the Committee of Management. 2. To provide funds to meet a large expedditure upon the School House, School Buildings, and premises, which is urgently needed and must be incurred. 3. To en- able the Committee to put in hand some necessary buildings. 4. To bank a sum of money. Some six months ago the idea of raising sufficient to clear the liabilities and establish a fund that would tide over the difficulties for a few years was mooted,and the suggestion was heartily taken up by the ladies of the district. Mrs. Peter Rylands at once placed Massey Hall and the well-laid and tastefully arranged grounds at the disposal of the committee, and on Wednesday the splendid array of articles, useful and ornamental, that loaded the stalls in a large room at Massey Hall, showed that the ladies had spared no pains to ensure the success of the undertaking. Arranged most tastefully round the sides were half a dozen stalls, and the emerald green of the lawn beyond, set off by a profusion of foliage, making the scene most charming. The Stall "Cedar Lawn" was, perhaps, the most prominent for its profuse stock and tasteful arrangement, amongst its collection being some very handsome rugs, and a number of ancient coins collected by the father of Major Pickmere, some of which date back to the time of the first of the first Georges. " Highfields " stall was well stocked with carvings, "the Hall" bearing an interesting show of foreign curios, Japanese mirrors and toys of a unique character. "The Vicarage" and " School ' stalls were tempting displays, a very good portrait of the vicar of Thelwall, the Rev. T. P. Williamson, being exhibited at the latter stall. "Thelwall Lea and Thelwall Heves "stall had an attrac- tive and artistically arranged stock and some splendid specimens of Dresden China were amongst the speciali- ties offered. The stallholders were as follows :—" High- fields," Mrs. T. G. Rylands, Miss Rylands, Miss P. Rvlands, Miss G. Rylands, Miss So wler, and Miss Farren ; "Cedar Lawn," Miss Pickinere ; "Thelwall Lea and Thelwall Reyes" Mrs. Bleckly, Mrs. Lrig, Miss Long, and Miss DeAngelus, Miss G. E. Milner and Miss Clarke; "School Stall' Miss Tudor; "The Vicarage," Mrs. Williamson, Mrs. W. Tinsley, Miss W. Williamson and Miss Holden ; "The Hall," Mrs. Jones Parry. There was a large attendance at the opening cere- mony on Wednesday afternoon, much disappointment being felt at the absence through accident of Lady Greenall, who had been announced to open the bazaar, but was prevented from attending through a sprained ankle. ' The Vicar in opening the sale , regretted the accident that had so unforttniately befallen their good friend Lady Greenall, and briefly explained the objects of the bazaar.

The sale then briskly proceeded, and during the even- ing quite a large programme of amusements, lawn tennis, bowls, and croquet were played. Dancing, a musical entertainment, and a May Pole dance were amongst the items, and the comedietta " On an Island" was given by Mr. T. P. Williamson and Miss William- son, In the farce" Modest Assurance," Messrs. T. P. Williamson and Rupert Crossley, and Miss Williamson and Miss Cattley were the dramatis persona. The Warrington Volunteer band Was present and played various selections during the afternoon and evening, Mr. Thomas Armstrong conducting.

div.head: WALKING DAY AT WA hItINGTON.
div.p: WALKING DAY AT WA hItINGTON.

The great children's festival held annually in Warrington, and known by the homely name of Walkihg Day, was observe lk yesterday; and, favoured with the sudden advent of most delicious weather, came off with imposing success. The day was, as usual, observed as a general holiday and the town presented the customary animated aspect. There was a profuse and picturesque ex- hibition of bunting in the main thoroughfares and numerous flags were displayed in other parts of the town. Occasionally the eye met, and some- times in quarters where it might not have been looked for, with pleasant diversifica- tion of the scene, in the display of plants, flowers, &c.. artistically and strikingly disposed. A publican, the landlord of the Bear's Paw Inn, in- troduced a decorative accessory in front of his pre- mises, somewhat of the grotesque element, by hanging out a characteristic-looking figure of Ally Sloper. The streOg were thronged as usual the Whole of the morning by passengers, who seemed to enter heartily into the spirieof the occasion, and to enjoy to the utmost the cheering and inspiriting sight presented to them of happy juvenility and of their really brilliant and beautiful procession. The children of the Church of England,Catholic, Noncon- formist and Ragged schools, and some 600 juveniles collected by the Salvation Army from among the pborest classes of the town, assembled in front of the Town Hall in the Park, about ten, o'clock, and started from there about a quarter past ten emerging from the Park by the west gate and making a circuit of the town, through Sankey-street, Akpley- street, Wilson-Patten-street ,past A rpley Station,through Bridge-street, Buttermarket-street and Church-street. The order of the procession was as follows :—Blue Coat School and band, Padgate Industrial Schools and band, Parish Church Schools and band, St. Anne's School and , band, St. Barnabas School and band, St. Paurs School and band, Holy Trinity School and band, St. James's School and band, St. Peter's School and band, Emmanuel I School, Primitive Methodist Schools (Legh-street and Latchford), Buckley-street School and band, Salvation Army and band, Ragged School and band. The children attending the Parish Church schools and the schools of the mission churches connected therewith,also the Blue Coat, Padgate Industrial,St. Anne's,and St. Barnabas's schools attended service at the Parish Church at the close of the procession. The preacher was the Rev. T. Rinch- cliffe, Rector of Mucklestone. Market Drayton, and he founded his discourse upon Mark ix. 41, "Ye belong to Christ." All the clergy connected with the Parish Church were present, the prayers being read by the Rector. There was a large congregation. The children belonging to all the schools taking part in the procession and to those which do not join in it had their usual treats later in the day.
In consequence of exceptional pressure of matter, we are compelled to hold over till next week the usual returns as to the schools taking part.

A FAMER'S CHILD DROWNED IN A WELL.—On Thursday forenoon, Robert Wilfred Ralph Avery Brooks, aged 16 months, son of Mr. It. Brookes, farmer, Camsley Farm, Lymm, was found dead in a small well in the farm yard. The child had been missed, and search being made, one 2f his brothers found him lying face downwards. It is supposed he had been chasing the dtwks and had fallen uto the water.

div.head: BIRTHS AND DEATHS.
div.p: BIRTHS AND DEATHS.
DEATH OF THE REGISTRAR OF

It is with regret,that we have this week to reCord the death of Mr. George Appleton, of High-st., Newton, registrar for births, marriages, and deaths, and authorised town crier for Newton-in-Maker- field, which took place at his residence, on SundaY, at noon, at the age of 07 years. 3lr. Appleton bad been in failing health for six months past, but he was not prevented from attending to his duties until Tues- day last week, when he was unable to leave his bed. ' He then gave up all hope of recovery, and gradupY sank until he died as stated. He was perfectly conscious• until the last and his death was totally unexpected. He leaves a widow and three sons and four daughters, all of whom are grown up. With the death of Mr. Apple- ton there passes from public life, almost the last of the old stock of Newton residents, for with a very short Fa- ception, he has resided in Newton the whole of his life. His father, Thomas Appleton, was a native of Newton, and held the position of registrar for upwards of 30 years, being also clerk of St. Peter's Church for that length of time, and a member of the choir some 20 yeara earlier. Just before the birth of the deceased his parents removed to Croft, but they only remained ithere i a very short time, and returned to Newton, and t s a noteworthy fact that Mr. Appleton has lived in the same house from his boyhood until his death. The deceased was apprenticed when young to a tailor, and on the com- pletion of his apprenticeship he started in business for himself, but on the death of his father in 1868. he took over the duties of Registrar, and Town Crier, the latter appointment being periodically renewed by the Court Leet. About 12 years ago however, he appointed a deputy crier, and this position is now held by Mr. J• Carlin. Mr. Appleton's parents at one time lived in the old " Cock pit," and he has often spoken of the lively scenes witnessed there, when the old aristocracy of Newton brought their birds to try conclusions in 936 ring. Cock-fighting, however, was not sport for which he had any respect, as the scenes were too cruel for his peaceful dispesition. He had also a lively recollection of bear-baiting scenes in the good old village, and next door to where his family now lives, were the stable!' from which the changes of horses for the old mail coaches, running between Liverpool and Manchester wire effected. He could also recite some interesting episodes with the old-fashioned mode of voting at the hustings. He was a man of steady habits, and NOB highly respected and esteemed by those to whom h.e came In contact, and his position, coupled with a chari- table disposition enabled him very often to assist maglt poor people in a time of need. He was a churchman 0 the evangelical school, and a Conservative, but he took little or no interest in politics. The funeral took Pl'ee on Wednesday, the body being interred in a grave, which already contains the remains of his father and mother, in Newton Churchyard. With the exception of the at- tendance of a few old friends, the funeral was of a private nature.

E THE STEAM NAVVY FATALITY.—On Friday rotor&g Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner,lield an inquest at the Waggo,a' and Horses Hotel, Haydock, near St. Helens, On the WO of Joseph English, labourer, who was killed by a steal navvy in a cutting ofthe new Liverpool, St. Helens, South Lancashire Railway, near Holly Bank, Haydock on Tuesday. Mr. John Keith, engineer for Messrs. W. Pilling and Co., the railway contractors, appearea. on behalf of the firm. The evidence was to the eflec'' that deceased was working near a steam navvy wheZ the door of the iron bucket suddenly opened. Deceas ran and attempted to close the door, when the bucket swung to one side and deceased's head was crushed be tween the bucket and the iron framework of the navq: He was instantaneously killed. It was stated that was deceased's duty to attend to the bucket, but he should not have gone towards it whilst the machinery • was in motion. The jury returned a verdict of 44 Acci dental death "and recommended that the men should he • particularly cautioned not to attempt to close the door of the bucket until the machinery was absolutslY stopped.

(Elution Slbbress. PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRIN GTO N Gtrriamesr.—For seven years past the voice of this great comeltuency has not been heard in the Councils of the Empire, You have been practically disfranchised. It is time to it an end to this humiliating state of things. I came at the invitation of a large, influential, and repre- sentative body of Electors to seek the high honour, and to undertake the serious duty, of serving you in Parliament. Their choice has been ratified by thousands among you, whom -I have met in public assembly, and in private conference. My political opinions are by this time well-known to you. I have expounded them on the platform, in meeting after meeting, from one end of the constituency to the other. I am a Home Ruler; I am no Separatist. I ask for the Sister Country a Local Legislature for the management of her domestic affairs, subject to the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament. I am in favour of shortening the duration of Parlia- ments, One Man One Vote, the Payment of Mem- bers, the Amendment of the Registration Laws by the appointment of responsible registration officers, the reduction of the qualifying period, the preservation Of the right to vote notwithstanding change of residence,and the securing to every duly qualified citizen his full electoral eights. I shall support whatever measures may be necessary to prevent the House of Lords being any longer an obstacle in the way of remedial legislation. I am in favour of the Disestablishment of the Welsh Church. I am in favour of providing public schools for Secondary and Technical Instruction.in agriculture and other industries. tam in favour of providing for the direct and Popular Contrel of the Liquor Traffic, and of Sunday Closing. I am in favour of the Restoration of the Land to the 73eop!e, by means of allotments and 'compulsory sales, so as to give to hibonrers and others the opportunity of acquiring as much land as they can advantageously cultivate ; and I am in favour of further improving Local Government in the Coun- ties by creating Distr jot and Parish Councils, with power to control charities, grant allotments, and take land compul- sorily for public purposes. By these measures vitality will be restored to our villages, and the excessive competition in the labour market, and the over-crowdingof our towns, will be prevented. tarn in favour of taking whatever steps are necessary to secure the proper Housing of the Working Classes. I am in favour of the Taxation of Ground Rents for local administrative purposes. I understand that the Iron Trade of Warrington has for a considerable time been in a more or less depressed condition, and, as a result, the large number of men employed in this great industry have suffered severely. I believe that the present heavy burden of Mining Royalties is a most serious hindrance to successful competition with Continental manufacturers, and a constant danger to the future prosperity of this important trade. lam therefore in favour of such a readjustment of Mining Royalties and Wayleaves as will effeetually and permanently remove all obstacles to the der elopmettt of a business which Is so vital to the, prosperity of this Borough, and which is so important a factor in the general triune of the United Kingdom. lam in favour of making the Sale and Transfer of Land cheap, simple, and easy; the Enfranchisement of Leaseholds ; and the protection of tenants from unjust exactions by their landloras. I am in favour of a Free Breakfast Table. I am in favour of establishing a juster system of Local and National Taxation, so as to distribute the burthen more equally. lam in favour of extending the Factory Acts, so as to do away with the evils of the Sweating System; I am in favour of reducing, by all feasible means, the Hours of Labour to such a point as will allow the working-man reasonable leisure for recreation and improvement ; and I shall support any practicable system by which the industrious and well-con- ducted workman shall, when broken down by age or infir- mity, be saved from the ignominy and misery of workhouse charity. From the opinions above enunciated you can judge of the line of policy which I shall pursue in Parliament, if you honour me with your confidence. I therefore earnestly appeal to you to unite in securing my return by such a majority as will prove this borough to be, what it really is, a Liberal and Progressive constituency. I have the Honour to be, Gentlemen, Your Obedient and Faithful Servant. ARTHUR HOUSTON. • Warrington, June 21, 1892.

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. GENTLEMEN, It is nigh upon twenty years since I settled among you, and during those years I have served you in every public office to which you could elect me. There is no community in all England than can show a nobler record of work done during those years for the well- being of all the dwellers within its borders. Northwich, Rune wn, Winsford, and Middlewich, in taxing themselves under. the Public Libraries Acts, have given to their people free access to the thoughts of Ole noblest minds of all time; in adoptitg the Technical Instruction Act they have gi-en to the young an opportunity, eagerly embraced by large and increasing numbers, of training for hand and eye and mind, fitting them for faller, brighter, happier lives. Verily this is a community a man may be proud to represent. With all this work I have sympathised, and to the fullest extent of my powers have joined, with all my heart. As I have worked and voted hitherto, I pledge myself to work and vote hereafter, if again you do me the honour to return use to Westminster. As President of the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council I fully endorse the platform it has adopted, every point in which has my heartiest approval. Five years ago I asked for your suffrages as a supp rter of Mr. Gladstone, and after a contest, during which the argu- ments for and against Home Rule were presented to you with a clearness and fulness rarely, if ever, equalled, you elected me by a majority as emphatic as it was decisive. To-day the same issue is before you, and my attitude towards it is unchanged. Once more I come before you as a devoted adherent of the statesman who, in the sixtith year of his public service—a service as unprecedented in its term as in the noble quality of its adhievements— is now and for the last time appealing Ito his fellow-countrymen for their approval and support. At such a time I may well be pardoned if. omitting any state- ment of my own. I refer you to his address to the Electors of Midlothian, and say that it is the clearest wish of my heart to be permitted to aid in the work of carrying to a successful Issue the reforms therein set forth, so fraught with happi- ness to millions of our fellow-men. Finally. I would ask every man in the Northwich Division to remember on the Polling Day that a vote given for me is a last vote for mr. Gladstone—a last opportunity of rewarding for a life's service thernan who has laboured so long, so stead- fastly,and so successfully for the people's good. I remain, Gentlemen Your faithful servant, JOHN TOMLINSON BRUNNER. Winnington Old Hall, Northwich, 30th June, 1892.

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. T° THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON DIVI— SION OF THE COUNTY OF LANCASTER. GENTLEMEN, A Dissolution of Parliament being imminent, I have the honour to again offer myself as your representative. I am a firm supporter of the party which, under the guid- ance of Lord Salisbury, has for nearly six years administered the affairs of the Empire with conspicuous success. The predictions that the alliance between Conservatives and Liberal Unionists would not stand the test of time have been completely falsified, and the country has seen that the policy of maintaining the Union is compatible with steady and :on/fawns progress in every department of public affairs. I claim, en behalf of the Unionist Administration, that it is entitled to a renewal of your. confidence on the following grounds : Peace has been uniformly preserved, and, owing to a firm and consistent policy, not only has our national influerwe been upheld, but our relations with foreign powers have seldom been Of a more harmonious character. The strength of the Navy, our chief line of defence, has been largely increased. Public Expenditure has been economised, the National Debt reduced, and the burden of Imperial and Local Taxa- tion lightened. Popular Representative Lwal Government has been ex- tended to England and Scotland. The interests of the Working Classes have been promoted, and beneficial results may be expected from the inquiries of the Commission appointed to investigate the conditions of Labour. School .Fees have practically been abolished, and an act has recently been passed which will facilitate the acquisition of Small Holdings of Land upon reasoitab it terms'. With regard to Ireland. the improvement and p rosperity of that part of the United Kingdom I believe to be entirely due to the resolute and straightforward policy which has steadily upheld the authority of the law. On the other hand, the attitude of the Irish Loyalists, the Report of the Special Commission, the divisions in the .Nation- 1 alist Ranks, and the apparent inability of Mr. Gladstone to I produce a scheme satisfactory to the various sections of his 1 party, show conclusively the folly and danger of any attempt to set up a separate Parliament in I: üblin. My views upon the principal politic al questions of the day are well known to you. While anxious to se, the Muss of Labour reduced as much as possible. lam of opinion that this can only he satisfac- torily effected by mutual arrangement between Employers and Employed. A legal limitation of the hours of adult male labour would, I believe, not only be prejudicial to the interests of the Employed, but would deprive men of the right of disp)sing freely of their own labour to the best advan- tage, besides constituting an Interference with the liberty of the subject. Opportunities for discussing these and other matters will be afforded at the meetings which I propose to attend throughout the Division prior to the Election. Should you honour me by re-election. I shall enieavour to conscientiously study the wants and interests of the consti- tuency to the best of my ability. I remain, Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, T. W. LEGH,

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1892. rro THE PARLIAMENTARY ELECTORS OF 1 THE KNUTSFORD DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. GENTLEMEN,—At the request of the Executive Council of the Liberal Association of this Division I have c 3rne forth to seek your suffrages on this occasion in opposition to the Conservative Candidate. Though returned to power in 1886, on the distinct promise that Ireland should be governed with equal rights and privi- leges, the Conservative party at the very outset of this rftime adopted the most stringent measures of coercion. in the administration of which they have violated every principle of justice and freedom and have only succeeded in intensify- ing that hatred of English rule with which our fellow-country- men in Ireland are naturally inspired, and which can only be eradicated by such just and conciliatory measures as Mr. Gladstone has proposed. To Ireland I would give an Irish Parliament for the management of exclusively Irish affairs, and I consider that with such a measure the ties which bind the twe nations would be drawn clorer,—agrarian crime in Ireland would disappear, and peace and prosperity would be established. The disestablishrnent of the Church In Wales is a reform that is immediately called for, and is one for which, if you honour me with your cmitidence, I would certainly vote. I am in favcur of perfect religious equality. Born and bred in an Agricultural District of Cheshire. I am fully conversant with the wants both of the Farmer and of the Agricultural Labourer, and I have not forgotten the lessons I learned in my boyhood from my father, the late Mr. G. W. Latham, formerly M.P, for Crewe. To the Farmer I would give every security and freedom, and would encourage him in all possible ways to make the best use of the land he farms, and to Increase wherever he can the yield per acre. This I consider the best remedy for the present agricultural depression. I advocate the enactment of a fresh Agricultural Holdings Act, largely amending that of 1883, abolishing the present law of distress, and substituting some simple means of ob- taining compensation in place of the present costly method of arbitration. I would also compensate the Farmer for all improvements, and, further give him security that his rent shall not be raised on account of such improvements. Every Labourer who wished for it should be ble to obtain his allotment or small holding, and the means of getting the same should be simple, speedy, and sure. The control and management of local affairs, including parochial cherities, I would place in the hands of parish or village and district councils elected by ballot by the parish- ioners, and to no man would I give more than one vote vrhetherin Parliamentary or local elections. Rates should be equally divided between owner and occu- pier. My opinion with regard to the Licensing laws is that the Ratepayers should be able to control the liquor traffic within their boundaries, and to say how many, If any, licenses should be granted, and during what hours the houses holding these licenses should remain open. I would have all education free and unsectarian, and leave the management of the schools in the hands of the Ratepayers , wherever there is any contribut ion of public money, how- ever small, there should be some form of representative con- ' trol. Though I have net yet seen any proposal for universally limiting the hourelof labour to (8) hours, which seems to be practicable, I am most strongly opposed to the hours of work being excessive, or in any way injurious to the worker, and I am inclined to support any measure which embodied the principle of" Trade Option "as defines at the Trades' Union Congress of 1891, which would secure for the workman more leisure without endangering the prosperity of our commerce or unduly trenching on the liberty of the individual. I shall hope before the day of the poll to address meetings In all parts of the constituency, and to 'elabomte my views on these and other questions on all of which it is impossible to , touch in this address. \ If my views commend themselves to you I trust that you will vote for me fearlessly and without favour, disregarding all outside influences, and remembering that the Ballot is absolutely secret and that, all statements to the contrary are false and lying. Should you consider me worthy of your support and return me as your member. it shall always be my endeavour in the future—as it has been in the past—to strive to render the lot of the working-man more tolerable, and to give to the farmer more security and comfort in his holding, and to promote all measures which will tend to establish the welfare of the nation and the peace and prosperity of this Empire on the sure and solid basis of a well-governed And contented people, I have the honour to remiln, Gentlemen, Your most obedient Servant, ALEXANDER MERE LATHAM. 1, Temple Gardens, London, E.C. June 18th, 1892.

Cation Mbrtso. PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION. 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON THE OF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. GENTLEMEN. Having been selected by the Liberals of this Division to contest the seat as their candidate at this General Election, it Is now my duty to lay before you on outline of my political principles. The most urgent question is now, as it was six years ago, that of the Government of Ireland. The Tories, after six years of power, having failed to devise any feasible scheme ot Local Government for Ireland, it is clear that there is no middle course between what is called Home Rule and a con- tinuation of the system of Coercion under which Ireland has for so long been misgoverned. And speaking as an Ulster Protestant as well as an Englishman by adoption, I believe that the integrity of this empire will be strengthened, and that prosperity and contentment will be promoted in Ireland, by the establishment of a Statutory Parliament in Dublin empowered to deal with purely Irish affairs, the control of all Imperial matters being retained by the Imperial Parlia- ment at Westminster. lam in complete sympathy with the leaders of the Labour Movement in their desire to obtain shorter hours of labour, to increase the opportun.ty for culture, and to gene rally improve their position. The attainment of an Eight Hours Working Day I regard as an important step, and though I consider the enforcing of an universal Eight Hours Day by legislative enactment as impracticable, I believe that the legislature can legitimately and usefully interfere to limit hours in certain cases, as, for instance, the hours of labour of Miners and Railway Servants. The establishment of a special State Department, for labour matters, controlled by a responsible minister, would, in my opinion, greatly promote, industrial interests. The existing Poor Laws, however suitable they may have been in the past, have become antiquated, and are no longer in accord withpopular requirements under altered conditions. They press harshly in sickness and old age upon deserving people, who through no fault of their own have been over- taken by poverty. I think the time has come when the whole question urgently requires reconsideration. Much can, I think, be done to check poverty add misery by curtailment of the excessive consumption of alcoholic liquors, and the promotion of Temperance by all legitimate means. One of the first steps towards this end is, to my mind, the placing of the Liquor Traffic under popular control, both as to I the granting of licences and the general regulation of Public- houses. I think that reconsideration and reform of the whole sub- ject of Incidence of Taxation, both Imperial and Local, is urgently demanded. Local Rates should be more fairly distributed, so that all sources, or possible sources, of income should bear their rela- tive share of Local Taxation ; and no form of Property should be allowed to escape, as is at present the case with Greund Rents and Mining Royalties. I consider the further extension of popular Local Govern- ment a matter of National importance, and regard as essential the establishment of popularly-elected Parish Councils, with sufficiently wide powers for the control and administration of local affairs. The thorough reconsideration and reform of the Land Laws is, to my mind, of great importance. I think reform of the system of Registration and the abolition of the Plural Vote is essential to political equality. I am in favour of perfect Religious, as well as Political. Freedom, and while myself a member of the Established Church, I consider the demand of the vast majority in Wales for Disestablishment of the Church in Wales as reasonable, and one which should be acceded to. II look upon the House of Lords, as at peesentconstituted, as opposed to the spirit of the age, and consider its reform as 1 essential to the proper working of Democraac Government. On any other special topics I shall be happy to give my views on the platform. If you should do 1T e the honour of returning me as your representative at Westminster. whatever energy and abliity I may have shall be spent in promoting the principles of Liberalism and the interests of this Constituency. I am. Gentlemen. Your obedient servant, W. NEILL.
